# MerkleForge

Authenticated data structures for Rust and TypeScript: Binary, Sparse, and Ethereum-compatible Patricia Merkle trees behind one API, with pluggable hashes and byte-identical stateless proofs.

  # Demos

  Each demo models a real system and runs the published
  [`@merkleforge/*`](https://www.npmjs.com/org/merkleforge) TypeScript packages in your browser.
  Nothing you type or pick is uploaded; the only network request is the optional live fetch on the
  Ethereum page, and only when you click it. Roots and proofs match the Rust crates byte for byte.

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # In-browser benchmarks

  Build a `BinaryMerkleTree` from 32-byte leaves on your own device, with each hash adapter, then
  generate and verify proofs for 500 of the leaves. Most published Merkle tree numbers come from a
  server. This page shows what your users' browsers will see, phones included.

  * **Keccak-256** and **SHA-256** come in two forms with identical output: pure JS from
    [`@merkleforge/hash`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash) and WebAssembly from
    [`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash-wasm). Trees,
    proofs, and JSON built with either are interchangeable.
  * **BLAKE3** is pure JS.

  <BrowserBenchmark />

  ## Use the faster adapter in your code

  ```ts [index.ts]
  import { createKeccak256Wasm } from '@merkleforge/hash-wasm'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const Keccak256 = await createKeccak256Wasm() // loads the WebAssembly module once
  const leaves = Array.from({ length: 16_384 }, (_, i) => new TextEncoder().encode(`leaf-${i}`))
  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, leaves)
  console.log(tree.leafCount, tree.generateProof(42).path.length)
  ```

  ```text
  16384 14
  ```

  The numbers depend on the `@merkleforge/*` version this site was built with. Server-side
  comparisons with other JavaScript libraries are on the [benchmarks page](/benchmarks).
</div>

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Airdrop claim

  Token airdrops, allowlists, and vesting contracts store one 32-byte Merkle root on-chain instead
  of every recipient. Each recipient later sends their allocation and a proof; the contract hashes
  the claim up to the root and pays out only if it matches.

  This demo uses `StandardMerkleTree` from
  [`@merkleforge/openzeppelin`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/openzeppelin), a drop-in
  for `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree` with identical roots, proofs, and `dump()` JSON. Edit the list,
  pick a recipient, then try to claim more than the allocation.

  <AirdropDemo />

  ## Build the tree

  TypeScript only: `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` has no Rust crate yet.

  ```ts [airdrop.ts]
  import { StandardMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/openzeppelin'

  const values = [
    ['0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111', '5000000000000000000'],
    ['0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222', '2500000000000000000'],
  ]
  const tree = StandardMerkleTree.of(values, ['address', 'uint256'])

  console.log(tree.root) // store this in the contract
  const proof = tree.getProof(0) // send this with the claim
  console.log(StandardMerkleTree.verify(tree.root, ['address', 'uint256'], values[0], proof))
  ```

  ```text
  0xd4dee0beab2d53f2cc83e567171bd2820e49898130a22622b10ead383e90bd77
  true
  ```

  ## Verify the claim on-chain

  ```solidity [Airdrop.sol]
  import {MerkleProof} from "@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/cryptography/MerkleProof.sol";

  function claim(bytes32[] calldata proof, uint256 amount) external {
      bytes32 leaf = keccak256(bytes.concat(keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, amount))));
      require(MerkleProof.verify(proof, root, leaf), "invalid proof");
      // mark claimed, then transfer `amount`
  }
  ```

  The double hash in the leaf stops a 64-byte internal node from being passed off as a leaf.
</div>

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Ethereum state proof

  Wallets, bridges, and light clients read Ethereum state from RPC providers they do not control.
  `eth_getProof` ([EIP-1186](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186)) returns an account and its
  storage together with Merkle Patricia trie proofs, so a client that trusts only a block's state
  root can check every value itself.

  The demo verifies a real response for the WETH contract with `verifyEthGetProof` from
  [`@merkleforge/ethereum`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/ethereum): the account in the
  state trie, then storage slots 0–2 (`name`, `symbol`, `decimals`) in WETH's storage trie. Pick a
  dishonest response to see it rejected, or fetch a live proof.

  <EthProofDemo />

  ## In code

  TypeScript only: `@merkleforge/ethereum` has no Rust crate yet. The Rust `MerklePatriciaTrie`
  produces the same roots.

  ```ts [proof.ts]
  import { verifyEthGetProof } from '@merkleforge/ethereum'

  const rpc = async (method: string, params: unknown[]) =>
    (
      await (
        await fetch('https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com', {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
          body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 1, method, params }),
        })
      ).json()
    ).result

  const block = await rpc('eth_getBlockByNumber', ['latest', false])
  const weth = '0xc02aaa39b223fe8d0a0e5c4f27ead9083c756cc2'
  const response = await rpc('eth_getProof', [weth, ['0x2'], block.number])

  // Throws if any proof or field does not match the state root.
  const { account, storage } = verifyEthGetProof(block.stateRoot, response)
  console.log(account?.nonce, storage[0]?.value)
  ```

  ```text
  1n 18n
  ```

  Here the state root comes from the same RPC; a light client takes it from a block header it has
  verified, for example through the beacon chain's sync committee.
</div>

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # File integrity

  Peer-to-peer and content-addressed systems (BitTorrent v2, IPFS, software update and backup
  tools) split a file into chunks and publish the Merkle root of the chunk hashes. A downloader
  that knows only the root can fetch chunks from untrusted peers in any order, check each one with
  a short proof the moment it arrives, and refetch just the chunk that fails, without waiting for
  the whole file.

  This demo splits a file into 64 KiB chunks and builds a `BinaryMerkleTree` with SHA-256 from
  [`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash-wasm) (it falls back
  to the pure-JS adapter if WebAssembly is unavailable). Your file is read locally and never
  uploaded.

  <FileIntegrityDemo />

  ## In code

  ```ts [chunks.ts]
  import { createSha256Wasm } from '@merkleforge/hash-wasm'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const CHUNK = 64 * 1024
  const file = new Uint8Array(1_000_000).map((_, i) => i % 251)
  const chunks = []
  for (let at = 0; at < file.length; at += CHUNK) chunks.push(file.subarray(at, at + CHUNK))

  const Sha256 = await createSha256Wasm()
  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, chunks)
  const root = tree.root()! // publish this

  // Downloader: check chunk 3 from an untrusted peer.
  const ok = BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, chunks[3]!, tree.generateProof(3))
  console.log(chunks.length, ok)
  ```

  ```text
  16 true
  ```

  Proofs for a file of `n` chunks hold `log2(n)` hashes: 14 hashes (448 bytes) for a 1 GiB file.
</div>

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Revocation list

  Certificate authorities, verifiable-credential issuers, and API gateways need to answer "has this
  been revoked?" for parties that should not download the whole list. A sparse Merkle tree puts
  every possible ID at a fixed position (here `keccak256(id)`), so the issuer can publish one root
  and hand out a short proof for either answer:

  * **membership**: the ID is in the tree, so it is revoked;
  * **non-membership**: the ID's slot is empty, so it is not revoked.

  The demo runs `SparseMerkleTree` from
  [`@merkleforge/variants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants) with Keccak-256.
  Revoke and reinstate IDs, then check one; the proof is verified against the root alone.

  <RevocationDemo />

  ## In code

  ```ts [revocation.ts]
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/ethereum'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const REVOKED = utf8('revoked')
  const key = (id: string) => keccak256(utf8(id))

  const list = new SparseMerkleTree(Keccak256)
  list.insert(key('cert-2041'), REVOKED)
  const root = list.root()! // publish this

  const yes = list.generateMembershipProof(key('cert-2041'))
  const no = list.generateMembershipProof(key('cert-1000')) // leaf: null, a non-membership proof
  console.log(SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(Keccak256, root, key('cert-2041'), REVOKED, yes))
  console.log(SparseMerkleTree.verifyNonMembership(Keccak256, root, key('cert-1000'), no))
  ```

  ```text
  true
  true
  ```

  The same tree type backs account state in rollups and nullifier sets in privacy protocols. See the
  [sparse Merkle tree guide](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree).
</div>

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Light-client demo

  A server commits rows to a Merkle root and sends one row plus its proof to a client. The client
  holds only the trusted root. Edit the rows, pick one to prove, then change the **claimed value** to
  see tampering rejected.

  The demo runs the real TypeScript library in your browser: `BinaryMerkleTree` from
  [`@merkleforge/variants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants) with the `Sha256`
  adapter from [`@merkleforge/hash`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash). Leaves are
  `SHA-256(0x00 ‖ row)`, internal nodes `SHA-256(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right)`, and the leaf layer is padded
  to a power of two with the empty-leaf hash. Roots and proofs are byte-identical to the Rust
  `BinaryMerkleTree<Sha256>` for the same rows, so a Rust server and this page agree.

  <LightClientDemo />

  ## The same flow in code

  <LangBar always />

  <Rust>
    ```rust [merkle-variants/examples/light_client.rs]
    use merkle_core::{error::MerkleError, types::LeafIndex};
    use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
    use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

    fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
        let proof;
        let root;

        {
            let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
            tree.insert(b"tx:alice->bob:100")?;
            tree.insert(b"tx:bob->carol:50")?;
            tree.insert(b"tx:carol->dave:25")?;

            root = *tree.root().expect("tree has inserted leaves");
            proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;

            println!("server: built tree and exported root + proof");
        }

        let valid = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(&root, b"tx:alice->bob:100", &proof);

        println!("client: tree dropped before verification");
        println!("Stateless verification: {valid}");

        Ok(())
    }
    ```

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
    cd MerkleForge
    cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
    ```

    ```text
    server: built tree and exported root + proof
    client: tree dropped before verification
    Stateless verification: true
    ```
  </Rust>

  <TypeScript>
    ```ts [index.ts]
    import { type Bytes, type MerkleProof, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
    import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
    import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

    function server(): { root: Bytes; proof: MerkleProof } {
      const tree = new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256)
      tree.insert(utf8('tx:alice->bob:100'))
      tree.insert(utf8('tx:bob->carol:50'))
      tree.insert(utf8('tx:carol->dave:25'))

      console.log('server: built tree and exported root + proof')
      return { root: tree.root()!, proof: tree.generateProof(0) }
    }

    // The tree goes out of scope when `server` returns; only the root and proof leave it.
    const { root, proof } = server()

    const valid = BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, utf8('tx:alice->bob:100'), proof)

    console.log('client: tree dropped before verification')
    console.log(`Stateless verification: ${valid}`)
    ```

    ```bash
    npm i @merkleforge/core @merkleforge/hash @merkleforge/variants
    npx tsx index.ts
    ```

    ```text
    server: built tree and exported root + proof
    client: tree dropped before verification
    Stateless verification: true
    ```
  </TypeScript>

  Learn more in [Proofs & stateless verification](/docs/guides/proofs).
</div>

# Why MerkleForge

MerkleForge is a framework for **authenticated data structures**, available as Rust crates and
TypeScript packages. You put data in, get a 32-byte root out, and hand out small proofs that
anyone holding the root can check, without downloading the rest of the data.

<LangBar />

## The problem

Data verification is one of the major bottlenecks in modern blockchain networks. As systems
process millions of transactions, checking the integrity of state data gets slow and
resource-intensive. Every state lookup, transaction batch, and light-client proof depends on the
speed and correctness of the underlying data structure.

<Rust>
  The Rust ecosystem has strong cryptographic building blocks, but Merkle tree support is spread
  across variant-specific crates. Libraries like `rs-merkle` focus on binary trees, while
  Ethereum-specific tries are maintained separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with
  different APIs, documentation depth, test coverage, and benchmark methodology.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  JavaScript and TypeScript have the same gap. Libraries like `merkletreejs` and
  `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree` focus on binary trees, while Ethereum-compatible tries are maintained
  separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with different APIs, proof formats, and test
  coverage, and proofs made in one language rarely verify in another.
</TypeScript>

## The solution

MerkleForge unifies the three Merkle tree variants used across production systems behind one
API:

<Rust>
  | Variant | Typical use |
  | --- | --- |
  | [`BinaryMerkleTree<H>`](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree) | Transaction batching, Bitcoin-style SPV, logs, file chunks |
  | [`SparseMerkleTree<H>`](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree) | Account state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollups |
  | [`MerklePatriciaTrie<H>`](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie) | Ethereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses |

  All three are generic over a [`HashFunction`](/docs/guides/hash-functions), implement the shared
  `MerkleTree<H>` trait, and produce proofs that verify **statelessly**.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  | Variant | Typical use |
  | --- | --- |
  | [`BinaryMerkleTree`](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree) | Transaction batching, airdrops and allowlists, logs, file chunks |
  | [`SparseMerkleTree`](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree) | Account state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollups |
  | [`MerklePatriciaTrie`](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie) | Ethereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses |

  All three take a [`HashFunction`](/docs/guides/hash-functions) object at construction, implement
  the shared `MerkleTree` interface, and produce proofs that verify **statelessly**.
</TypeScript>

## Features

<Rust>
  * **Unified API.** `BinaryMerkleTree<H>`, `SparseMerkleTree<H>`, and `MerklePatriciaTrie<H>` all
    implement `MerkleTree<H>`, so generic code works with any of them.
  * **Pluggable hash functions.** Swap SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 by changing one type
    parameter. Generics are monomorphised at compile time, so there is no runtime dispatch.
  * **Stateless verification.** A light client verifies a leaf with the trusted root, the proof, and
    the leaf bytes. See [Proofs & stateless verification](/docs/guides/proofs).
  * **Domain separation built in.** Leaves hash as `H(0x00 ‖ data)` and internal nodes as
    `H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right)`, which blocks second-preimage attacks. See the
    [mental model](/docs/mental-model).
  * **Reproducible benchmarks.** A dedicated Criterion suite compares hashes, tree variants, and
    other Rust Merkle libraries. See [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks).
  * **Tested.** Unit, integration, property-based (Proptest), and Ethereum test-vector tests.
  * **`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`** in every published crate.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  * **Unified API.** `BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`, and `MerklePatriciaTrie` all implement
    the `MerkleTree` interface, so generic code works with any of them.
  * **Pluggable hash functions.** Swap SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 by passing a different
    `HashFunction` object, for example `BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, leaves)`. The hash is
    a value, not a type parameter. `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` adds WebAssembly Keccak-256 and SHA-256
    with identical output.
  * **Byte-identical with Rust.** Roots, proofs, and proof encodings (bincode and JSON) match the Rust
    crates byte for byte, so a Rust server can prove and a browser can verify, or the other way round.
  * **Stateless verification.** A light client verifies a leaf with the trusted root, the proof, and
    the leaf bytes. See [Proofs & stateless verification](/docs/guides/proofs).
  * **Domain separation built in.** Leaves hash as `H(0x00 ‖ data)` and internal nodes as
    `H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right)`, which blocks second-preimage attacks. See the
    [mental model](/docs/mental-model).
  * **Runs anywhere.** ESM only, on Node.js 22+, browsers, Deno, and Bun. The only runtime dependency
    is [`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes).
  * **Ethereum and on-chain.** `eth_getProof` verification, an OpenZeppelin-compatible
    `StandardMerkleTree`, and Solidity verifiers for Keccak-256 proofs.
  * **Tested.** Unit, property-based (fast-check), cross-implementation vectors generated from the
    Rust crates, and Ethereum test-vector tests.
</TypeScript>

## Crates and packages

<Rust>
  | Crate | Role |
  | --- | --- |
  | [`merkle-core`](https://crates.io/crates/merkle-core) | Traits, proof types, serialization helpers, and errors. `no_std` + `alloc` capable. |
  | [`merkleforge-hash`](https://crates.io/crates/merkleforge-hash) | `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, and `Blake3` adapters. |
  | [`merkle-variants`](https://crates.io/crates/merkle-variants) | `BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`, and `MerklePatriciaTrie`. |
  | `merkle-bench` | Criterion benchmarks. Not published. |

  :::note
  The hash crate is published as `merkleforge-hash` (the original name was taken) and imported in
  Rust as `merkleforge_hash`. In the repository it lives in the `merkle-hash/` folder.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  | Package | Role |
  | --- | --- |
  | [`@merkleforge/core`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/core) | `HashFunction` and `MerkleTree` interfaces, proof types, `MerkleError`, byte helpers. No runtime dependencies. |
  | [`@merkleforge/hash`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash) | `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, and `Blake3` adapters, built on `@noble/hashes`. |
  | [`@merkleforge/variants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants) | `BinaryMerkleTree` (with multiproofs), `SparseMerkleTree`, `MerklePatriciaTrie`, and proof codecs. |
  | [`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash-wasm) | WebAssembly `Keccak256` and `Sha256` with identical output. Optional. |
  | [`@merkleforge/ethereum`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/ethereum) | Verify `eth_getProof` account and storage proofs against a state root. |
  | [`@merkleforge/openzeppelin`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/openzeppelin) | Drop-in `StandardMerkleTree` and `SimpleMerkleTree` for `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`, with the same roots, proofs, and dumps. |

  The last three have no Rust counterpart. The source lives in
  [1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts).
</TypeScript>

## Rust and TypeScript together

The same trees, hashes, and proof formats are available on npm as
[`@merkleforge/*`](https://www.npmjs.com/org/merkleforge) packages. Roots and proofs match the Rust
crates byte for byte, so a Rust server can prove and a browser can verify. Every guide shows both
languages: pick one with the **Rust / TypeScript** switch in the sidebar. See
[TypeScript packages](/docs/reference/typescript) for the package list and how the APIs map.

:::warning
MerkleForge has **not** completed an independent security audit. Review the code against your
threat model before using it in security-critical systems. See [Security](/docs/reference/security).
:::

* [Choosing a tree](/docs/guides/choosing-a-tree): which variant fits your data.

# Getting started

This page takes you from an empty project to a verified inclusion proof in a few minutes. MerkleForge
ships as Rust crates and as TypeScript packages with the same trees, hashes, and byte-identical proofs.
Pick your language with the switch in the sidebar; your choice applies to every page.

<LangBar />

## Requirements

<Rust>
  MerkleForge targets **Rust 1.97.1** or newer (edition 2024), the `rust-version` declared by every
  crate. Check your toolchain with:

  ```bash
  rustc --version
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The TypeScript packages are ESM only and run on **Node.js 22** or newer, in browsers, Deno, and Bun.
  Check your Node.js version with:

  ```bash
  node --version
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Install

::::steps
### Create a project

<Rust>
  ```bash
  cargo new merkle-hello
  cd merkle-hello
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```bash
  mkdir merkle-hello && cd merkle-hello
  npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
  ```
</TypeScript>

### Add the packages

<Rust>
  :::code-group
  ```bash [cargo add]
  cargo add merkle-core merkleforge-hash merkle-variants
  ```

  ```toml [Cargo.toml]
  [dependencies]
  merkle-core = "0.5.2"
  merkleforge-hash = "0.5.2"
  merkle-variants = "0.5.2"
  ```
  :::

  Most applications want all three:

  * `merkle-core` provides the traits (`MerkleTree`, `ProofVerifier`, `HashFunction`), the proof
    types, and `MerkleError`.
  * `merkleforge-hash` provides the `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, and `Blake3` adapters.
  * `merkle-variants` provides the trees.

  Depend on `merkle-core` alone if you are writing your own tree or hash adapter.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  :::code-group
  ```bash [npm]
  npm i @merkleforge/core @merkleforge/hash @merkleforge/variants
  ```

  ```bash [pnpm]
  pnpm add @merkleforge/core @merkleforge/hash @merkleforge/variants
  ```

  ```bash [yarn]
  yarn add @merkleforge/core @merkleforge/hash @merkleforge/variants
  ```

  ```bash [bun]
  bun add @merkleforge/core @merkleforge/hash @merkleforge/variants
  ```
  :::

  Most applications want all three:

  * `@merkleforge/core` provides the interfaces (`MerkleTree`, `HashFunction`), the proof types,
    `MerkleError`, and byte helpers such as `utf8`, `toHex`, and `bytesEqual`.
  * `@merkleforge/hash` provides the `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, and `Blake3` adapters.
  * `@merkleforge/variants` provides the trees.

  The other packages are optional: `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` (faster WebAssembly hashes),
  `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` (a drop-in for `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`), and
  `@merkleforge/ethereum` (`eth_getProof` verification). See the [package overview](/docs/reference/typescript).
</TypeScript>

### Write your first proof

<Rust>
  Replace `src/main.rs` with:

  ```rust [src/main.rs]
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

      tree.insert(b"alice:100")?;
      tree.insert(b"bob:250")?;
      tree.insert(b"carol:75")?;

      let root = tree.root().expect("tree is non-empty");
      println!("root: {root:02x?}");

      // Generate an inclusion proof for leaf 0 (alice).
      let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;
      println!("proof depth: {}", proof.depth());

      // Stateless verification: no tree needed, only the root, leaf bytes, and proof.
      let valid = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, b"alice:100", &proof);
      assert!(valid);

      // A different value for the same leaf is rejected.
      assert!(!BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, b"alice:999", &proof));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Create `index.ts`:

  ```ts [index.ts]
  import { proofDepth, toHex, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256)

  tree.insert(utf8('alice:100'))
  tree.insert(utf8('bob:250'))
  tree.insert(utf8('carol:75'))

  const root = tree.root()
  if (!root) throw new Error('tree is non-empty')
  console.log('root:', toHex(root))

  // Generate an inclusion proof for leaf 0 (alice).
  const proof = tree.generateProof(0)
  console.log('proof depth:', proofDepth(proof))

  // Stateless verification: no tree needed, only the root, leaf bytes, and proof.
  const valid = BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, utf8('alice:100'), proof)
  console.assert(valid)

  // A different value for the same leaf is rejected.
  console.assert(!BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, utf8('alice:999'), proof))
  ```
</TypeScript>

### Run it

<Rust>
  ```bash
  cargo run
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```bash
  npx tsx index.ts
  ```

  Node.js 23.6 and newer can also run it directly with `node index.ts`.
</TypeScript>

You should see the root, then `proof depth: 2` (three leaves are padded to four, so the proof has
two sibling hashes). The root is the same in both languages:
`0xbe8688d2a521ee5e1757a093610029e743c0f627a5d4e3fbf7f5a07962370d61`.
::::

## What just happened?

1. Each <Rust inline>`insert`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`insert`</TypeScript> hashed the raw bytes
   into a leaf, `H(0x00 ‖ data)`, and recomputed the path to the root.
2. `root()` returned the 32-byte commitment to all three leaves.
3. <Rust inline>`generate_proof`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`generateProof`</TypeScript> collected the
   sibling hashes from leaf 0 up to the root.
4. `verify` rebuilt the root from the bytes of `alice:100` and those siblings, and compared it with
   the trusted root. It never touched the tree.

That last step is the **light-client pattern**: whoever holds a trusted root can check one value
without the dataset. The [Mental model](/docs/mental-model) page explains each piece.

## Build from many leaves at once

When you already have the full leaf set,
<Rust inline>`from_leaves`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`fromLeaves`</TypeScript> builds the tree in one
`O(n)` pass. The root, indices, and proofs are identical to sequential inserts.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let rows = ["alice:100", "bob:250", "carol:75"];
      let batch = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(rows)?;

      let mut sequential = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      for row in rows {
          sequential.insert(row.as_bytes())?;
      }

      assert_eq!(batch.root(), sequential.root());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  :::note
  `BinaryMerkleTree::from_leaves` was added in v0.5.0. On v0.4.x, use sequential `insert` calls.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const rows = ['alice:100', 'bob:250', 'carol:75'].map(utf8)
  const batch = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, rows)

  const sequential = new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256)
  for (const row of rows) sequential.insert(row)

  console.assert(bytesEqual(batch.root()!, sequential.root()!))
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Swap the hash function

<Rust>
  Every tree is generic over its hash. Change one type parameter and nothing else:

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Keccak256};

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut fast = BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();
      let mut evm = BinaryMerkleTree::<Keccak256>::new();

      fast.insert(b"alice:100")?;
      evm.insert(b"alice:100")?;

      // Different algorithms, different roots.
      assert_ne!(fast.root(), evm.root());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Every tree takes its hash as a constructor argument. Pass a different one and nothing else changes:

  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Blake3, Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const fast = new BinaryMerkleTree(Blake3)
  const evm = new BinaryMerkleTree(Keccak256)

  fast.insert(utf8('alice:100'))
  evm.insert(utf8('alice:100'))

  // Different algorithms, different roots.
  console.assert(!bytesEqual(fast.root()!, evm.root()!))
  ```
</TypeScript>

See [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions) for when to pick each one.

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
  cd MerkleForge
  cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
  ```

  ```text

  client: tree dropped before verification
  Stateless verification: true
  ```

</TypeScript>

The same flow runs in your browser on the [light-client demo](/demo/light-client).

* [Choosing a tree](/docs/guides/choosing-a-tree) when your data is a key-value map rather than a list.

# Mental model

Think of a Merkle root as a **fingerprint for many values**. Change any value and the fingerprint
changes. A proof is the short path that lets another machine check one value against that
fingerprint.

<LangBar />

## The four pieces

| Piece | What it is | In MerkleForge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Leaf** | The hash of one value you inserted. | <Rust inline>`H::hash(data)`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.hash(data)`</TypeScript>, computed for you by `insert`. |
| **Root** | One digest that commits to every leaf. | `tree.root()` returns <Rust inline>`Option<&H::Digest>`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`Uint8Array` or `undefined`</TypeScript>. |
| **Proof** | The sibling hashes on the path from one leaf to the root. | <Rust inline>`MerkleProof<D>` (binary), `SparseMerkleProof<D>`, `MptProof<D>`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`MerkleProof` (binary), `SparseMerkleProof`, `MptProof`</TypeScript>. |
| **Verifier** | Code that rebuilds the root from a leaf and a proof. | <Rust inline>`ProofVerifier::verify` and the per-tree `verify*` functions</Rust><TypeScript inline>The static `verify*` functions on each tree class</TypeScript>. |

```text
                 root = H(0x01 ‖ n01 ‖ n23)
                /                          \
     n01 = H(0x01 ‖ l0 ‖ l1)      n23 = H(0x01 ‖ l2 ‖ l3)
        /            \               /            \
 l0 = H(0x00‖a)  l1 = H(0x00‖b)  l2 = H(0x00‖c)  l3 = H(0x00‖d)
```

To prove `a` is leaf 0, the prover sends `l1` and `n23`. The verifier computes `l0` from `a`, then
`n01`, then the root, and compares it with the root it already trusts. For `n` leaves that is
`⌈log₂ n⌉` hashes, no matter how big the dataset is.

## Who holds what

* The **prover** (a server, indexer, or full node) holds the full tree. It publishes the root and
  answers proof requests.
* The **verifier** (a light client, browser, contract, or embedded device) holds only a **trusted
  root**, for example from a block header or a signed checkpoint.

A proof is only as good as the root you check it against. Get the root from a source you trust.

## Domain separation: `0x00` and `0x01`

MerkleForge hashes leaves and internal nodes in different **domains**:

| Hash | Pre-image |
| --- | --- |
| Leaf | `H(0x00 ‖ data)` |
| Internal node | `H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right)` |

Without the prefixes, an internal node's pre-image (`left ‖ right`, 64 bytes) is also a valid leaf
value. An attacker could then present an internal node as if it were a leaf and forge a "proof"
for data that was never inserted. This is a **second-preimage attack**. With distinct prefixes, a
leaf hash can never equal an internal node hash for a different structure.

The `Sha256` and `Keccak256` adapters use the byte prefixes above. `Blake3` gets the same
separation from BLAKE3's `derive_key` mode with two context strings. See
[Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions) for the exact constructions.

## Verifying by hand

Nothing in a proof is magic. This program rebuilds the root manually and checks it against the
library's own verifier:

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c", "d"])?;
      let root = *tree.root().expect("non-empty");
      let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;

      // 1. current = H(0x00 ‖ leaf)
      let mut current = Sha256::hash(b"a");
      // 2. Walk the siblings from the leaf level up to the root.
      for node in &proof.path {
          current = match node.side {
              ProofSide::Left => Sha256::hash_nodes(&node.hash, &current),
              ProofSide::Right => Sha256::hash_nodes(&current, &node.hash),
          };
      }
      // 3. Compare with the trusted root.
      assert_eq!(current, root);
      assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(&root, b"a", &proof));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'].map(utf8))
  const root = tree.root()!
  const proof = tree.generateProof(0)

  // 1. current = H(0x00 ‖ leaf)
  let current = Sha256.hash(utf8('a'))
  // 2. Walk the siblings from the leaf level up to the root.
  for (const node of proof.path) {
    current =
      node.side === 'left' ? Sha256.hashNodes(node.hash, current) : Sha256.hashNodes(current, node.hash)
  }
  // 3. Compare with the trusted root.
  console.assert(bytesEqual(current, root))
  console.assert(BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, utf8('a'), proof))
  ```
</TypeScript>

<Rust inline>`ProofSide::Left`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`side: 'left'`</TypeScript> means the sibling sits on the left, so it goes first in the concatenation.

## Padding and empty slots

* `BinaryMerkleTree` pads the leaf layer to the next power of two with <Rust inline>`H::empty()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.empty()`</TypeScript>,
  the hash of an empty leaf. Five leaves become eight slots.
* `SparseMerkleTree` has 2²⁵⁶ slots and precomputes the root of an empty subtree at every level,
  so empty regions cost nothing to store.
* `MerklePatriciaTrie` follows Ethereum's node layout and has no padding.

Because empty slots hash to <Rust inline>`H::empty()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.empty()`</TypeScript>, **empty leaf data is rejected** with
<Rust inline>`MerkleError::EmptyLeafData`</Rust><TypeScript inline>a `MerkleError` with code `'EmptyLeafData'`</TypeScript>; otherwise an inserted empty value would be indistinguishable from
padding.

## One caveat: the leaf count is not committed

<Rust inline>`MerkleProof::leaf_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`MerkleProof.leafCount`</TypeScript> tells the verifier how deep the path should be. The root does **not**
commit to it, so any count with the same padded size verifies. If the exact number of leaves matters
to you, get it from a trusted source and compare.

# Use cases

Every use case below has the same shape: someone commits to a lot of data with one 32-byte
**root**, publishes or signs that root, and later hands out small **proofs** that a specific piece
is (or is not) part of it. Whoever checks the proof needs only the root, the piece, and the proof,
not the rest of the data.

Each section names the tree, hash, and packages to use. Items marked **planned** are on the
[roadmap](/roadmap) and not in the libraries yet.

## Blockchain and Ethereum

### Airdrops, allowlists, and claims

Commit a list of `(address, amount)` pairs on-chain as one root, and let each user claim with a
proof. Nobody stores the full list on-chain, and gas stays constant as the list grows.

* **Tree:** `StandardMerkleTree` from `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` (same roots and proofs as
  `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`), or `BinaryMerkleTree` with `Keccak256` and the MerkleForge
  Solidity verifier.
* **Verify on-chain:** OpenZeppelin's `MerkleProof.verify`, or the MerkleForge verifiers in
  [`contracts/`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/contracts).
* **Try it:** [airdrop claim demo](/demo/airdrop).

### Light clients and Ethereum state proofs

Check an account balance, nonce, or contract storage slot against a trusted block's state root
instead of trusting an RPC provider's answer.

* **Tree:** `MerklePatriciaTrie` with `Keccak256` (matches Ethereum roots).
* **Packages:** `@merkleforge/ethereum` (`verifyEthGetProof`) in TypeScript;
  `MerkleForgeEthereum` on-chain.
* **Try it:** [Ethereum state proof demo](/demo/ethereum).

### Rollup and app-chain state

Keep account or application state as a key-value map, prove reads, and prove a key is absent.

* **Tree:** `SparseMerkleTree` (membership and non-membership proofs over 32-byte keys).
* **Hash:** `Sha256` or `Blake3` off-chain, `Keccak256` when proofs are checked by Solidity.
  SNARK-friendly hashes such as Poseidon2 are **planned** for proofs checked inside circuits.

### Transaction batches, receipts, and bridges

Commit a batch of transactions or messages, post the root, and prove inclusion of any one of them
on the other side, one at a time or with a [multiproof](/docs/guides/proofs).

* **Tree:** `BinaryMerkleTree`, `generateMultiProof` for many items at once.

## Beyond blockchain

### File integrity and chunked downloads

Split a file into fixed-size chunks and commit to them. A downloader that trusts only the root can
verify every chunk as it arrives, from any mirror or peer, and pinpoint a corrupted chunk instead of
re-downloading the whole file. This is how BitTorrent v2 and content-addressed storage work.

* **Tree:** `BinaryMerkleTree`, one leaf per chunk, `Sha256` or `Blake3`.
* **Try it:** [file integrity demo](/demo/file-integrity), which runs on a file you pick without uploading it.

### Revocation lists and allowlists with "not in the list" proofs

Publish a root over revoked certificate or credential IDs. A verifier can check a membership proof
(revoked) or a non-membership proof (still valid) without downloading the whole list.

* **Tree:** `SparseMerkleTree`, keyed by a hash of the ID.
* **Try it:** [revocation list demo](/demo/revocation).

### Transparency and audit logs

Append events to a log and publish its root, so anyone can check an entry is in the log. Certificate
Transparency uses this to catch mis-issued TLS certificates.

* **Today:** `BinaryMerkleTree` gives inclusion proofs for a log you rebuild or append to.
* **Planned:** RFC 9162 append-only trees with consistency proofs (proof that a newer log extends
  an older one without rewriting it).

### Databases and replicas

Compare two replicas of a dataset by comparing roots, then walk down only the subtrees that differ.
Serve reads with a proof so clients can check them against a root they trust.

* **Tree:** `SparseMerkleTree` for key-value data, `BinaryMerkleTree` for ordered data.
* **Planned:** replica diffing helpers and on-disk authenticated storage.

## AI and data

### Dataset commitments

Publish a root over a training or evaluation set, one leaf per example or shard. Later, prove a
given example was in the set (for licensing and attribution), or with a sparse tree prove it was
not (for test-set contamination checks), without releasing the dataset.

* **Tree:** `BinaryMerkleTree` for an ordered list of shards, `SparseMerkleTree` keyed by a hash of
  each example when you need non-membership proofs.
* **Planned:** dataset tooling and Python bindings.

### Model weights and checkpoints

Commit to a model file in fixed-size chunks. Mirrors and caches can serve the chunks, and a loader
verifies each one against the published root before using it, so a corrupted or swapped shard is
caught early.

* **Tree:** `BinaryMerkleTree` with `Sha256` or `Blake3`, exactly as in the
  [file integrity demo](/demo/file-integrity).
* **Planned:** GPU-accelerated builds for very large checkpoints.

### Agent and inference logs

Record prompts, tool calls, and outputs of an AI system in an append-only log and publish its root,
so the operator cannot quietly rewrite history.

* **Today:** `BinaryMerkleTree` inclusion proofs over log entries.
* **Planned:** append-only trees with consistency proofs.

## Zero-knowledge

### Anonymous membership and private claims

Prove "I am in this group" or "I own a note in this pool" inside a zero-knowledge proof, without
revealing which member. These systems use Merkle trees with SNARK-friendly hashes.

* **Planned:** Poseidon2 adapters, incremental append-only trees, and Noir and Circom verifiers
  generated from MerkleForge proof formats. See the [roadmap](/roadmap).

## Picking a tree

If you are unsure which tree fits, start with [Choosing a tree](/docs/guides/choosing-a-tree). In
short: an ordered list proved by position is a `BinaryMerkleTree`; a key-value map that needs "not
present" proofs is a `SparseMerkleTree`; anything that must match Ethereum roots is a
`MerklePatriciaTrie` with `Keccak256`.

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Roadmap

  MerkleForge started as fast, correct Merkle trees for blockchains. The same idea, a 32-byte root
  that commits to a large dataset plus small proofs anyone can check, applies anywhere data has to be
  trusted without being re-downloaded: files, logs, databases, machine-learning datasets and models,
  and zero-knowledge circuits. This page is where we are taking MerkleForge across **CPU**, **GPU**,
  **ZK**, and **AI** systems.

  Plans are grouped as **Now** (in review or being built), **Next** (designed, starting soon), and
  **Later** (direction, open to discussion). Nothing below is a promise of a date. If something
  matters to you, say so in [Rust issues](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/issues) or
  [TypeScript issues](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/issues), which is how items move up.

  Two rules hold for everything here: roots and proofs stay byte-identical across Rust, TypeScript,
  and Solidity, and a faster backend never changes an output. Every new backend is tested against
  the reference implementation.

  ## Shipped

  ## CPU and WebAssembly

  The fastest hash call is the one you batch. Tree builds are a sequence of independent node hashes
  per layer, which is ideal for SIMD and for multiple cores.

  | Status | Item |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Now** | **Batch hashing API** in TypeScript ([in review](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/pull/29)): hash adapters can hash a whole tree layer in one call (`hashNodePairs`, `hashLeaves`). `BinaryMerkleTree` stores nodes in one flat buffer and skips hashing padding subtrees. |
  | **Now** | **New WebAssembly backend** for `@merkleforge/hash-wasm`: a 9 KB `no_std` Rust module with SIMD Keccak-256 (two permutations at once). Keccak-256 tree builds are about 5x faster than in 0.2.2 (485 ms to 98 ms at 131,072 leaves), and pure-JS tree builds about 3x faster, with byte-for-byte identical output ([benchmarks and parity](/docs/performance/benchmarks)). |
  | **Now** | **CI on every runtime**: the full test suite in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, and the built packages on Node.js, Deno, and Bun. |
  | Next | One-call proof verification in WebAssembly (fold the whole path in one call), batched multiproofs, and batch hashing for `SparseMerkleTree` updates. |
  | Next | BLAKE3 in WebAssembly, and SHA-256 SIMD (multi-buffer). |
  | Next | Rust: multi-buffer SIMD hashing (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON) behind the same `HashFunction` trait, so a layer of nodes is hashed 4 to 8 at a time. |
  | Later | Parallel tree builds: `rayon` in Rust and Web Workers in JavaScript for trees with millions of leaves. |
  | Later | Embedded and `no_std` targets for `merkle-variants` (RISC-V, Cortex-M) for device attestation and firmware updates. |

  ## GPU

  Large trees (10⁸ leaves and more: rollup state, data availability, dataset commitments) spend
  nearly all their time hashing. The batch API above is shaped for GPUs on purpose: one layer is one
  dispatch of independent pair hashes.

  | Status | Item |
  | --- | --- |
  | Next | **WebGPU backend** for the browser and Deno: a `HashFunction` whose `hashNodePairs` runs Keccak-256, SHA-256, and Poseidon2 compute shaders. Same digests, tested against the CPU adapters. |
  | Later | **Native GPU backend** in Rust through `wgpu` (Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12), with CUDA where it pays off, for building and updating very large trees. |
  | Later | Published crossover measurements: at what tree size the GPU beats the CPU on common hardware, so the library can choose for you. The CPU stays the default. |

  ## Zero-knowledge proofs

  Zero-knowledge systems prove statements about Merkle trees inside a circuit, where Keccak-256 and
  SHA-256 are expensive. They need SNARK-friendly hashes and proof formats that circuits can consume.

  | Status | Item |
  | --- | --- |
  | Next | **Poseidon2 and Poseidon adapters** over BN254 (and other fields), with parameters that match circomlib, Noir, and gnark, so roots agree with existing circuits. |
  | Next | **Incremental (append-only) Merkle trees** for commitments and nullifiers, the shape used by Semaphore-style anonymous signalling and privacy pools. |
  | Later | **Circuit verifiers generated from the same proof format**: Noir and Circom templates that verify binary and sparse MerkleForge proofs, alongside the existing Solidity verifiers. |
  | Later | Interop with proving systems (Halo2, Plonky3, SP1 and RISC Zero guests) so the Rust crates can run inside zkVMs and their proofs verify on-chain. |

  ## AI and data systems

  Machine-learning pipelines move huge datasets and model files between parties that need to trust
  them. A Merkle root is a compact, verifiable fingerprint of any of these, and a proof shows that
  one piece belongs without sharing the rest.

  | Status | Item |
  | --- | --- |
  | Next | **Dataset commitments**: commit to a training or evaluation set (one leaf per example or shard), then prove a specific example was or was not included, for audits, licensing, and contamination checks. |
  | Next | **Model and checkpoint integrity**: a root over fixed-size chunks of model weights, so downloads verify chunk by chunk and a corrupted or swapped shard is caught before loading. Try it with the [file integrity demo](/demo/file-integrity). |
  | Later | **Verifiable AI agent and inference logs**: an append-only log of prompts, tool calls, and outputs with consistency proofs, so anyone can check the log was never rewritten. |
  | Later | **Retrieval provenance (RAG)**: prove that a retrieved passage comes from a committed corpus version. |
  | Later | Python bindings (PyO3) so data and ML tooling can use the Rust crates directly. |

  ## Other systems beyond blockchain

  | Status | Item |
  | --- | --- |
  | Next | **Transparency logs**: an append-only tree with RFC 9162 (Certificate Transparency) inclusion and consistency proofs. |
  | Next | **File sync and content-addressed storage**: chunked file verification and fast diffing between two replicas by comparing subtree roots. |
  | Later | Authenticated key-value storage on disk for databases that need verifiable reads and audits. |
  | Later | Supply-chain attestations: commit to SBOMs and build outputs and prove a component was part of a release. |
  | Later | More language bindings (Go, Swift, Kotlin) generated from the Rust crates. |

  ## Docs and examples

  | Status | Item |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Now** | A [demo section](/demo) that runs the TypeScript packages in your browser: light client, in-browser benchmarks, airdrop claims, file integrity, revocation lists, and Ethereum state proofs. |
  | **Now** | A [use cases](/docs/use-cases) guide that maps real systems to trees, hashes, and packages. |
  | Next | End-to-end examples per use case, from building a tree to verifying on-chain or in a client. |

  MerkleForge has not completed an independent security audit. See the
  [security notes](/docs/reference/security) before using it in production.
</div>

# Choosing a tree

MerkleForge ships three tree variants. They share the <Rust inline>`MerkleTree<H>` trait</Rust><TypeScript inline>`MerkleTree` interface</TypeScript> but are built for
different shapes of data.

<LangBar />

| | `BinaryMerkleTree<H>` | `SparseMerkleTree<H>` | `MerklePatriciaTrie<H>` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data shape** | Ordered list | Map from 32-byte keys to values | Map from byte keys to values |
| **Addressed by** | <Rust inline>`LeafIndex`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`number` index</TypeScript> | 32-byte key | Byte-string key |
| **Proofs** | Inclusion | Membership and non-membership | Membership and non-membership (RLP witness) |
| **Proof size** | `⌈log₂ n⌉` siblings | 256 siblings, empty ones compressed to `None` | One RLP node per trie level on the path |
| **Best hash** | `Sha256` or `Blake3` | `Sha256` or `Blake3` | `Keccak256` for Ethereum roots |
| **Typical use** | Transaction batches, logs, file chunks, SPV | Account state, rollups, allowlists | Ethereum state, receipts, storage proofs |

## Quick decision guide

* **You have a list and prove items by position:** use
  [`BinaryMerkleTree`](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree). It has the smallest proofs and the fastest
  construction.
* **You have a key-value map and need to prove a key is absent:** use
  [`SparseMerkleTree`](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree). Keys are 32 bytes, so hash longer keys
  first.
* **You need roots or witnesses that Ethereum tooling understands:** use
  [`MerklePatriciaTrie<Keccak256>`](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie).

## Writing code that works with any variant

The shared <Rust inline>trait</Rust><TypeScript inline>interface</TypeScript> lets you write generic code. Each variant also has a native API (keys
for the sparse tree and trie); the <Rust inline>trait</Rust><TypeScript inline>interface</TypeScript> maps leaf indices onto it.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::{BinaryMerkleTree, MerklePatriciaTrie, SparseMerkleTree};
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  /// Insert rows through the shared trait and return a metadata snapshot.
  fn commit<H, T>(tree: &mut T, rows: &[&[u8]]) -> Result<TreeMetadata, MerkleError>
  where
      H: HashFunction,
      T: MerkleTree<H>,
  {
      for row in rows {
          tree.insert(row)?;
      }
      Ok(tree.metadata())
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let rows: &[&[u8]] = &[b"alice:100", b"bob:250", b"carol:75"];

      let binary = commit(&mut BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
      let sparse = commit(&mut SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
      let trie = commit(&mut MerklePatriciaTrie::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;

      for meta in [binary, sparse, trie] {
          println!("{:<18} leaves={} height={}", meta.variant, meta.leaf_count, meta.height);
      }
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The sparse tree and trie implement `MerkleTree` through an `indexed()` view that shares the tree's
  state:

  ```ts
  import { type Bytes, type MerkleTree, type TreeMetadata, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree, MerklePatriciaTrie, SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  /** Insert rows through the shared interface and return a metadata snapshot. */
  function commit(tree: MerkleTree, rows: Bytes[]): TreeMetadata {
    for (const row of rows) tree.insert(row)
    return tree.metadata()
  }

  const rows = ['alice:100', 'bob:250', 'carol:75'].map(utf8)

  const binary = commit(new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256), rows)
  const sparse = commit(new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256).indexed(), rows)
  const trie = commit(new MerklePatriciaTrie(Sha256).indexed(), rows)

  for (const meta of [binary, sparse, trie]) {
    console.log(`${meta.variant.padEnd(18)} leaves=${meta.leafCount} height=${meta.height}`)
  }
  ```
</TypeScript>

### How the shared interface maps onto each variant

* **Binary:** `insert` appends and returns the next index. `remove` replaces the leaf with
  <Rust inline>`H::empty()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.empty()`</TypeScript>; later indices are unchanged.
* **Sparse:** leaf index `i` is stored at a key whose last 8 bytes are `i` in big-endian order.
  `insert` returns the first unoccupied index at or above the leaf count, so it never overwrites a
  leaf after a removal. <Rust inline>`generate_proof`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`generateProof`</TypeScript> returns a `MerkleProof` with 256 path nodes.
* **Patricia:** leaf index `i` is stored under the key `merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf: ‖ i`
  (8 bytes, big-endian). <Rust inline>`generate_proof` through the trait returns
  `MerkleError::UnsupportedOperation`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`generateProof` through the view throws
  `MerkleError` with code `'UnsupportedOperation'`</TypeScript>, because Patricia proofs are key-addressed. Use
  <Rust inline>`MerklePatriciaTrie::generate_proof(key)`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`trie.generateProof(key)`</TypeScript> instead.

:::tip
Use the <Rust inline>trait</Rust><TypeScript inline>interface</TypeScript> for generic plumbing (ingestion, metadata, benchmarks). Use each variant's native API
when you need key-addressed proofs.
:::

# Binary Merkle tree

<Rust inline>`BinaryMerkleTree<H>`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`BinaryMerkleTree`</TypeScript> is a
balanced binary tree over an ordered list of leaves. It stores leaves and internal nodes in one flat,
cache-friendly array, pads the leaf layer to a power of two, and gives `O(log n)` inclusion proofs
addressed by <Rust inline>`LeafIndex`</Rust><TypeScript inline>a numeric leaf index</TypeScript>.

Use it for transaction batches, logs, file chunks, snapshot commitments, and Bitcoin-style SPV.

<LangBar />

## Create a tree

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      // Empty tree, grows as you insert.
      let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      assert!(tree.is_empty());
      assert_eq!(tree.root(), None);

      // Pre-size the leaf layer for at least 1,000 leaves (rounded up to 1,024).
      // Reserving storage adds no logical leaves.
      let reserved = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::with_capacity(1_000);
      assert_eq!(reserved.leaf_count(), 0);

      // Build from a known leaf set in one O(n) pass.
      let batch = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves([b"tx1".as_slice(), b"tx2", b"tx3"])?;
      assert_eq!(batch.leaf_count(), 3);

      tree.insert(b"tx1")?;
      tree.insert(b"tx2")?;
      tree.insert(b"tx3")?;
      assert_eq!(tree.root(), batch.root());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  `from_leaves` accepts anything that iterates over `AsRef<[u8]>`: `&str`, `&[u8]`, `Vec<u8>`,
  `String`. It returns `MerkleError::EmptyLeafData` if any leaf is empty.

  :::note
  `from_leaves` was added in v0.5.0.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  // Empty tree, grows as you insert.
  const tree = new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256)
  console.assert(tree.isEmpty())
  console.assert(tree.root() === undefined)

  // Pre-size the leaf layer for at least 1,000 leaves (rounded up to 1,024).
  // Reserving storage adds no logical leaves.
  const reserved = BinaryMerkleTree.withCapacity(Sha256, 1_000)
  console.assert(reserved.leafCount === 0)

  // Build from a known leaf set in one O(n) pass.
  const batch = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['tx1', 'tx2', 'tx3'].map(utf8))
  console.assert(batch.leafCount === 3)

  tree.insert(utf8('tx1'))
  tree.insert(utf8('tx2'))
  tree.insert(utf8('tx3'))
  console.assert(bytesEqual(tree.root()!, batch.root()!))
  ```

  `fromLeaves` accepts any `Iterable<Uint8Array>` (an array, a generator, a `Set`). Encode strings
  with `utf8` first. It throws a `MerkleError` with code `EmptyLeafData` if any leaf is empty.
</TypeScript>

## Insert and remove

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

      // insert returns the stable index of the new leaf.
      let alice = tree.insert(b"alice:100")?;
      let bob = tree.insert(b"bob:250")?;
      let carol = tree.insert(b"carol:75")?;
      assert_eq!((alice, bob, carol), (LeafIndex(0), LeafIndex(1), LeafIndex(2)));
      assert_eq!(tree.height(), 3); // 3 leaves pad to 4 slots: 4 -> 2 -> 1

      // Removing an interior leaf replaces it with H::empty(); later indices stay put.
      tree.remove(bob)?;
      assert_eq!(tree.leaf_count(), 3);

      // Removing the last leaf shrinks the logical leaf count.
      tree.remove(carol)?;
      assert_eq!(tree.leaf_count(), 1);

      // Empty data is rejected so it can't be confused with padding.
      assert_eq!(tree.insert(b""), Err(MerkleError::EmptyLeafData));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { isMerkleError, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256)

  // insert returns the stable index of the new leaf.
  const alice = tree.insert(utf8('alice:100'))
  const bob = tree.insert(utf8('bob:250'))
  const carol = tree.insert(utf8('carol:75'))
  console.assert(alice === 0 && bob === 1 && carol === 2)
  console.assert(tree.height === 3) // 3 leaves pad to 4 slots: 4 -> 2 -> 1

  // Removing an interior leaf replaces it with hasher.empty(); later indices stay put.
  tree.remove(bob)
  console.assert(tree.leafCount === 3)

  // Removing the last leaf shrinks the logical leaf count.
  tree.remove(carol)
  console.assert(tree.leafCount === 1)

  // Empty data is rejected so it can't be confused with padding.
  let error: unknown
  try {
    tree.insert(new Uint8Array())
  } catch (e) {
    error = e
  }
  console.assert(isMerkleError(error, 'EmptyLeafData'))
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Generate and verify proofs

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let txs = ["tx:alice->bob:100", "tx:bob->carol:50", "tx:carol->dave:25"];
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(txs)?;
      let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");

      for (i, tx) in txs.iter().enumerate() {
          let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(i))?;
          assert_eq!(proof.leaf_index, LeafIndex(i));
          assert_eq!(proof.depth(), 2);
          assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, tx.as_bytes(), &proof));
      }

      // Out-of-range indices are an error, not a panic.
      assert_eq!(
          tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(9)).unwrap_err(),
          MerkleError::IndexOutOfBounds { index: 9, len: 3 },
      );
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  `verify` is an associated function: it needs no tree instance. It returns `false` (never panics)
  for empty leaf data, a wrong leaf, a tampered sibling, a path of the wrong length, or sides that
  don't match the leaf index.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { isMerkleError, proofDepth, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const txs = ['tx:alice->bob:100', 'tx:bob->carol:50', 'tx:carol->dave:25']
  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, txs.map(utf8))
  const root = tree.root()!

  txs.forEach((tx, i) => {
    const proof = tree.generateProof(i)
    console.assert(proof.leafIndex === i)
    console.assert(proofDepth(proof) === 2)
    console.assert(BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, utf8(tx), proof))
  })

  // Out-of-range indices throw a MerkleError, never a bare exception.
  let error: unknown
  try {
    tree.generateProof(9)
  } catch (e) {
    error = e
  }
  console.assert(
    isMerkleError(error, 'IndexOutOfBounds') && error.detail.index === 9 && error.detail.len === 3,
  )
  ```

  `BinaryMerkleTree.verify` is a static method: it needs no tree instance, only the hash function.
  It returns `false` (never throws) for empty leaf data, a wrong leaf, a tampered sibling, a path of
  the wrong length, sides that don't match the leaf index, or an index or leaf count that isn't a
  non-negative safe integer.
</TypeScript>

## Prove several leaves at once

A multiproof covers several leaves with one set of sibling hashes. Neighbouring leaves share
siblings, so it is usually much smaller than one proof per leaf.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let txs: Vec<String> = (0..8).map(|i| format!("tx-{i}")).collect();
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(&txs)?;
      let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");

      // Indices may be unsorted or repeated; the proof stores them sorted and unique.
      let proof = tree.generate_multi_proof(&[LeafIndex(5), LeafIndex(4), LeafIndex(6), LeafIndex(7)])?;
      assert_eq!(proof.leaf_indices, vec![4, 5, 6, 7]);
      assert_eq!(proof.hashes.len(), 1); // vs. 12 hashes for four separate proofs

      let leaves: Vec<&[u8]> = proof.leaf_indices.iter().map(|&i| txs[i].as_bytes()).collect();
      assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_multi_proof(root, &leaves, &proof));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  `verify_multi_proof` returns `false` for unsorted or repeated indices, a wrong leaf, a tampered,
  missing, or extra hash, or a `leaf_count` with a different tree depth. `BinaryMultiProof`
  serializes with serde and `Serializable`, in the same format as the TypeScript package
  [`@merkleforge/variants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const txs = Array.from({ length: 8 }, (_, i) => utf8(`tx-${i}`))
  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, txs)
  const root = tree.root()!

  // Indices may be unsorted or repeated; the proof stores them sorted and unique.
  const proof = tree.generateMultiProof([5, 4, 6, 7])
  console.assert(proof.leafIndices.join() === '4,5,6,7')
  console.assert(proof.hashes.length === 1) // vs. 12 hashes for four separate proofs

  const leaves = proof.leafIndices.map((i) => txs[i]!)
  console.assert(BinaryMerkleTree.verifyMultiProof(Sha256, root, leaves, proof))
  ```

  `verifyMultiProof` returns `false` for unsorted or repeated indices, a wrong leaf, a tampered,
  missing, or extra hash, or a `leafCount` with a different tree depth. Calling
  `generateMultiProof` with no indices throws `InvalidProofStructure`. `encodeBinaryMultiProof` /
  `decodeBinaryMultiProof` and `multiProofToSerdeJSON` / `multiProofFromSerdeJSON` produce the same
  bytes and JSON as the Rust `BinaryMultiProof`, and `toSolidityBinaryMultiProof` formats a
  Keccak-256 multiproof for the Solidity verifier.
</TypeScript>

## Height and padding

| Leaves | Padded slots | <Rust inline>`height()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`height`</TypeScript> | Proof depth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | – |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 (trivial proof) |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| 3–4 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| 5–8 | 8 | 4 | 3 |
| 1,000 | 1,024 | 11 | 10 |

A single-leaf tree has a **trivial** proof
(<Rust inline>`proof.is_trivial()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`isTrivialProof(proof)`</TypeScript>):
the leaf hash is the root.

## Through the generic trait

<Rust>
  `BinaryMerkleTree` implements both `MerkleTree<H>` and `ProofVerifier<H>`:

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Blake3;

  fn verify_with<V: ProofVerifier<Blake3>>(
      root: &[u8; 32],
      leaf: &[u8],
      proof: &MerkleProof<[u8; 32]>,
  ) -> bool {
      V::verify(root, leaf, proof)
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();
      MerkleTree::insert(&mut tree, b"leaf")?;
      let proof = MerkleTree::generate_proof(&tree, LeafIndex(0))?;
      let root = *MerkleTree::root(&tree).expect("non-empty");

      assert!(verify_with::<BinaryMerkleTree<Blake3>>(&root, b"leaf", &proof));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `BinaryMerkleTree` implements the `MerkleTree` interface from `@merkleforge/core`, and its static
  `verify` matches the `ProofVerifier` function type, so code written against the interfaces works
  with any tree:

  ```ts
  import { type MerkleTree, type ProofVerifier, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Blake3 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  // Code written against the interfaces works with any tree.
  const tree: MerkleTree = new BinaryMerkleTree(Blake3)
  const verify: ProofVerifier = BinaryMerkleTree.verify

  tree.insert(utf8('leaf'))
  const proof = tree.generateProof(0)
  const root = tree.root()!

  console.assert(verify(tree.hasher, root, utf8('leaf'), proof))
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Clone, Debug, and serde

<Rust>
  `BinaryMerkleTree` implements `Clone`, `Debug`, `Default`, `Serialize`, and `Deserialize`. The
  serialized form stores only the hash algorithm name and the leaf hashes; internal nodes are
  recomputed on load. See [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  There is no `clone` or debug formatting in TypeScript. `toJSON()` returns the hash algorithm name
  and the leaf hashes in hex (so `JSON.stringify(tree)` works directly), and
  `BinaryMerkleTree.fromJSON` recomputes the internal nodes on load. A round trip is also the way to
  copy a tree. `fromJSON` throws `DeserializationError` if the JSON was written with a different hash.

  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['a', 'b', 'c'].map(utf8))

  // toJSON keeps the hash name and leaf hashes; fromJSON rebuilds the rest.
  const json = JSON.stringify(tree)
  const copy = BinaryMerkleTree.fromJSON(Sha256, JSON.parse(json))
  console.assert(bytesEqual(copy.root()!, tree.root()!))
  ```

  See [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization).
</TypeScript>

## Performance

<Rust>
  On the reference machine (i7-1185G7), building a 100,000-leaf SHA-256 tree takes about 268 ms,
  proof generation about 79 ns, and verification about 3 µs. See
  [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks) for the full tables.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  In the published TypeScript run at 131,072 Keccak-256 leaves, `BinaryMerkleTree` generates one
  proof in 8–11 µs and verifies one in about 148 µs with pure-JavaScript Keccak-256, or 41 µs with
  [`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`](/docs/guides/hash-functions). See
  [BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md) for the full
  comparison with other JavaScript libraries.
</TypeScript>

# Sparse Merkle tree

<Rust inline>`SparseMerkleTree<H>`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`SparseMerkleTree`</TypeScript> models a fixed-depth **256-bit key space**: 2²⁵⁶ leaf slots, almost all
empty. It stores only non-empty nodes, precomputes the empty-subtree hash at every level, and
compresses single-leaf subtrees into shortcut nodes (Buterin, 2018) and small subtrees into batch
entries (Ouvrard, 2018/2019).

Use it for account state, key-value commitments, allowlists, and rollup state, especially when you
must prove that a key is **absent**.

<LangBar />

## Keys and values

* A key is <Rust inline>`[u8; 32]`</Rust><TypeScript inline>a 32-byte `Uint8Array`</TypeScript>. If your natural key is longer or variable-length (an address, a user ID),
  hash it to 32 bytes first.
* A value is any non-empty byte string. The tree stores <Rust inline>`H::hash(value)`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.hash(value)`</TypeScript>.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  /// Derive a 32-byte tree key from an arbitrary identifier.
  fn key_for(id: &str) -> [u8; 32] {
      Sha256::hash(id.as_bytes())
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      assert_eq!(state.root(), None); // root() is None while empty
      assert_eq!(state.depth(), 256);

      state.insert(key_for("alice"), b"balance:100")?;
      state.insert(key_for("bob"), b"balance:250")?;

      // Inserting an existing key overwrites its value.
      state.insert(key_for("alice"), b"balance:90")?;
      assert_eq!(state.leaf_count(), 2);

      // get() returns the stored leaf *hash*, not the value.
      assert_eq!(state.get(key_for("alice")), Some(&Sha256::hash(b"balance:90")));
      assert_eq!(state.get(key_for("carol")), None);

      state.remove(key_for("bob"))?;
      assert_eq!(state.leaf_count(), 1);
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  /** Derive a 32-byte tree key from an arbitrary identifier. */
  const keyFor = (id: string) => Sha256.hash(utf8(id))

  const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)
  console.assert(state.root() === undefined) // root() is undefined while empty
  console.assert(state.depth === 256)

  state.insert(keyFor('alice'), utf8('balance:100'))
  state.insert(keyFor('bob'), utf8('balance:250'))

  // Inserting an existing key overwrites its value.
  state.insert(keyFor('alice'), utf8('balance:90'))
  console.assert(state.leafCount === 2)

  // get() returns the stored leaf *hash*, not the value.
  console.assert(bytesEqual(state.get(keyFor('alice'))!, Sha256.hash(utf8('balance:90'))))
  console.assert(state.get(keyFor('carol')) === undefined)

  state.remove(keyFor('bob'))
  console.assert(state.leafCount === 1)
  ```
</TypeScript>

`root()` returns <Rust inline>`None`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`undefined`</TypeScript> for an empty tree. If you need the canonical root of an empty tree (for
example as a genesis state), use <Rust inline>`empty_root()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`emptyRoot()`</TypeScript>.

## Membership proofs

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
      let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      let alice = [7_u8; 32];
      let bob = [9_u8; 32];

      state.insert(alice, b"balance:100")?;
      state.insert(bob, b"balance:250")?;

      let proof = state.generate_membership_proof(alice)?;
      let root = state.root().expect("state is not empty");

      assert!(proof.is_membership());
      assert_eq!(proof.siblings.len(), 256);

      // Checks the key, the value, and the path.
      assert!(SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(
          root,
          alice,
          b"balance:100",
          &proof,
      ));
      // The same proof does not verify for another key or value.
      assert!(!SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(root, bob, b"balance:100", &proof));
      assert!(!SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(root, alice, b"balance:999", &proof));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { isSparseMembershipProof, SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)
  const alice = new Uint8Array(32).fill(7)
  const bob = new Uint8Array(32).fill(9)

  state.insert(alice, utf8('balance:100'))
  state.insert(bob, utf8('balance:250'))

  const proof = state.generateMembershipProof(alice)
  const root = state.root()!

  console.assert(isSparseMembershipProof(proof))
  console.assert(proof.siblings.length === 256)

  // Checks the key, the value, and the path.
  console.assert(SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(Sha256, root, alice, utf8('balance:100'), proof))
  // The same proof does not verify for another key or value.
  console.assert(!SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(Sha256, root, bob, utf8('balance:100'), proof))
  console.assert(!SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(Sha256, root, alice, utf8('balance:999'), proof))
  ```
</TypeScript>

<Rust>
  A `SparseMerkleProof<D>` has three public fields: `key`, `siblings` (256 entries ordered leaf to
  root, with `None` for empty subtrees), and `leaf` (the stored leaf hash, or `None`).

  :::warning
  Use `verify_membership`, which checks that the proof is for the key you expect. The older
  `SparseMerkleTree::verify` does **not** check the key and is deprecated.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  A `SparseMerkleProof` is a plain object with three fields: `key`, `siblings` (256 entries ordered
  leaf to root, with `null` for empty subtrees), and `leaf` (the stored leaf hash, or `null`).
  `verifyMembership` and `verifyNonMembership` always check that the proof is for the key you
  expect; there is no key-blind `verify`.
</TypeScript>

## Non-membership proofs

The same function proves absence. For a missing key,
<Rust inline>`generate_membership_proof` returns a proof with `leaf: None`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`generateMembershipProof` returns a proof with `leaf: null`</TypeScript>,
and the verifier rebuilds the root with <Rust inline>`H::empty()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.empty()`</TypeScript>
in the leaf slot.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
      let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      state.insert([1_u8; 32], b"registered")?;

      let missing = [2_u8; 32];
      let proof = state.generate_membership_proof(missing)?;
      let root = state.root().expect("non-empty");

      assert!(proof.is_non_membership());
      assert!(SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_non_membership(root, missing, &proof));

      // A non-membership proof can't be replayed for a key that *is* present.
      let present = state.generate_membership_proof([1_u8; 32])?;
      assert!(!SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_non_membership(root, [1_u8; 32], &present));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { isSparseMembershipProof, SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)
  const registered = new Uint8Array(32).fill(1)
  state.insert(registered, utf8('registered'))

  const missing = new Uint8Array(32).fill(2)
  const proof = state.generateMembershipProof(missing)
  const root = state.root()!

  console.assert(!isSparseMembershipProof(proof)) // proof.leaf === null
  console.assert(SparseMerkleTree.verifyNonMembership(Sha256, root, missing, proof))

  // A non-membership proof can't be replayed for a key that *is* present.
  const present = state.generateMembershipProof(registered)
  console.assert(!SparseMerkleTree.verifyNonMembership(Sha256, root, registered, present))
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Batch operations

<Rust inline>`batch_insert` and `batch_remove`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`batchInsert` and `batchRemove`</TypeScript> apply every change first, then recompute each affected node
once (one-phase batch update, Ma et al.). For many updates this is much faster than a loop of
single inserts.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
      let mut batched = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      let mut sequential = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

      let updates: Vec<([u8; 32], Vec<u8>)> = (0_u8..100)
          .map(|i| ([i; 32], format!("account:{i}").into_bytes()))
          .collect();

      batched.batch_insert(&updates)?;
      for (key, value) in &updates {
          sequential.insert(*key, value)?;
      }
      assert_eq!(batched.root(), sequential.root());
      assert_eq!(batched.leaf_count(), 100);

      // Remove several keys in one pass. Every key must exist.
      batched.batch_remove(&[[0_u8; 32], [1_u8; 32], [2_u8; 32]])?;
      assert_eq!(batched.leaf_count(), 97);
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const batched = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)
  const sequential = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)

  const key = (i: number) => new Uint8Array(32).fill(i)
  const updates = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => [key(i), utf8(`account:${i}`)] as const)

  batched.batchInsert(updates)
  for (const [k, value] of updates) sequential.insert(k, value)
  console.assert(bytesEqual(batched.root()!, sequential.root()!))
  console.assert(batched.leafCount === 100)

  // Remove several keys in one pass. Every key must exist.
  batched.batchRemove([key(0), key(1), key(2)])
  console.assert(batched.leafCount === 97)
  ```
</TypeScript>

Rules:

* If a key appears more than once in <Rust inline>`batch_insert`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`batchInsert`</TypeScript>, the **last** value wins.
* <Rust inline>`batch_insert` fails</Rust><TypeScript inline>`batchInsert` throws</TypeScript> with `EmptyLeafData` if any value is empty, before changing the tree.
* <Rust inline>`batch_remove` fails</Rust><TypeScript inline>`batchRemove` throws</TypeScript> with `UnsupportedOperation` if any key is missing, before changing the tree.
* Single `remove` of a missing key also <Rust inline>returns</Rust><TypeScript inline>throws</TypeScript> `UnsupportedOperation`.

In the published Rust benchmark run (2026-08-17), a 1,000-key batch insert took 20.33 ms versus 8.69 s
for 1,000 sequential inserts. That run predates the v0.5.0 fix that makes single inserts
recompute only the changed path, so today's sequential numbers are far lower; batching still saves
work on shared ancestors. See [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks).

## Empty hashes and storage introspection

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut tree = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

      // Level 0 is the empty leaf; level 256 is the empty-tree root.
      assert_eq!(tree.empty_hash_at(0), &Sha256::empty());
      assert_eq!(tree.empty_root(), tree.empty_hash_at(256));
      assert_eq!(tree.empty_hashes().len(), 257);

      tree.insert([0xAB; 32], b"value")?;
  ```
