  ```rust
      println!("materialized nodes: {}", tree.stored_node_count());
      println!("nodes written by last mutation: {}", tree.last_node_access_count());
      println!("estimate without batching: {}", tree.unbatched_node_count_estimate());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)

  // Level 0 is the empty leaf; level 256 is the empty-tree root.
  console.assert(bytesEqual(tree.emptyHashAt(0), Sha256.empty()))
  console.assert(bytesEqual(tree.emptyRoot(), tree.emptyHashAt(256)))
  console.assert(tree.emptyHashes().length === 257)

  tree.insert(new Uint8Array(32).fill(0xab), utf8('value'))
  console.log('materialized nodes:', tree.storedNodeCount)
  console.log('nodes written by last mutation:', tree.lastNodeAccessCount)
  console.log('estimate without batching:', tree.unbatchedNodeCountEstimate())
  ```
</TypeScript>

<Rust>
  The `merkle_variants::sparse` module also exports the constants `SPARSE_TREE_DEPTH` (256),
  `EMPTY_HASH_LEVELS` (257), and `BATCH_DEPTH` (4), and the helper `bit_at(key, depth)` that
  returns the path bit for a key at a depth (bit 0 is the high bit of `key[0]`).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `@merkleforge/variants` also exports the constants `SPARSE_TREE_DEPTH` (256),
  `EMPTY_HASH_LEVELS` (257), `BATCH_DEPTH` (4), and `SPARSE_KEY_BYTES` (32), and the helper
  `bitAt(key, depth)` that returns the path bit for a key at a depth as a boolean (bit 0 is the high
  bit of `key[0]`).
</TypeScript>

## Verifying on-chain

<Rust>
  Proof formatting for Solidity is TypeScript only. Switch to TypeScript to see it, or encode the
  proof yourself for the `MerkleForgeSparse` contract in
  [MerkleForge-ts/contracts](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/contracts).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  A Keccak-256 sparse proof carries 256 siblings, most of them empty. `toSoliditySparseProof`
  drops the empty ones and records which levels are present in a bitmap, producing the arguments
  for `MerkleForgeSparse.verifyMembership` / `verifyNonMembership` (see
  [contracts/](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/contracts)). Values are
  `0x` hex strings and a `bigint`, ready for viem or ethers.

  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree, toSoliditySparseProof } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Keccak256)
  const alice = Keccak256.hash(utf8('alice'))
  state.insert(alice, utf8('balance:100'))
  state.insert(Keccak256.hash(utf8('bob')), utf8('balance:250'))

  const proof = toSoliditySparseProof(state.generateMembershipProof(alice))
  // Only the one non-empty sibling is kept; bit `level` of `bitmap` marks where it sits.
  console.assert(proof.siblings.length === 1)
  console.log(proof)
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Through the generic trait

<Rust>
  `SparseMerkleTree` implements `MerkleTree<H>` by mapping leaf index `i` to a key whose last 8 bytes
  are `i` (big-endian). `MerkleTree::generate_proof` returns an ordinary `MerkleProof` with 256 path
  nodes. Prefer the key-addressed API above for real state.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `smt.indexed()` returns a `MerkleTree` view that shares the tree's state and maps leaf index `i`
  to a key whose last 8 bytes are `i` (big-endian). Its `insert` takes the first free index at or
  above the leaf count, so it never overwrites a leaf. `generateProof` returns an ordinary
  `MerkleProof` with 256 path nodes. Prefer the key-addressed API above for real state.

  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)
  const view = state.indexed()

  const index = view.insert(utf8('first'))
  const proof = view.generateProof(index)
  console.assert(proof.path.length === 256)
  ```
</TypeScript>

# Merkle Patricia trie

<Rust inline>`MerklePatriciaTrie<H>`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`MerklePatriciaTrie`</TypeScript> implements Ethereum's Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT): nibble-addressed byte
keys, four node types (empty, leaf, extension, branch), hex-prefix path encoding, RLP-encoded
nodes, and Ethereum's inline-or-hash node references.

With `Keccak256`, roots **match Ethereum**: the implementation is tested against the official
`trietest.json` and `trieanyorder.json` vectors from the Ethereum test suite.

<LangBar />

## Insert, get, remove

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
  use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
      let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();

      trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"100")?;
      trie.insert(b"account:bob", b"250")?;
      trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"90")?; // overwrite

      assert_eq!(trie.get(b"account:alice"), Some(b"90".as_slice()));
      assert_eq!(trie.get(b"account:carol"), None);
      assert_eq!(trie.leaf_count(), 2);

      // Removal collapses branches and extensions, so the root equals that of a
      // trie built from the remaining entries.
      trie.remove(b"account:bob")?;

      let mut fresh = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
      fresh.insert(b"account:alice", b"90")?;
      assert_eq!(trie.root(), fresh.root());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { MerklePatriciaTrie } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const trie = new MerklePatriciaTrie(Keccak256)

  trie.insert(utf8('account:alice'), utf8('100'))
  trie.insert(utf8('account:bob'), utf8('250'))
  trie.insert(utf8('account:alice'), utf8('90')) // overwrite

  console.assert(bytesEqual(trie.get(utf8('account:alice'))!, utf8('90')))
  console.assert(trie.get(utf8('account:carol')) === undefined)
  console.assert(trie.leafCount === 2)

  // Removal collapses branches and extensions, so the root equals that of a
  // trie built from the remaining entries.
  trie.remove(utf8('account:bob'))

  const fresh = new MerklePatriciaTrie(Keccak256)
  fresh.insert(utf8('account:alice'), utf8('90'))
  console.assert(bytesEqual(trie.root()!, fresh.root()!))
  ```
</TypeScript>

Unlike the sparse tree, `get` returns the stored **value** bytes. Values must be non-empty
(`EmptyLeafData`), and removing a missing key <Rust inline>returns</Rust><TypeScript inline>throws</TypeScript>
`UnsupportedOperation`. `root()` is <Rust inline>`None`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`undefined`</TypeScript>
for an empty trie.

## Ethereum compatibility

The trie produces the same root as Ethereum clients for the same key-value set. This is the
`dogs` case from Ethereum's `trieanyorder.json`:

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
  use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

  fn hex32(s: &str) -> [u8; 32] {
      let s = s.trim_start_matches("0x");
      let mut out = [0_u8; 32];
      for (i, byte) in out.iter_mut().enumerate() {
          *byte = u8::from_str_radix(&s[2 * i..2 * i + 2], 16).expect("valid hex");
      }
      out
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
      let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
      trie.insert(b"doe", b"reindeer")?;
      trie.insert(b"dog", b"puppy")?;
      trie.insert(b"dogglesworth", b"cat")?;

      let expected = hex32("0x8aad789dff2f538bca5d8ea56e8abe10f4c7ba3a5dea95fea4cd6e7c3a1168d3");
      assert_eq!(trie.root(), Some(&expected));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { toHex, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { MerklePatriciaTrie } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const trie = new MerklePatriciaTrie(Keccak256)
  trie.insert(utf8('doe'), utf8('reindeer'))
  trie.insert(utf8('dog'), utf8('puppy'))
  trie.insert(utf8('dogglesworth'), utf8('cat'))

  const expected = '0x8aad789dff2f538bca5d8ea56e8abe10f4c7ba3a5dea95fea4cd6e7c3a1168d3'
  console.assert(toHex(trie.root()!) === expected)
  ```
</TypeScript>

Insertion order does not matter: the trie is canonical.

How compatibility works: the `Keccak256` adapter overrides
<Rust inline>`HashFunction::hash_encoded_node`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`HashFunction.hashEncodedNode`</TypeScript> to
return plain `Keccak-256(rlp)`, with no domain prefix, exactly as Ethereum hashes nodes. RLP already
distinguishes node types, so the `0x00`/`0x01` prefixes used by binary and sparse trees are not
needed here.

:::note
With `Sha256` or `Blake3` the trie works the same way but its roots are not Ethereum roots. A
custom adapter needs to override <Rust inline>`hash_encoded_node`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashEncodedNode` (a `defineHashFunction` option)</TypeScript>
to produce Ethereum-compatible roots; matching on the algorithm name no longer works (changed in
v0.5.0). The WebAssembly `createKeccak256Wasm()` from `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` already does this.
:::

## Witnesses (proofs)

<Rust inline>`generate_proof(key)` returns an `MptProof<D>`: the key, the value (or `None`)</Rust><TypeScript inline>`generateProof(key)` returns an `MptProof`: the key, the value (or `null`)</TypeScript>,
and the RLP-encoded nodes on the key's path, root first. It has the shape of an
[EIP-1186](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186) `accountProof` / `storageProof` entry.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::{MerklePatriciaTrie, MptProof};
  use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
      let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
      trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"100")?;
      trie.insert(b"account:bob", b"250")?;
      let root = *trie.root().expect("trie is not empty");

      // Membership
      let proof = trie.generate_proof(b"account:alice")?;
      assert!(proof.is_membership());
      assert_eq!(proof.value.as_deref(), Some(b"100".as_slice()));
      assert!(MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(&root, &proof));

      // Non-membership: the path ends at an empty slot or a divergent node.
      let absent = trie.generate_proof(b"account:carol")?;
      assert!(absent.is_non_membership());
      assert!(MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(&root, &absent));

      // A forged value fails verification.
      let forged: MptProof<[u8; 32]> = MptProof::new(
          proof.key.clone(),
          Some(b"1000000".to_vec()),
          proof.proof_nodes.clone(),
      );
      assert!(!MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(&root, &forged));
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { MerklePatriciaTrie, type MptProof } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const trie = new MerklePatriciaTrie(Keccak256)
  trie.insert(utf8('account:alice'), utf8('100'))
  trie.insert(utf8('account:bob'), utf8('250'))
  const root = trie.root()!

  // Membership
  const proof = trie.generateProof(utf8('account:alice'))
  console.assert(proof.value !== null && bytesEqual(proof.value, utf8('100')))
  console.assert(MerklePatriciaTrie.verifyProof(Keccak256, root, proof))

  // Non-membership: the path ends at an empty slot or a divergent node.
  const absent = trie.generateProof(utf8('account:carol'))
  console.assert(absent.value === null)
  console.assert(MerklePatriciaTrie.verifyProof(Keccak256, root, absent))

  // A forged value fails verification.
  const forged: MptProof = { ...proof, value: utf8('1000000') }
  console.assert(!MerklePatriciaTrie.verifyProof(Keccak256, root, forged))
  ```
</TypeScript>

<Rust inline>`verify_proof`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`verifyProof`</TypeScript> checks that the first
node hashes to the trusted root, then walks the key's nibble path through the witness. The
verifier needs only the root and the proof, so it works for light clients and cross-chain bridges.

<Rust>
  `MptProof` derives `Serialize` / `Deserialize`, so you can send it over the network directly.

  `generate_proof` on an empty trie returns `MerkleError::EmptyTree`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `MptProof` is a plain object with `key`, `value`, and `proofNodes`. To send it over the network,
  use `encodeMptProof` / `decodeMptProof` or `mptProofToSerdeJSON` / `mptProofFromSerdeJSON`, which
  produce the same bytes and JSON as the Rust crate (see [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization)).
  TypeScript has no `isMembership()` helper: a proof with `value !== null` is a membership proof.

  `generateProof` on an empty trie throws `MerkleError` with code `EmptyTree`.

  `MerklePatriciaTrie.proveValue(hasher, root, key, proofNodes)` is the lower-level verifier: it
  returns the value the witness proves, `null` for a proven absence, or throws `InvalidProof`. It
  also accepts `eth_getProof`-style witnesses, where short child nodes are embedded in their parent
  rather than listed.
</TypeScript>

## Verifying `eth_getProof`

<Rust>
  `eth_getProof` verification is TypeScript only. Switch to TypeScript to see
  `@merkleforge/ethereum`, or verify the `accountProof` and `storageProof` node lists yourself with
  `verify_proof`: the account key is `keccak256(address)` and storage keys are `keccak256(slot)`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `@merkleforge/ethereum` verifies [EIP-1186](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186) responses
  against a state root. `verifyEthGetProof` checks the account proof, every storage proof, and that
  the response's own fields agree with them, and returns the decoded account (`null` if it does not
  exist) and slot values as `bigint`. It throws `InvalidProof` on any mismatch.
  `verifyAccountProof`, `verifyStorageProof`, and `mappingSlot` are also exported.

  ```bash
  npm i @merkleforge/ethereum
  ```

  ```ts
  import { toHex } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { mappingSlot, verifyEthGetProof } from '@merkleforge/ethereum'

  const RPC_URL = 'https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com'
  const rpc = async (method: string, params: unknown[]) => {
    const res = await fetch(RPC_URL, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 1, method, params }),
    })
    return (await res.json()).result
  }

  // USDC on mainnet: balances live in the mapping at slot 9.
  const usdc = '0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48'
  const holder = '0x37305B1cD40574E4C5Ce33f8e8306Be057fD7341'
  const slot = toHex(mappingSlot(holder, 9n))

  // Take the state root from a block header you trust (a light client, a
  // checkpoint). Here it comes from the same RPC, for brevity.
  const block = await rpc('eth_getBlockByNumber', ['latest', false])
  const response = await rpc('eth_getProof', [usdc, [slot], block.number])

  // Throws InvalidProof if any part of the response disagrees with the root.
  const { account, storage } = verifyEthGetProof(block.stateRoot, response)
  console.log('contract nonce:', account?.nonce)
  console.log('USDC balance (6 decimals):', storage[0]?.value)
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Low-level building blocks

<Rust>
  The `merkle_variants::patricia` module exposes the encoding primitives for tooling and tests:

  | Item | Purpose |
  | --- | --- |
  | `NibblePath` | Byte key to 4-bit nibble path (`from_key`, `len`, `get`, `slice`, `common_prefix_len`) |
  | `hp_encode` / `hp_decode` | Hex-prefix encoding for leaf and extension paths |
  | `rlp_encode` / `rlp_decode` | RLP for `MptNode` values |
  | `MptNode<D>` | `Empty`, `Leaf`, `Extension`, `Branch` |
  | `NodeRef<D>` | `Hash(D)` for nodes ≥ 32 bytes of RLP, `Inline(Vec<u8>)` otherwise |
  | `hash_node::<H>` | Ethereum-style reference for a node |
  | `compute_root_hash::<H>` | Root digest for a root node (always hashed) |

  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::patricia::{compute_root_hash, hp_encode, MptNode, NibblePath};
  use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

  fn main() {
      // The empty trie root, keccak256(rlp("")), well known from Ethereum.
      let empty = compute_root_hash::<Keccak256>(&MptNode::Empty);
      assert_eq!(empty[..4], [0x56, 0xe8, 0x1f, 0x17]);

      let path = NibblePath::from_key(b"key");
      assert_eq!(path.len(), 6); // two nibbles per byte

      // Hex-prefix flag for a leaf with an even-length path is 0x20.
      assert_eq!(hp_encode(&path, true)[0], 0x20);
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `@merkleforge/variants` exports the same encoding primitives:

  | Item | Purpose |
  | --- | --- |
  | `bytesToNibbles` / `Nibbles` | Byte key to 4-bit nibble path (a plain `number[]`) |
  | `hpEncode` / `hpDecode` | Hex-prefix encoding for leaf and extension paths |
  | `rlpEncode` / `rlpDecode` | RLP for `MptNode` values |
  | `encodeRlp` / `decodeRlp` / `RlpValue` | General RLP for byte strings and nested lists |
  | `MptNode` | `{ kind: 'empty' \| 'leaf' \| 'extension' \| 'branch', … }` |
  | `NodeRef` | `{ kind: 'hash', hash }` for nodes ≥ 32 bytes of RLP, `{ kind: 'inline', rlp }` otherwise |
  | `hashNode(hasher, node)` | Ethereum-style reference for a node |
  | `computeRootHash(hasher, node)` | Root digest for a root node (always hashed) |

  ```ts
  import { toHex, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { bytesToNibbles, computeRootHash, hpEncode } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  // The empty trie root, keccak256(rlp("")), well known from Ethereum.
  const empty = computeRootHash(Keccak256, { kind: 'empty' })
  console.assert(toHex(empty).startsWith('0x56e81f17'))

  const path = bytesToNibbles(utf8('key'))
  console.assert(path.length === 6) // two nibbles per byte

  // Hex-prefix flag for a leaf with an even-length path is 0x20.
  console.assert(hpEncode(path, true)[0] === 0x20)
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Through the generic trait

<Rust>
  `MerklePatriciaTrie` implements `MerkleTree<H>`: leaf index `i` is stored under
  `b"merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf:" ‖ i` (8 bytes, big-endian). `MerkleTree::generate_proof` returns
  `UnsupportedOperation` because Patricia proofs are key-addressed; call the inherent
  `generate_proof(key)` instead.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `trie.indexed()` returns a `MerkleTree` view that shares the trie's state: leaf index `i` is stored
  under `utf8('merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf:') ‖ i` (8 bytes, big-endian). Its `generateProof` throws
  `UnsupportedOperation` because Patricia proofs are key-addressed; call
  `trie.generateProof(key)` instead.
</TypeScript>

# Hash functions

Every MerkleForge tree is parameterised by a `HashFunction`. The hash decides the digest, how
leaves and internal nodes are hashed, and what an empty slot looks like.

<LangBar />

<Rust>
  Trees are generic over `H: HashFunction`. Swapping the hash is a type-level change: Rust
  monomorphises the generics, so there is no runtime dispatch.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  A `HashFunction` is a plain object passed to the tree's constructor (and to the static verifiers).
  Swapping the hash means passing a different object; no other code changes.
</TypeScript>

## The adapters

<Rust inline>`merkleforge-hash`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`@merkleforge/hash`</TypeScript> ships
three adapters. All produce 32-byte
<Rust inline>`[u8; 32]`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`Uint8Array`</TypeScript> digests.

| Type | Algorithm | <Rust inline>`algorithm_name()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`algorithmName`</TypeScript> | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Sha256` | SHA-256 | `"SHA-256"` | Interoperable binary and sparse trees; hardware SHA extensions |
| `Keccak256` | Keccak-256 | `"Keccak-256"` | Ethereum-compatible Patricia roots |
| `Blake3` | BLAKE3 | `"BLAKE3"` | Highest software throughput when Ethereum compatibility isn't needed |

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::traits::HashFunction;
  use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Keccak256, Sha256};

  fn main() {
      let sha = Sha256::hash(b"alice:100");
      let keccak = Keccak256::hash(b"alice:100");
      let blake = Blake3::hash(b"alice:100");

      assert_eq!(sha.len(), 32);
      assert_ne!(sha, keccak);
      assert_ne!(sha, blake);

      assert_eq!(Blake3::algorithm_name(), "BLAKE3");
      assert_eq!(Blake3::digest_size(), 32);

      // Combine two child digests into a parent.
      let left = Blake3::hash(b"left leaf");
      let right = Blake3::hash(b"right leaf");
      let _parent = Blake3::hash_nodes(&left, &right);
  }
  ```

  `merkleforge_hash` re-exports `HashFunction`, so `use merkleforge_hash::HashFunction;` also works.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Blake3, Keccak256, Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'

  const sha = Sha256.hash(utf8('alice:100'))
  const keccak = Keccak256.hash(utf8('alice:100'))
  const blake = Blake3.hash(utf8('alice:100'))

  console.assert(sha.length === 32)
  console.assert(!bytesEqual(sha, keccak))
  console.assert(!bytesEqual(sha, blake))

  console.assert(Blake3.algorithmName === 'BLAKE3')
  console.assert(Blake3.digestSize === 32)

  // Combine two child digests into a parent.
  const left = Blake3.hash(utf8('left leaf'))
  const right = Blake3.hash(utf8('right leaf'))
  const parent = Blake3.hashNodes(left, right)
  ```

  The `HashFunction` type itself is exported from `@merkleforge/core`. The adapters are built on
  [`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes), so they run unchanged in Node.js,
  browsers, Deno, and Bun.
</TypeScript>

## Domain separation

| Adapter | Leaf: `hash(data)` | Internal node: <Rust inline>`hash_nodes(l, r)`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashNodes(l, r)`</TypeScript> | Encoded node: <Rust inline>`hash_encoded_node(rlp)`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashEncodedNode(rlp)`</TypeScript> |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Sha256` | `SHA-256(0x00 ‖ data)` | `SHA-256(0x01 ‖ l ‖ r)` | `SHA-256(0x00 ‖ rlp)` (default) |
| `Keccak256` | `Keccak-256(0x00 ‖ data)` | `Keccak-256(0x01 ‖ l ‖ r)` | `Keccak-256(rlp)`, plain, Ethereum-compatible |
| `Blake3` | `derive_key("MerkleForge 2026 leaf v1", data)` | `derive_key("MerkleForge 2026 internal-node v1", l ‖ r)` | Same as leaf (default) |

`empty()` is the leaf hash of an empty slice,
<Rust inline>`hash(b"")`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hash(new Uint8Array())`</TypeScript>, for all
three adapters. Binary trees pad with it and sparse trees use it for vacant slots.

Why it matters: see [Mental model → Domain separation](/docs/mental-model#domain-separation-0x00-and-0x01).

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::traits::HashFunction;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;
  use sha2::{Digest, Sha256 as RawSha256};

  fn main() {
      // The adapter's leaf hash is SHA-256 over 0x00 ‖ data.
      let mut raw = RawSha256::new();
      raw.update([0x00]);
      raw.update(b"alice:100");
      let expected: [u8; 32] = raw.finalize().into();

      assert_eq!(Sha256::hash(b"alice:100"), expected);
      assert_eq!(Sha256::empty(), Sha256::hash(b""));
  }
  ```

  (This snippet uses the [`sha2`](https://crates.io/crates/sha2) crate directly to show the
  pre-image. You don't need it to use MerkleForge.)
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { sha256 } from '@noble/hashes/sha2.js'

  // The adapter's leaf hash is SHA-256 over 0x00 ‖ data.
  const expected = sha256.create().update(Uint8Array.of(0x00)).update(utf8('alice:100')).digest()

  console.assert(bytesEqual(Sha256.hash(utf8('alice:100')), expected))
  console.assert(bytesEqual(Sha256.empty(), Sha256.hash(new Uint8Array())))
  ```

  (This snippet uses [`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes) directly to show
  the pre-image. It is already a dependency of `@merkleforge/hash`, but import it explicitly only if
  you need raw hashes.)
</TypeScript>

## Choosing one

* **Ethereum interop:** `Keccak256`. Required for Patricia roots that match Ethereum.
* **Broad interoperability:** `Sha256`. Ubiquitous, and fast on CPUs with SHA extensions.
* **Raw speed:** `Blake3`. In the published run it hashed 1 MB at 5.99 GiB/s versus 1.28 GiB/s for
  SHA-256 and 291 MiB/s for Keccak-256. See [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks).

<TypeScript>
  Those throughput figures are for the Rust crates. In JavaScript, the WebAssembly adapters below are
  the fastest option for Keccak-256 and SHA-256.
</TypeScript>

A tree built with one hash can't be read with another: serialized trees store the algorithm
name and deserialization rejects a mismatch.

## WebAssembly hashes

<Rust>
  This is a TypeScript-only package: the Rust adapters are already native code. Switch to
  **TypeScript** to see it.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  [`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash-wasm) provides
  WebAssembly versions of `Keccak256` and `Sha256`. With Keccak-256 they build trees 3–7x faster
  than the pure-JS `Keccak256` in Node.js (6.5x at 131,072 leaves, [measured](/docs/performance/benchmarks)). Their
  output and `algorithmName` are identical to `@merkleforge/hash`, so trees, proofs, and JSON built
  with either are interchangeable. The factories are async because they load the WebAssembly module;
  the returned adapter is synchronous.

  ```bash
  npm i @merkleforge/hash-wasm
  ```

  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { createKeccak256Wasm } from '@merkleforge/hash-wasm'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  // Loads the WebAssembly module once; the adapter is synchronous after that.
  const KeccakWasm = await createKeccak256Wasm()

  const rows = ['alice:100', 'bob:250', 'carol:75'].map(utf8)
  const fast = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(KeccakWasm, rows)
  const plain = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, rows)

  // Same output and algorithmName: trees and proofs are interchangeable.
  console.assert(bytesEqual(fast.root()!, plain.root()!))
  console.assert(KeccakWasm.algorithmName === Keccak256.algorithmName)
  ```

  `createSha256Wasm()` works the same way. There is no WebAssembly BLAKE3.
</TypeScript>

## The `HashFunction` trait

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use core::fmt::Debug;

  pub trait HashFunction: Send + Sync + 'static {
      type Digest: AsRef<[u8]> + Clone + Debug + PartialEq + Eq + Send + Sync + 'static;

      /// Leaf hash. Must apply the leaf domain, e.g. H(0x00 ‖ data).
      fn hash(data: &[u8]) -> Self::Digest;

      /// Parent of two children. Default: hash(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right).
      fn hash_nodes(left: &Self::Digest, right: &Self::Digest) -> Self::Digest {
          let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(1 + left.as_ref().len() + right.as_ref().len());
          buf.push(0x01);
          buf.extend_from_slice(left.as_ref());
          buf.extend_from_slice(right.as_ref());
          Self::hash(&buf)
      }

      /// Hash of a self-describing encoding such as an RLP Patricia node. Default: hash(encoded).
      fn hash_encoded_node(encoded: &[u8]) -> Self::Digest {
          Self::hash(encoded)
      }

      /// Digest of an empty slot. Default: hash(&[]).
      fn empty() -> Self::Digest {
          Self::hash(&[])
      }

      fn algorithm_name() -> &'static str;
      fn digest_size() -> usize;
  }
  ```

  This mirrors the definition in `merkle_core::traits::hash_function` (doc comments shortened).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  In TypeScript it is an interface; digests are always `Uint8Array`, so there is no associated
  `Digest` type:

  ```ts
  import type { Bytes } from '@merkleforge/core'

  export interface HashFunction {
    /** Human-readable name, e.g. "SHA-256". Stored in tree metadata. */
    readonly algorithmName: string
    /** Digest length in bytes. */
    readonly digestSize: number
    /** Leaf hash. Must apply the leaf domain, e.g. H(0x00 ‖ data). */
    hash(data: Bytes): Bytes
    /** Parent of two children, e.g. H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right). */
    hashNodes(left: Bytes, right: Bytes): Bytes
    /** Hash of a self-describing encoding such as an RLP Patricia node. */
    hashEncodedNode(encoded: Bytes): Bytes
    /** Digest of an empty slot. */
    empty(): Bytes
  }
  ```

  This mirrors the definition in `@merkleforge/core` (doc comments shortened). Interfaces can't
  carry default methods, so the defaults come from `defineHashFunction` instead: `hashNodes` hashes
  `0x01 ‖ left ‖ right` with `hash`, `hashEncodedNode` delegates to `hash`, and `empty` is `hash` of
  no bytes, the same defaults as the Rust trait.
</TypeScript>

## Writing a custom adapter

<Rust>
  Implement `hash`, `algorithm_name`, and `digest_size`. Apply the `0x00` leaf prefix in `hash`; the
  default `hash_nodes` applies `0x01`. This example wraps the `sha2` crate's SHA-512/256:

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use sha2::{Digest, Sha512_256};

  pub struct Sha512Trunc;

  impl HashFunction for Sha512Trunc {
      type Digest = [u8; 32];

      fn hash(data: &[u8]) -> [u8; 32] {
          let mut hasher = Sha512_256::new();
          hasher.update([0x00]); // leaf domain
          hasher.update(data);
          hasher.finalize().into()
      }

      // hash_nodes, hash_encoded_node, and empty use the defaults.

      fn algorithm_name() -> &'static str {
          "SHA-512/256"
      }

      fn digest_size() -> usize {
          32
      }
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha512Trunc>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c"])?;
      let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");
      let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(2))?;
      assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha512Trunc>::verify(root, b"c", &proof));
      assert_eq!(tree.metadata().hash_algorithm, "SHA-512/256");
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Pass `algorithmName`, `digestSize`, and `hash` to `defineHashFunction`, which fills in the rest
  and returns a frozen `HashFunction`. Apply the `0x00` leaf prefix (`LEAF_PREFIX`) in `hash`; the
  default `hashNodes` applies `0x01` (`NODE_PREFIX`). This example wraps `@noble/hashes`'
  SHA-512/256:

  ```ts
  import { concatBytes, defineHashFunction, LEAF_PREFIX, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'
  import { sha512_256 } from '@noble/hashes/sha2.js'

  export const Sha512Trunc = defineHashFunction({
    algorithmName: 'SHA-512/256',
    digestSize: 32,
    hash: (data) => sha512_256(concatBytes(Uint8Array.of(LEAF_PREFIX), data)), // leaf domain
    // hashNodes, hashEncodedNode, and empty use the defaults.
  })

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha512Trunc, ['a', 'b', 'c'].map(utf8))
  const root = tree.root()!
  const proof = tree.generateProof(2)
  console.assert(BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha512Trunc, root, utf8('c'), proof))
  console.assert(tree.metadata().hashAlgorithm === 'SHA-512/256')
  ```

  An adapter built this way works with every tree and verifier, but only matches a Rust tree if both
  sides compute the same bytes.
</TypeScript>

Checklist for a custom adapter:

1. **Separate the domains.** `hash` must not collide with
   <Rust inline>`hash_nodes`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashNodes`</TypeScript> for different
   structures. Prefix leaves with `0x00`, or override both methods with your own separation (as
   `Blake3` does with context strings).
2. **Override for speed if you like.**
   <Rust inline>`hash_nodes` can hash `0x01 ‖ l ‖ r` without the intermediate `Vec`, as the shipped
   adapters do.</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashNodes` can hash `0x01 ‖ l ‖ r` with an incremental
   hasher instead of concatenating, as `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` does.</TypeScript> Keep the same
   output.
3. **Ethereum roots** need
   <Rust inline>`hash_encoded_node`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashEncodedNode`</TypeScript> to
   return the plain hash of the RLP bytes.
4. **Use a unique <Rust inline>`algorithm_name`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`algorithmName`</TypeScript>.**
   Serialized trees store it to reject mismatched hashes.

<Rust>
  :::warning
  Since v0.5.0, the default `hash_nodes` hashes `0x01 ‖ left ‖ right` instead of
  `left ‖ right`. Custom adapters that relied on the old default now produce different roots.
  The shipped adapters override `hash_nodes` and are unaffected.
  :::
</Rust>

# Proofs & stateless verification

A MerkleForge proof lets a verifier check one value against a trusted root, with no access to the
tree. This is the property that makes Merkle trees useful for light clients, bridges, browsers, and
embedded devices. Proofs are byte-compatible between the two languages: a proof generated by a Rust
server verifies in a TypeScript client, and the other way round.

<LangBar />

## Proof types

<Rust>
  | Tree | Proof type | Verify with |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree` | `MerkleProof<D>` | `BinaryMerkleTree::<H>::verify(root, leaf, &proof)` |
  | `SparseMerkleTree` | `SparseMerkleProof<D>` | `verify_membership(root, key, leaf, &proof)`, `verify_non_membership(root, key, &proof)` |
  | `MerklePatriciaTrie` | `MptProof<D>` | `verify_proof(root, &proof)` |

  The binary proof lives in `merkle-core`, so a verifier can depend on the shared types:

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::types::{LeafIndex, ProofSide};

  /// One step on the path: a sibling hash and the side it sits on.
  pub struct ProofNode<D> {
      pub hash: D,
      pub side: ProofSide,
  }

  /// Inclusion proof for one leaf of a binary tree.
  pub struct MerkleProof<D> {
      pub leaf_index: LeafIndex,
      pub leaf_count: usize,
      pub path: Vec<ProofNode<D>>, // O(log n) siblings, leaf level first
  }
  ```

  (Shown without derives and docs; `MerkleProof` also has `depth()` and `is_trivial()`.)
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  | Tree | Proof type | Verify with |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree` | `MerkleProof` | `BinaryMerkleTree.verify(H, root, leaf, proof)` |
  | `SparseMerkleTree` | `SparseMerkleProof` | `SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(H, root, key, leaf, proof)`, `SparseMerkleTree.verifyNonMembership(H, root, key, proof)` |
  | `MerklePatriciaTrie` | `MptProof` | `MerklePatriciaTrie.verifyProof(H, root, proof)` |

  Every verifier is a static method that takes the hash function `H` as its first argument. The
  binary proof type lives in `@merkleforge/core`, so a verifier can depend on the shared types:

  ```ts
  import type { Bytes } from '@merkleforge/core'

  /** Which side of the running hash a proof sibling sits on. */
  export type ProofSide = 'left' | 'right'

  /** One step on the path: a sibling hash and the side it sits on. */
  export interface ProofNode {
    readonly hash: Bytes
    readonly side: ProofSide
  }

  /** Inclusion proof for one leaf of a binary tree. */
  export interface MerkleProof {
    readonly leafIndex: number
    readonly leafCount: number
    readonly path: readonly ProofNode[] // O(log n) siblings, leaf level first
  }
  ```

  (Proofs are plain objects; use `proofDepth(proof)` and `isTrivialProof(proof)` from
  `@merkleforge/core` for the depth and trivial-proof checks.)
</TypeScript>

## The verification algorithm

```text
1. current = H(0x00 ‖ leaf_data)
2. for each node in proof.path:
     if node.side == Left:  current = H(0x01 ‖ node.hash ‖ current)
     if node.side == Right: current = H(0x01 ‖ current ‖ node.hash)
3. return current == expected_root
```

<Rust inline>`BinaryMerkleTree::verify`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`BinaryMerkleTree.verify`</TypeScript>
also rejects proofs whose structure is inconsistent: empty leaf data,
<Rust inline>`leaf_index >= leaf_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`leafIndex >= leafCount`</TypeScript>,
a path length that doesn't match the padded size, or sides that don't match the bits of
<Rust inline>`leaf_index`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`leafIndex`</TypeScript>. It returns `false`
and never <Rust inline>panics</Rust><TypeScript inline>throws</TypeScript> on malformed input.

## The `ProofVerifier` trait

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::{traits::HashFunction, types::MerkleProof};

  pub trait ProofVerifier<H: HashFunction> {
      fn verify(expected_root: &H::Digest, leaf_data: &[u8], proof: &MerkleProof<H::Digest>) -> bool;
  }
  ```

  It is separate from `MerkleTree` so it can be implemented by a type with no tree state at all.
  `BinaryMerkleTree<H>` implements it, and its inherent `verify` delegates to it.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  TypeScript has no static trait methods, so `ProofVerifier` in `@merkleforge/core` is a function
  type, with the hash function passed as an argument instead of a type parameter:

  ```ts
  import type { Bytes, HashFunction, MerkleProof } from '@merkleforge/core'

  export type ProofVerifier = (
    hasher: HashFunction,
    expectedRoot: Bytes,
    leafData: Bytes,
    proof: MerkleProof,
  ) => boolean
  ```

  It is separate from `MerkleTree` so a verifier needs no tree state at all.
  `BinaryMerkleTree.verify` satisfies it and can be passed around as a plain function.
</TypeScript>

## Light-client example

The server builds the tree and exports the root and a serialized proof. The client receives bytes,
decodes the proof, and verifies, with the tree long gone.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  /// What the server publishes: a root (e.g. in a block header) and proof bytes.
  struct Published {
      root: [u8; 32],
      proof_bytes: Vec<u8>,
  }

  fn server(transactions: &[&str], index: usize) -> Result<Published, MerkleError> {
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(transactions)?;
      let root = *tree.root().ok_or(MerkleError::EmptyTree)?;
      let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(index))?;
      Ok(Published { root, proof_bytes: proof.to_bytes()? })
      // `tree` is dropped here.
  }

  fn client(trusted_root: &[u8; 32], claimed_tx: &str, proof_bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<bool, MerkleError> {
      let proof = MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(proof_bytes)?;
      Ok(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(trusted_root, claimed_tx.as_bytes(), &proof))
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let txs = ["tx:alice->bob:100", "tx:bob->carol:50", "tx:carol->dave:25"];
      let published = server(&txs, 0)?;

      println!("proof is {} bytes", published.proof_bytes.len());
      assert!(client(&published.root, "tx:alice->bob:100", &published.proof_bytes)?);
      assert!(!client(&published.root, "tx:alice->bob:1000", &published.proof_bytes)?);
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  The repository ships the same flow as a runnable example:

  ```bash
  cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `encodeMerkleProof` and `decodeMerkleProof` use the same bytes as the Rust `to_bytes` /
  `from_bytes`, so either side can be written in either language.

  ```ts
  import { type Bytes, decodeMerkleProof, encodeMerkleProof, MerkleError, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  /** What the server publishes: a root (e.g. in a block header) and proof bytes. */
  interface Published {
    root: Bytes
    proofBytes: Bytes
  }

  function server(transactions: string[], index: number): Published {
    const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, transactions.map(utf8))
    const root = tree.root()
    if (!root) throw new MerkleError({ code: 'EmptyTree' })
    const proof = tree.generateProof(index)
    return { root, proofBytes: encodeMerkleProof(proof) }
    // `tree` is garbage once this returns.
  }

  function client(trustedRoot: Bytes, claimedTx: string, proofBytes: Bytes): boolean {
    const proof = decodeMerkleProof(proofBytes)
    return BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, trustedRoot, utf8(claimedTx), proof)
  }

  const txs = ['tx:alice->bob:100', 'tx:bob->carol:50', 'tx:carol->dave:25']
  const published = server(txs, 0)

  console.log(`proof is ${published.proofBytes.length} bytes`)
  console.assert(client(published.root, 'tx:alice->bob:100', published.proofBytes))
  console.assert(!client(published.root, 'tx:alice->bob:1000', published.proofBytes))
  ```

  `decodeMerkleProof` throws `DeserializationError` on malformed bytes. A runnable TypeScript
  version of the server/client split is on the [Examples](/examples) page.
</TypeScript>

Try it interactively on the [light-client demo](/demo/light-client): change the claimed value and watch verification
fail.

## Verifying on-chain

<Rust>
  The Rust crates have no Solidity helpers. The Solidity verifier contracts and the functions that
  format proofs for them ship with the TypeScript packages; switch to **TypeScript** to see them.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The TypeScript packages can also format a proof for the Solidity verifier contracts
  (`MerkleForgeBinary`, `MerkleForgeSparse`) in
  [contracts/](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/contracts).
  `toSolidityBinaryProof`, `toSolidityBinaryMultiProof`, and `toSoliditySparseProof` from
  `@merkleforge/variants` turn proofs into `bigint` and `0x` hex arguments ready for viem or ethers.
  The contracts hash with Keccak-256, so the tree must use `Keccak256`.

  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree, toSolidityBinaryProof } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  // The Solidity verifiers hash with Keccak-256, so build the tree with Keccak256.
  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, ['alice:100', 'bob:250', 'carol:75'].map(utf8))

  const args = toSolidityBinaryProof(tree.generateProof(0))
  // { leafIndex: 0n, leafCount: 3n, siblings: ['0x…', '0x…'] }, ready for viem or ethers
  console.assert(args.leafCount === 3n && args.siblings.length === 2)
  ```

  `toSoliditySparseProof` also compresses a sparse proof: empty siblings are dropped and marked in a
  bitmap, so calldata holds only real hashes.
</TypeScript>

## What a verifier must trust

* **The root.** A proof only shows that a leaf is consistent with *some* root. Get the root from a
  trusted source: a block header, a signed checkpoint, a contract.
* **The leaf encoding.** Verify the exact bytes that were inserted. Agree on a canonical encoding
  (field order, separators, number formats) between prover and verifier.
* **Not <Rust inline>`leaf_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`leafCount`</TypeScript>.** The binary
  root doesn't commit to
  <Rust inline>`MerkleProof::leaf_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`proof.leafCount`</TypeScript>.
  If the number of leaves matters, obtain it independently.
* **The key, for sparse proofs.** Use
  <Rust inline>`verify_membership`, which checks the proof's key. The deprecated
  `SparseMerkleTree::verify` does not.</Rust><TypeScript inline>`SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership`
  or `verifyNonMembership`, which check the proof's key against the key you pass.</TypeScript>

## Proof sizes

From the published comparison run on a 10,000-leaf tree:

| Library | Serialized proof size |
| --- | --- |
| MerkleForge | 469 bytes |
| `rs-merkle` | 448 bytes |
| `merkle_light` | 512 bytes |

A binary proof carries `⌈log₂ n⌉` 32-byte siblings plus a side tag each, the leaf index, and the
leaf count. <TypeScript inline>`encodeMerkleProof` produces the same bytes as the Rust crate, so
the MerkleForge size applies to both languages. </TypeScript>See
[Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization) for encoding options.

# Serialization

Proofs have two wire formats shared by both languages: a compact binary encoding
([`bincode`](https://crates.io/crates/bincode) 2, standard config) and a JSON shape (what
`serde_json` produces). A proof encoded in Rust decodes in TypeScript, and the other way round.

<LangBar />

<Rust>
  Proofs and trees implement `serde`'s `Serialize` and `Deserialize`. On top of that, `merkle-core`
  provides the `Serializable` trait with compact binary helpers backed by bincode.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Proofs are plain objects and trees are classes, so there is no `serde` or trait to derive.
  Instead, each proof type has a pair of explicit codecs for each format, all of which produce the
  same bytes or JSON as the Rust crates:

  | Proof | Binary (bincode) | Rust-compatible JSON |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `MerkleProof` (`@merkleforge/core`) | `encodeMerkleProof` / `decodeMerkleProof` | `merkleProofToSerdeJSON` / `merkleProofFromSerdeJSON` |
  | `SparseMerkleProof` | `encodeSparseProof` / `decodeSparseProof` | `sparseProofToSerdeJSON` / `sparseProofFromSerdeJSON` |
  | `MptProof` | `encodeMptProof` / `decodeMptProof` | `mptProofToSerdeJSON` / `mptProofFromSerdeJSON` |
  | `BinaryMultiProof` | `encodeBinaryMultiProof` / `decodeBinaryMultiProof` | `multiProofToSerdeJSON` / `multiProofFromSerdeJSON` |

  The sparse, Patricia, and multiproof codecs are exported from `@merkleforge/variants`. Decoders
  take an optional `digestSize` (default 32) where the proof holds fixed-size digests.
</TypeScript>

## The `Serializable` trait

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::error::MerkleError;

  pub trait Serializable: Sized {
      fn to_bytes(&self) -> Result<Vec<u8>, MerkleError>;
      fn from_bytes(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, MerkleError>;
      fn serialized_size(&self) -> Result<usize, MerkleError> {
          Ok(self.to_bytes()?.len())
      }
  }
  ```

  A blanket implementation covers **every** type that is `Serialize + DeserializeOwned`, so you
  never implement it by hand. Errors map to `MerkleError::SerializationError` and
  `MerkleError::DeserializationError`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The trait is Rust only. Its TypeScript counterpart is the `encode*` / `decode*` codecs above:
  `encodeMerkleProof(proof)` returns the same bytes as Rust's `proof.to_bytes()`, and
  `decodeMerkleProof(bytes)` reads them. For the size, take `.length` of the encoded bytes.
  Malformed input throws `MerkleError` with code `DeserializationError`. Unlike Rust's `from_bytes`,
  the decoders also reject trailing bytes after the proof.
</TypeScript>

## Proofs

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["alice", "bob", "carol", "dave"])?;
      let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(2))?;

      let bytes = proof.to_bytes()?;
      let recovered = MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(&bytes)?;
      assert_eq!(proof, recovered);
      println!("{} bytes", proof.serialized_size()?);

      // Garbage input is an error, not a panic.
      assert!(MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(b"not a proof").is_err());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  `SparseMerkleProof<D>` and `MptProof<D>` work the same way.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { decodeMerkleProof, encodeMerkleProof, isMerkleError, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dave'].map(utf8))
  const proof = tree.generateProof(2)

  // Same bytes as the Rust proof.to_bytes().
  const bytes = encodeMerkleProof(proof)
  const recovered = decodeMerkleProof(bytes)
  console.assert(BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, tree.root()!, utf8('carol'), recovered))
  console.log(`${bytes.length} bytes`)

  // Garbage input throws a MerkleError, not some other exception.
  try {
    decodeMerkleProof(utf8('not a proof'))
    console.assert(false)
  } catch (error) {
    console.assert(isMerkleError(error, 'DeserializationError'))
  }
  ```

  `encodeSparseProof` / `decodeSparseProof` and `encodeMptProof` / `decodeMptProof` work the same way.
</TypeScript>

## Any serde format

<Rust>
  Because the types are plain `serde` types, you can use JSON, CBOR, or anything else. With
  [`serde_json`](https://crates.io/crates/serde_json):

  ```rust
  use merkle_variants::{SparseMerkleTree, sparse::SparseMerkleProof};
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
      let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      state.insert([7_u8; 32], b"balance:100")?;
      let proof = state.generate_membership_proof([7_u8; 32])?;

      let json = serde_json::to_string(&proof)?;
      let decoded: SparseMerkleProof<[u8; 32]> = serde_json::from_str(&json)?;
      assert_eq!(proof, decoded);
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  :::tip
  JSON encodes `[u8; 32]` as an array of numbers. A TypeScript client reads that shape directly with
  `@merkleforge/variants` (`sparseProofFromSerdeJSON` and friends). For other languages, define a
  small wire format with hex strings and convert at the boundary.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `JSON.stringify` on a proof object does not give you a portable format (`Uint8Array` fields
  become `{"0": …}` objects). Convert with the `*ToSerdeJSON` helpers first: they produce exactly
  the objects `serde_json` writes for the Rust types (snake_case fields, bytes as arrays of numbers,
  `"Left"` / `"Right"` sides), so a Rust service can read them with `serde_json::from_str`.

  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import {
    SparseMerkleTree,
    sparseProofFromSerdeJSON,
    sparseProofToSerdeJSON,
  } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const state = new SparseMerkleTree(Sha256)
  const key = new Uint8Array(32).fill(7)
  state.insert(key, utf8('balance:100'))
  const proof = state.generateMembershipProof(key)

  // The same JSON as serde_json::to_string(&proof) in Rust.
  const json = JSON.stringify(sparseProofToSerdeJSON(proof))
  const decoded = sparseProofFromSerdeJSON(JSON.parse(json))
  console.assert(
    SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(Sha256, state.root()!, key, utf8('balance:100'), decoded),
  )
  ```

  For CBOR, MessagePack, or another format, encode the same `*ToSerdeJSON` object with the library of
  your choice, or send the bincode bytes.
</TypeScript>

## Trees

`BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`, and `MerklePatriciaTrie` serialize compactly. The encoding
stores only:

| Tree | Stored |
| --- | --- |
| `BinaryMerkleTree` | Hash algorithm name + leaf hashes |
| `SparseMerkleTree` | Hash algorithm name + `(key, leaf hash)` pairs in key order |
| `MerklePatriciaTrie` | Hash algorithm name + `(key, value)` entries in key order |

<TypeScript>
  In TypeScript, each tree has `toJSON()` (so `JSON.stringify(tree)` works) and a static
  `fromJSON(hasher, json)`. The JSON is `{ hashAlgorithm, leaves }` (binary and sparse) or
  `{ hashAlgorithm, entries }` (Patricia), with every byte string as `0x` hex. This tree format is
  TypeScript's own: it is not the Rust serde or bincode tree encoding, so move proofs (not whole
  trees) between the two languages, or rebuild the tree from its leaves.
</TypeScript>

Internal nodes are **recomputed** on load, so a decoded tree is always internally consistent.
Deserialization rejects data written with a different hash algorithm.

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Sha256};

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["alice", "bob", "carol"])?;
      tree.remove(LeafIndex(1))?;

      let bytes = tree.to_bytes()?;
      let restored = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_bytes(&bytes)?;
      assert_eq!(restored.root(), tree.root());
      assert_eq!(restored.leaf_count(), tree.leaf_count());

      // Bytes from a SHA-256 tree can't be loaded as a BLAKE3 tree.
      assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::from_bytes(&bytes).is_err());
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  :::note
  Tree `Serialize` / `Deserialize` (and `Clone` / `Debug`) were added in v0.5.0. Proof
  serialization is available in earlier releases too.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { bytesEqual, isMerkleError, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Blake3, Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'].map(utf8))
  tree.remove(1)

  // toJSON() makes JSON.stringify work directly; leaf hashes are hex strings.
  const json = JSON.stringify(tree)
  const restored = BinaryMerkleTree.fromJSON(Sha256, JSON.parse(json))
  console.assert(bytesEqual(restored.root()!, tree.root()!))
  console.assert(restored.leafCount === tree.leafCount)

  // JSON from a SHA-256 tree can't be loaded as a BLAKE3 tree.
  try {
    BinaryMerkleTree.fromJSON(Blake3, JSON.parse(json))
    console.assert(false)
  } catch (error) {
    console.assert(isMerkleError(error, 'DeserializationError'))
  }
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Metadata

<Rust>
  `TreeMetadata` implements `Serialize` and `Deserialize`, but its string fields are
  `&'static str`, so it can't be deserialized from an owned buffer and is **not** `Serializable`.
  Serialize it for logs and dashboards, for example with `serde_json::to_string(&tree.metadata())`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `TreeMetadata` is a plain object, so `JSON.stringify(tree.metadata())` works and `JSON.parse`
  reads it back. Its keys are camelCase (`leafCount`, `nodeCount`, …), not the snake_case keys Rust
  writes.
</TypeScript>

See [Metadata](/docs/guides/metadata).

# Metadata

Every tree returns a `TreeMetadata` snapshot through the
<Rust inline>`MerkleTree` trait</Rust><TypeScript inline>`MerkleTree` interface</TypeScript>. It is
cheap to build and useful for logging, dashboards, health checks, and benchmarks.

<LangBar />

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <Rust inline>`leaf_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`leafCount`</TypeScript> | <Rust inline>`usize`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`number`</TypeScript> | Logical leaves stored |
| `height` | <Rust inline>`usize`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`number`</TypeScript> | `0` for an empty tree, `1` for a single leaf |
| <Rust inline>`node_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`nodeCount`</TypeScript> | <Rust inline>`usize`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`number`</TypeScript> | Allocated or materialized nodes (see below) |
| <Rust inline>`hash_algorithm`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hashAlgorithm`</TypeScript> | <Rust inline>`&'static str`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`string`</TypeScript> | <Rust inline>`H::algorithm_name()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`hasher.algorithmName`</TypeScript>, e.g. `"SHA-256"` |
| `variant` | <Rust inline>`&'static str`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`string`</TypeScript> | `"BinaryMerkleTree"`, `"SparseMerkleTree"`, or `"MerklePatriciaTrie"` |

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])?;
      let metadata = tree.metadata();

      println!("variant: {}", metadata.variant);
      println!("algorithm: {}", metadata.hash_algorithm);
      println!("leaves: {}", metadata.leaf_count);
      println!("height: {}", metadata.height);
      println!("allocated nodes: {}", metadata.node_count);

      assert_eq!(metadata.variant, "BinaryMerkleTree");
      assert_eq!(metadata.hash_algorithm, "SHA-256");
      assert_eq!(metadata.leaf_count, 5);
      assert_eq!(metadata.height, 4); // 5 leaves pad to 8: 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1
      assert_eq!(metadata.node_count, 15); // 8 + 4 + 2 + 1
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  `metadata()` is a trait method, so bring `MerkleTree` into scope (the prelude does).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'].map(utf8))
  const metadata = tree.metadata()

  console.log('variant:', metadata.variant)
  console.log('algorithm:', metadata.hashAlgorithm)
  console.log('leaves:', metadata.leafCount)
  console.log('height:', metadata.height)
  console.log('allocated nodes:', metadata.nodeCount)

  console.assert(metadata.variant === 'BinaryMerkleTree')
  console.assert(metadata.hashAlgorithm === 'SHA-256')
  console.assert(metadata.leafCount === 5)
  console.assert(metadata.height === 4) // 5 leaves pad to 8: 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1
  console.assert(metadata.nodeCount === 15) // 8 + 4 + 2 + 1
  ```

  `metadata()` is a method on every tree class (and on `indexed()` views), so no import is needed
  beyond the tree itself.
</TypeScript>

## What `node_count` means per variant

* **Binary:** the length of the flat node array, padding included (`2 × capacity − 1`).
* **Sparse:** materialized storage entries (internal, shortcut, and batch nodes). Thanks to
  shortcut and batch compression this is far smaller than 256 per leaf. Compare with
  <Rust inline>`stored_node_count()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`storedNodeCount`</TypeScript> and <Rust inline>`unbatched_node_count_estimate()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`unbatchedNodeCountEstimate()`</TypeScript>.
* **Patricia:** materialized trie nodes, also available as <Rust inline>`node_count()`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`nodeCount`</TypeScript>.

## Serializing metadata

<Rust>
  `TreeMetadata` implements `Serialize`, so you can log it as JSON:

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Blake3;

  fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
      let mut tree = SparseMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();
      tree.insert([1_u8; 32], b"value")?;

      let json = serde_json::to_string(&tree.metadata())?;
      assert!(json.contains("\"variant\":\"SparseMerkleTree\""));
      println!("{json}");
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  Because its string fields are `&'static str`, `TreeMetadata` can't be deserialized from an owned
  buffer. Treat it as output only.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `TreeMetadata` is a plain object, so `JSON.stringify` logs it directly:

  ```ts
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Blake3 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { SparseMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = new SparseMerkleTree(Blake3)
  tree.insert(new Uint8Array(32).fill(1), utf8('value'))

  const json = JSON.stringify(tree.metadata())
  console.assert(json.includes('"variant":"SparseMerkleTree"'))
  console.log(json) // keys are camelCase: leafCount, nodeCount, hashAlgorithm
  ```

  The JSON keys are camelCase (`leafCount`, `nodeCount`, `hashAlgorithm`), while Rust's
  `serde_json` writes snake_case (`leaf_count`, …). Rename the keys if a dashboard reads both. Unlike
  Rust, `JSON.parse` reads it back without restriction.
</TypeScript>

# Errors

Fallible MerkleForge operations report a `MerkleError`. Verification functions return a boolean
instead: a bad proof is an expected outcome, not an error.

<LangBar />

<Rust>
  Every fallible MerkleForge API returns `Result<T, MerkleError>`.

  `MerkleError` lives in `merkle_core::error` (and the prelude). It implements `Debug`, `Clone`,
  `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Display`, and, with the default `std` feature, `std::error::Error`, so it works
  with `?`, `Box<dyn Error>`, `anyhow`, and `thiserror`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Every fallible MerkleForge API throws a `MerkleError`. It is exported from `@merkleforge/core` and
  extends the built-in `Error`, so `try`/`catch`, `instanceof Error`, and error reporting tools work
  as usual. Each error carries a `detail` object whose `code` names the case (also available as
  `error.code`), plus that case's fields. `isMerkleError(error, code?)` is a type guard that narrows
  `detail` to the given code.
</TypeScript>

## Variants

<Rust>
  | Variant | Raised when |
  | --- | --- |
  | `EmptyTree` | Proof generation (or binary `remove`) on a tree with no leaves |
  | `IndexOutOfBounds { index, len }` | A `LeafIndex` past the last logical leaf |
  | `InvalidProof` | Available to APIs that report failed verification as an error (the shipped verifiers return `false` instead) |
  | `InvalidProofStructure(String)` | A proof's shape is inconsistent (e.g. sparse proof generation with a non-256 depth) |
  | `EmptyLeafData` | Inserting an empty value (empty data would be indistinguishable from padding) |
  | `SerializationError(String)` | `to_bytes` failed |
  | `DeserializationError(String)` | `from_bytes` got malformed data |
  | `HashError(String)` | An internal hashing step failed (for custom adapters; not raised by the shipped ones) |
  | `UnsupportedOperation(&'static str)` | The variant can't do this, e.g. removing a missing sparse or Patricia key, or index-based Patricia proofs |
  | `RlpError(String)` | Malformed RLP or hex-prefix data in the Patricia trie |
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The codes and messages match the Rust variants. Rust's tuple payloads become named fields.

  | `detail` | Raised when |
  | --- | --- |
  | `{ code: 'EmptyTree' }` | Proof generation (or binary `remove`) on a tree with no leaves |
  | `{ code: 'IndexOutOfBounds', index, len }` | A leaf index past the last logical leaf, negative, or not an integer |
  | `{ code: 'InvalidProof' }` | A witness doesn't connect to the root in APIs that return the proven value, such as `MerklePatriciaTrie.proveValue` and `@merkleforge/ethereum` (the `verify*` functions return `false` instead) |
  | `{ code: 'InvalidProofStructure', reason }` | A proof's shape is inconsistent (e.g. `generateMultiProof` with no indices) |
  | `{ code: 'EmptyLeafData' }` | Inserting an empty value (empty data would be indistinguishable from padding) |
  | `{ code: 'SerializationError', reason }` | Reserved for parity with Rust; the shipped encoders don't fail |
  | `{ code: 'DeserializationError', reason }` | `decode*`, `*FromSerdeJSON`, or `fromJSON` got malformed data, or JSON written with a different hash |
  | `{ code: 'HashError', reason }` | For custom adapters; not raised by the shipped ones |
  | `{ code: 'UnsupportedOperation', operation }` | The variant can't do this, e.g. removing a missing sparse or Patricia key, or index-based Patricia proofs |
  | `{ code: 'RlpError', reason }` | Malformed RLP or hex-prefix data in the Patricia trie |

  Misusing a helper outside the tree types, such as passing an odd-length string to `fromHex`, throws
  a plain `TypeError` or `RangeError` instead.
</TypeScript>

## Handling errors

<Rust>
  `MerkleError` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: new variants may arrive in minor releases, so keep a
  fallback arm.

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn describe(result: Result<MerkleProof<[u8; 32]>, MerkleError>) -> String {
      match result {
          Ok(proof) => format!("proof with {} siblings", proof.depth()),
          Err(MerkleError::EmptyTree) => "tree has no leaves".into(),
          Err(MerkleError::IndexOutOfBounds { index, len }) => {
              format!("leaf {index} is outside the current leaf count {len}")
          }
          Err(MerkleError::EmptyLeafData) => "empty leaves are rejected".into(),
          Err(other) => other.to_string(),
      }
  }

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
      assert_eq!(describe(tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))), "tree has no leaves");

      tree.insert(b"alice")?;
      assert_eq!(
          describe(tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(3))),
          "leaf 3 is outside the current leaf count 1",
      );
      assert_eq!(describe(tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))), "proof with 0 siblings");
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Switch on `error.detail.code`; TypeScript narrows `detail` in each case. New codes may arrive in
  minor releases, so keep a `default` branch, and rethrow anything that isn't a `MerkleError`.

  ```ts
  import { isMerkleError, type MerkleProof, proofDepth, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  function describe(attempt: () => MerkleProof): string {
    try {
      return `proof with ${proofDepth(attempt())} siblings`
    } catch (error) {
      if (!isMerkleError(error)) throw error
      switch (error.detail.code) {
        case 'EmptyTree':
          return 'tree has no leaves'
        case 'IndexOutOfBounds':
          return `leaf ${error.detail.index} is outside the current leaf count ${error.detail.len}`
        case 'EmptyLeafData':
          return 'empty leaves are rejected'
        default:
          return error.message
      }
    }
  }

  const tree = new BinaryMerkleTree(Sha256)
  console.assert(describe(() => tree.generateProof(0)) === 'tree has no leaves')

  tree.insert(utf8('alice'))
  console.assert(
    describe(() => tree.generateProof(3)) === 'leaf 3 is outside the current leaf count 1',
  )
  console.assert(describe(() => tree.generateProof(0)) === 'proof with 0 siblings')
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Display messages

<Rust>
  ```rust
  use merkle_core::error::MerkleError;

  fn main() {
      let err = MerkleError::IndexOutOfBounds { index: 5, len: 3 };
      assert_eq!(err.to_string(), "index 5 is out of bounds for a tree with 3 leaves");
      assert_eq!(MerkleError::EmptyLeafData.to_string(), "leaf data must not be empty");
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `error.message` holds the same text as the Rust `Display` output, and `error.name` is
  `'MerkleError'`.

  ```ts
  import { MerkleError } from '@merkleforge/core'

  const err = new MerkleError({ code: 'IndexOutOfBounds', index: 5, len: 3 })
  console.assert(err.message === 'index 5 is out of bounds for a tree with 3 leaves')
  console.assert(new MerkleError({ code: 'EmptyLeafData' }).message === 'leaf data must not be empty')
  ```
</TypeScript>

## Generic error handling

<Rust>
  `MerkleError` implements `std::error::Error`, so it converts into `Box<dyn Error>` with `?`:

  ```rust
  use std::error::Error;

  use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
  use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
      let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
      trie.insert(b"key", b"value")?;

      // Removing a key that isn't there is an error.
      let err = trie.remove(b"missing").unwrap_err();
      println!("{err}");
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Because `MerkleError` extends `Error`, code that only handles errors generically needs nothing
  MerkleForge-specific:

  ```ts
  import { MerkleError, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { MerklePatriciaTrie } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const trie = new MerklePatriciaTrie(Keccak256)
  trie.insert(utf8('key'), utf8('value'))

  // Removing a key that isn't there is an error.
  try {
    trie.remove(utf8('missing'))
  } catch (error) {
    console.assert(error instanceof MerkleError && error instanceof Error)
    console.log(`${error}`)
  }
  ```

  This prints
  `MerkleError: operation 'remove missing Patricia key' is not supported for this tree variant`.
</TypeScript>

# no_std

<LangBar />

<TypeScript>
  :::info
  This page is about the Rust crates. The TypeScript packages have no `std` / `no_std` split: they are
  plain ESM with one runtime dependency ([`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes))
  and run unchanged in Node.js, browsers, Deno, Bun, and edge or worker runtimes. To verify proofs on
  a constrained device, use the Rust crates below, or verify on-chain with the Solidity verifiers in
  [MerkleForge-ts/contracts](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/contracts).
  :::
</TypeScript>

`merkle-core`, the crate with the traits, proof types, and errors, supports `no_std` targets with
a global allocator. That lets embedded devices, enclaves, and WebAssembly modules share proof types
with your servers and implement their own verifiers.

## Feature flags

| Feature | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `std` | Yes | Standard-library integration, including `std::error::Error` for `MerkleError`. Implies `alloc`. |
| `alloc` | Via `std` | Heap-backed types (`Vec`, `String`) for `no_std` builds. Required. |

Disabling both is a compile error: proofs need `Vec`.

```toml [Cargo.toml]
[dependencies]
merkle-core = { version = "0.5.2", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```

Check a bare-metal build from the repository:

```bash
rustup target add thumbv7em-none-eabihf
cargo check -p merkle-core \
  --no-default-features \
  --features alloc \
  --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf
```

## What is available without `std`

Everything in `merkle-core`: `HashFunction`, `MerkleTree`, `ProofVerifier`, `Serializable`
(bincode), `MerkleProof`, `ProofNode`, `ProofSide`, `LeafIndex`, `NodeIndex`, `TreeMetadata`, and
`MerkleError` (without the `std::error::Error` impl).

:::warning
`merkleforge-hash` and `merkle-variants` currently depend on `merkle-core` with default features
and use `std` (the sparse tree uses `std::collections::HashMap`), so they are **std-only**. On a
`no_std` target, depend on `merkle-core` alone and supply a `HashFunction` adapter and verifier.
:::

## A no_std verifier

This verifier uses only `merkle-core` types and `core`, so it compiles in a `#![no_std]` crate with
`alloc`. It follows the same algorithm as `BinaryMerkleTree::verify`. Shown here with a host-side
`main` that cross-checks it against the real tree:

```rust
use merkle_core::{
    traits::HashFunction,
    types::{MerkleProof, ProofSide},
};

/// Stateless binary-proof check using only merkle-core.
pub fn verify_binary<H: HashFunction>(
    expected_root: &H::Digest,
    leaf_data: &[u8],
    proof: &MerkleProof<H::Digest>,
) -> bool {
    if leaf_data.is_empty() || proof.leaf_index.value() >= proof.leaf_count {
        return false;
    }
    let Some(capacity) = proof.leaf_count.checked_next_power_of_two() else {
        return false;
    };
    if proof.path.len() != capacity.ilog2() as usize {
        return false;
    }

    let mut current = H::hash(leaf_data);
    let mut offset = proof.leaf_index.value();
    for node in &proof.path {
        let expected = if offset % 2 == 0 { ProofSide::Right } else { ProofSide::Left };
        if node.side != expected {
            return false;
        }
        current = match node.side {
            ProofSide::Left => H::hash_nodes(&node.hash, &current),
            ProofSide::Right => H::hash_nodes(&current, &node.hash),
        };
        offset /= 2;
    }
    current == *expected_root
}

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    use merkle_core::types::LeafIndex;
    use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
    use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c"])?;
    let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(2))?;
    assert!(verify_binary::<Sha256>(root, b"c", &proof));
    assert!(!verify_binary::<Sha256>(root, b"x", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

On the device, provide a `HashFunction` implementation backed by a `no_std` hash crate (for
example `sha2` with `default-features = false`), following the
[custom adapter guide](/docs/guides/hash-functions#writing-a-custom-adapter).

# Benchmarks

The Rust crates and the TypeScript packages are benchmarked separately, each with its own harness.
Lower latency is better; higher throughput is better. Results are hardware-specific: compare
trends across machines, not absolute values.

<LangBar />

<Rust>
  MerkleForge uses [Criterion](https://crates.io/crates/criterion) benchmarks in the unpublished
  `merkle-bench` crate to compare hash adapters, tree variants, proof generation, proof
  verification, and other Rust Merkle libraries. Criterion reports mean, median, and standard
  deviation to filter out noise. For the latest CI numbers with links to every Criterion report, see
  the [live benchmark explorer](/benchmarks).

  :::note
  The tables below are copied from [`BENCHMARKS.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)
  (run date 2026-08-17). That run predates the v0.5.0 sparse-tree and Patricia-trie
  performance fixes, which cut 4,000 sequential sparse inserts from about 223 s to 0.2 s and
  4,000 Patricia inserts from about 5.9 s to 0.02 s. Sparse and Patricia numbers here are therefore
  pessimistic. Cells marked *not captured* were not completed in that run. The comparison with
  `rs-merkle` and `merkle_light` was rerun on 2026-11-06 for 0.5.2.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The TypeScript packages are compared with other JavaScript Merkle tree libraries:
  [`@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/merkle-tree),
  [`merkletreejs`](https://github.com/merkletreejs/merkletreejs),
  [`@aztec/merkle-tree`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@aztec/merkle-tree), and
  [`@aztec/world-state`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@aztec/world-state). The suite lives in
  [`bench/`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/bench) in the MerkleForge-ts
  repository. All numbers come from one run on one machine, so read them as ratios, not absolutes.
  The same results are on the [benchmarks page](/benchmarks#typescript).

  :::note
  The tables below are copied from
  [`BENCHMARKS.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md) in the
  MerkleForge-ts repository (MerkleForge 0.2.3, run date 2026-11-01).
  :::
</TypeScript>

## Faster than what?

<Rust>
  Measured 2026-11-06 for MerkleForge 0.5.2 (i7-1185G7, 4 cores / 8 threads, rustc 1.97.1), SHA-256 everywhere, the same 32-byte leaves for every library, Criterion medians. Every ratio is MerkleForge against the named library, same operation, same leaves, same hash, same run. The libraries produce different roots (MerkleForge domain-separates leaves and nodes), so this compares speed for the same job, not identical output.

  Against [`rs-merkle`](https://crates.io/crates/rs_merkle) 1.5, at 1,048,576 leaves:

  | Operation | MerkleForge | `rs-merkle` | Faster | Threads (MerkleForge / rs-merkle) |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
  | Generate one proof | 191 ns | 2.26 µs | **11.8x** | 1 / 1 |
  | Generate a multiproof (100 leaves) | 8.1 µs | 48.3 µs | **6.0x** | 1 / 1 |
  | Build the tree (`parallel` feature) | 72.3 ms | 458 ms | **6.3x** | 8 / 1 |
  | Verify 10,000 proofs (`verify_batch`, `parallel`) | 6.1 ms | 89.0 ms | **14.5x** | 8 / 1 |
  | Verify 10,000 proofs (`verify_batch`, one thread) | 19.3 ms | 88.7 ms | **4.6x** | 1 / 1 |
  | Verify one proof | 1.86 µs | 8.36 µs | **4.5x** | 1 / 1 |
  | Build the tree (one thread) | 183 ms | 437 ms | **2.4x** | 1 / 1 |
  | Verify a multiproof (100 leaves) | 144 µs | 290 µs | **2.0x** | 1 / 1 |

  Against [`merkle_light`](https://crates.io/crates/merkle_light) at 1,048,576
  leaves, MerkleForge builds **2.7x** faster and verifies 10,000 proofs **3.7x**
  faster with `parallel`; single-threaded, the two are within about 20% on every
  operation. `merkle_light` has no multiproofs.

  What favours whom:

  * MerkleForge hashes every leaf with a `0x00` prefix and every node with a
    `0x01` prefix, which blocks second-preimage attacks. That is extra work the
    other libraries skip, and it is counted in MerkleForge's times.
  * `rs-merkle` is given its leaves already hashed in verification (its API
    takes leaf hashes); MerkleForge hashes the raw leaf inside `verify`. In
    construction, `rs-merkle`'s leaf hashing is timed.
  * Rows marked 8 threads use the `parallel` feature (rayon) on this 4-core
    laptop; the other libraries have no multi-threaded build or batch verifier.
    The one-thread rows are the like-for-like comparison.

  Full tables and caveats: [`BENCHMARKS.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md#faster-than-what) in the Rust repository.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Every TypeScript speed ratio names its baseline. There are three, and they are never mixed:

  | Baseline | What is compared | Headline (131,072 leaves) |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | **Another JavaScript library** | `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` against [`@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/merkle-tree) 1.0.8, the library it replaces, on the same leaves in the same run | builds 8–15x faster across sizes; 12.3x for an `[address, uint256]` airdrop tree (1,708 ms vs 21,021 ms), with byte-for-byte identical output |
  | **The previous MerkleForge release** | 0.2.3 against 0.2.2, same harness and machine | `BinaryMerkleTree` with `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` builds 5x faster (485 ms to 98 ms) |
  | **A Keccak-256 implementation** | `keccak256` from `@merkleforge/hash` against `keccak_256` from `@noble/hashes` | about 2x faster per hash, identical digests |

  **There is no speed claim against the Rust crates.** The TypeScript packages are a port of them and
  are checked against them for identical output, not raced against them.
</TypeScript>

## Parity: same bytes first

<Rust>
  The Rust crates are the reference implementation. The TypeScript packages are checked against them
  byte for byte, live, in the TypeScript repository's CI: roots and the bincode bytes of every
  sampled proof for Keccak-256 and SHA-256 trees of up to 131,072 leaves, plus generated test vectors
  for every tree, proof, and codec. Switch to TypeScript above for the full table.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  A speedup only counts if the output is the same. `bench/parity.mjs` builds the benchmark's own
  trees (the same leaves that are timed) and compares the output byte for byte with OpenZeppelin,
  `@noble/hashes`, and the Rust crates, which it runs live. It runs in CI on every pull request and
  fails the build on any difference.

  | MerkleForge | Compared with | Leaves | What must match | Result |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `keccak256` (@merkleforge/hash) | `keccak_256` (@noble/hashes 2.4.0) | — | 101,025 digests, lengths 0–1024 + random | identical |
  | `SimpleMerkleTree` (@merkleforge/openzeppelin) | @openzeppelin/merkle-tree 1.0.8 | 1,024, 16,384, 131,072 | root, full dump (every node), 2000 proofs, 1 multiproof | identical |
  | `StandardMerkleTree` (@merkleforge/openzeppelin) | @openzeppelin/merkle-tree 1.0.8 | 1,024, 16,384, 131,072 | root, full dump (every node), 2000 proofs, 1 multiproof | identical |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree` + @merkleforge/hash-wasm | `BinaryMerkleTree` + @merkleforge/hash (pure JS) | 1,024, 16,384, 131,072 | root, 2000 encoded proofs | identical |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree` Keccak-256 (@merkleforge/variants) | Rust `merkle-variants` `BinaryMerkleTree` | 1,024, 16,384, 131,072 | root, bincode bytes of 2000 proofs | identical |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree` SHA-256 (@merkleforge/variants) | Rust `merkle-variants` `BinaryMerkleTree` | 1,024, 16,384, 131,072 | root, bincode bytes of 2000 proofs | identical |

  16 checks, all identical. Node v24.15.0, run 2026-11-06.

  The unit tests add property tests against the real `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree` (150 random trees
  per tree type, random leaf types, values, and sizes), test vectors generated by the Rust crates for
  every tree, proof, multiproof, and codec (`serde_json` and bincode), and the Solidity verifiers
  checked with Foundry against fixtures produced by the TypeScript packages.

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts.git
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git      # the Rust crates, next to it
  cd MerkleForge-ts && pnpm install && pnpm build
  cd bench && npm install
  npm run parity    # about 45 s; exits non-zero on any difference (RUST=0 skips the Rust rows)
  ```
</TypeScript>
