## What is measured

<Rust>
  Each table below names the Criterion benchmark that produced it. Latency is the time for one
  operation; construction builds a fresh tree from the given number of leaves.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Each library builds a tree from the same random 32-byte leaves, generates proofs for the same
  2,000 random leaves, and verifies every proof (a run fails if any proof does not verify). Build
  time is the median of 3 builds; proof and verify times are the mean per operation after a warm-up.
  Database setup (Aztec) is not counted.

  Sizes are powers of two, so the fixed-depth Aztec trees are full and have the same depth as the
  other trees, except `@aztec/world-state`, whose note hash tree is always 42 levels deep.

  What differs between libraries, so the numbers are not like for like:

  * **Hash.** OpenZeppelin, merkletreejs, and one Aztec `StandardTree` run use Keccak-256 from
    `@noble/hashes`; MerkleForge uses its own pure-JS Keccak-256 (identical digests, see
    [Parity](#parity-same-bytes-first)) or WebAssembly where noted. The other Aztec runs use Poseidon2,
    a SNARK-friendly hash that costs more per call in JavaScript.
  * **Storage.** The Aztec trees keep nodes in LMDB and support commit, rollback, and snapshots.
    `@aztec/world-state` is Aztec's native C++ rollup state. The other libraries keep the tree in
    memory.
  * **Verification.** OpenZeppelin, merkletreejs, and MerkleForge verify with their own functions.
    The Aztec trees have no verifier on the tree, so their proofs are checked with Aztec's
    `computeRootFromSiblingPath` and Aztec's synchronous Poseidon2. For world-state that means 42
    Poseidon2 hashes in JavaScript per proof, which is why its verify column is high.
  * **Proof generation in the OpenZeppelin-compatible trees** re-verifies every proof before
    returning it (both libraries do this), so it is slower than in `BinaryMerkleTree`.
  * **Leaf hashing.** `BinaryMerkleTree` hashes every leaf with a domain prefix (`H(0x00 || leaf)`),
    which protects against second-preimage attacks. That is twice the hashing of merkletreejs, which
    uses leaves as nodes directly.
</TypeScript>

## Results

<Rust>
  **Hash function throughput** · `cargo bench --bench hash_throughput`

  | Algorithm | 32 B latency | 64 B latency | 1 MB throughput |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | SHA-256 | 109.60 ns | 177.40 ns | 1.28 GiB/s |
  | Keccak-256 | 1.23 µs | 660.99 ns | 291.12 MiB/s |
  | BLAKE3 | 230.70 ns | 247.83 ns | 5.99 GiB/s |

  **Binary Merkle tree** · `cargo bench --bench binary_tree`

  | Leaves | Construction (SHA-256) | Construction (BLAKE3) | Proof gen | Proof verify |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 100 | 147.19 µs | 140.96 µs | 45.22 ns | 1.09 µs |
  | 1,000 | 1.80 ms | 1.83 ms | 57.21 ns | 1.87 µs |
  | 10,000 | 30.53 ms | 39.07 ms | 74.18 ns | 2.06 µs |
  | 100,000 | 268.23 ms | 274.93 ms | 78.69 ns | 2.95 µs |

  Construction builds a fresh `BinaryMerkleTree<H>`. Proof generation uses `LeafIndex(0)`. Proof
  verification checks the proof against the recorded root and the original leaf bytes.

  **Sparse Merkle tree** · `cargo bench --bench sparse_tree` (SHA-256)

  | Existing keys | Insert | Proof gen | Proof verify | Non-membership proof | Non-membership verify |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 10 | 189.85 µs | 244.18 µs | 91.43 µs | 268.20 µs | 74.38 µs |
  | 100 | 2.11 ms | 2.25 ms | 75.74 µs | 2.32 ms | 76.86 µs |
  | 1,000 | 20.24 ms | 20.32 ms | 81.58 µs | 20.12 ms | 71.28 µs |
  | 10,000 | 181.05 ms | 198.84 ms | 63.00 µs | 203.49 ms | 76.41 µs |

  **Sparse Merkle tree, batch updates**

  | Batch size | Batch insert | Sequential insert | Speedup |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 10 | 288.97 µs | 1.53 ms | 5.30× |
  | 100 | 2.08 ms | 88.12 ms | 42.46× |
  | 1,000 | 20.33 ms | 8.69 s | 427.72× |

  **Merkle Patricia trie** · `cargo bench --bench patricia_trie` (Keccak-256)

  | Existing entries | Insert | Get | Proof gen | Proof verify |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 10 | 20.61 µs | 159.00 ns | not captured | not captured |
  | 100 | 217.63 µs | 200.07 ns | not captured | not captured |
  | 1,000 | 2.11 ms | 270.26 ns | not captured | not captured |
  | 10,000 | not captured | 387.44 ns | not captured | not captured |

  State-root timings (`patricia_trie/state_root`) were not captured in this run.

  **Energy-aware construction** · `cargo bench --bench bench_energy` builds a 100,000-leaf binary
  tree.

  | Algorithm | 100K construction time | CPU cycles | Package energy |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | SHA-256 | 463.52 ms | not captured | not captured |
  | Keccak-256 | 1.49 s | not captured | not captured |
  | BLAKE3 | 261.02 ms | not captured | not captured |

  These are Criterion wall-clock numbers only. See [Profiling & energy](/docs/performance/profiling)
  to collect RAPL counters.

  **MerkleForge, `rs-merkle`, and `merkle_light`** · `cargo bench -p merkle-bench --bench comparison` (2026-11-06)

  **10,000 leaves**

  | Operation | MerkleForge | MerkleForge `parallel` | `rs-merkle` | `merkle_light` |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | Build (`from_leaves`) | 1.59 ms | 1.20 ms | 3.02 ms | 1.73 ms |
  | Build (one `insert` at a time) | 13.6 ms | 14.6 ms | n/a | n/a |
  | Generate one proof | 193 ns | 172 ns | 1.61 µs | 181 ns |
  | Verify one proof | 1.46 µs | 1.36 µs | 5.93 µs | 1.57 µs |
  | Verify 10,000 proofs | 15.0 ms | 4.55 ms | 68.2 ms | 16.5 ms |
  | Generate a multiproof (100 leaves) | 3.89 µs | 4.29 µs | 24.5 µs | n/a |
  | Verify a multiproof (100 leaves) | 84.6 µs | 82.5 µs | 168 µs | n/a |

  **1,048,576 leaves**

  | Operation | MerkleForge | MerkleForge `parallel` | `rs-merkle` | `merkle_light` |
  | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
  | Build (`from_leaves`) | 183 ms | 72.3 ms | 437 ms | 196 ms |
  | Build (one `insert` at a time) | 2.01 s | 2.10 s | n/a | n/a |
  | Generate one proof | 191 ns | 193 ns | 2.26 µs | 261 ns |
  | Verify one proof | 2.33 µs | 1.86 µs | 8.63 µs | 2.15 µs |
  | Verify 10,000 proofs | 19.3 ms | 6.15 ms | 88.7 ms | 22.6 ms |
  | Generate a multiproof (100 leaves) | 8.11 µs | 7.88 µs | 48.3 µs | n/a |
  | Verify a multiproof (100 leaves) | 144 µs | 142 µs | 290 µs | n/a |

  The `rs-merkle` and `merkle_light` columns come from the single-thread run;
  their numbers in the `parallel` run were within noise (they do not use the
  feature). Proof sizes for a 10,000-leaf tree: MerkleForge 469 bytes,
  `rs-merkle` 448, `merkle_light` 512.
</Rust>

  | Library | Hash | Build (ms) | Proof (µs) | Verify (µs) |
  |---|---|---:|---:|---:|
  | @merkleforge/openzeppelin StandardMerkleTree | Keccak-256 (MerkleForge JS) | 196 | 53.6 | 55.1 |
  | @openzeppelin/merkle-tree StandardMerkleTree | Keccak-256 (noble) | 1960 | 283 | 270 |

  **OpenZeppelin `[address, uint256]` leaves, 131,072 leaves**

  | Library | Hash | Build (ms) | Proof (µs) | Verify (µs) |
  |---|---|---:|---:|---:|
  | @merkleforge/openzeppelin StandardMerkleTree | Keccak-256 (MerkleForge JS) | 1708 | 74.8 | 78.7 |
  | @openzeppelin/merkle-tree StandardMerkleTree | Keccak-256 (noble) | 21021 | 347 | 344 |

  Node v24.15.0, 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1185G7 @ 3.00GHz, linux 7.0.0-38-generic. Build is the median of 3 runs; proof and verify are the mean over 2000 random leaves.

  **Keccak-256 per call**

  Plain Keccak-256 (`keccak256` from `@merkleforge/hash`, no domain prefix)
  against `keccak_256` from `@noble/hashes` 2.4.0, on the input sizes trees hash:
  32-byte leaves, 33-byte prefixed leaves, 64- and 65-byte node pairs, and one
  full 136-byte block. Both produce the same digests; the script checks this
  before timing.

  | Input | @noble/hashes keccak_256 | @merkleforge/hash keccak256 | Speedup |
  |---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | 32 B | 7.00 µs | 3.25 µs | 2.2x |
  | 33 B | 8.86 µs | 3.32 µs | 2.7x |
  | 64 B | 7.85 µs | 3.37 µs | 2.3x |
  | 65 B | 7.57 µs | 3.43 µs | 2.2x |
  | 136 B | 14.44 µs | 5.30 µs | 2.7x |

  Node v24.15.0, 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1185G7 @ 3.00GHz, linux 7.0.0-38-generic. Median of 5 rounds of 200,000 calls per size.

  **Install footprint**

  Dependencies installed with each library, not counting the library itself,
  and the total size of the library plus its dependencies.

  | Library | Dependencies | Size |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | `@merkleforge/core` + `hash` + `variants` | 1 (`@noble/hashes`) | 1.4 MB |
  | `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` | 3 (`@merkleforge/core`, `@merkleforge/hash`, `@noble/hashes`) | 1.1 MB |
  | `merkletreejs` 0.6.0 | 3 | 1 MB |
  | `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree` 1.0.8 | 38 | 16 MB |
  | `@aztec/merkle-tree` 4.4.0 | 362 | 395 MB |
  | `@aztec/world-state` 5.2.1 | 377 | 1.1 GB |

  The Aztec packages bring Aztec's prover (`bb.js`), native bindings, LMDB, an
  HTTP server, and Ethereum tooling. They are built for running an Aztec node,
  not as general-purpose tree libraries.
</TypeScript>

## Reproduce

<Rust>
  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
  cd MerkleForge

  # Everything (long: the Patricia insert group alone can take many minutes)
  cargo bench --workspace
  xdg-open target/criterion/report/index.html   # `open` on macOS

  # Focused groups
  cargo bench --bench hash_throughput
  cargo bench --bench binary_tree
  cargo bench --bench sparse_tree
  cargo bench --bench patricia_trie
  cargo bench --bench comparison
  cargo bench --bench comparison --features parallel   # multi-threaded build and verify_batch
  COMPARISON_LEAVES=1048576 cargo bench --bench comparison
  cargo bench --bench bench_energy

  # Print comparative proof sizes
  MERKLEFORGE_PRINT_COMPARISON_SIZES=1 cargo bench --bench comparison -- --list
  ```

  Record the machine, kernel, CPU governor, Rust version, and command next to any numbers you
  publish.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts.git
  cd MerkleForge-ts
  pnpm install && pnpm build   # in the repo root
  cd bench
  npm install                  # comparison libraries, kept out of the pnpm workspace
  npm run bench                # writes results.json; SIZES, OPS, and BUILD_RUNS env vars adjust the run
  node report.mjs              # prints the tables above
  npm run bench:keccak         # Keccak-256 per call against @noble/hashes
  npm run parity               # byte-for-byte parity; needs the Rust repo cloned next to MerkleForge-ts
  ```

  The 0.2.2 comparison reruns the same harness at the `v0.2.2` tag; the steps are in
  [BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md#reproduce).

  Record the machine, Node.js version, and command next to any numbers you publish.
</TypeScript>

## Reading the tables

* **Latency:** time for one operation.
* **Throughput:** bytes or elements processed per second.
* **Proof generation:** time to produce the witness sent to a verifier.
* **Proof verification:** time for a stateless client to check the witness against a trusted root.
* **Proof size:** bytes sent over the network or stored as evidence.

# Profiling & energy

Benchmarks answer *how long did this take?* Profiling answers *where did the CPU time go?* Use the
tools below when investigating construction, proof generation, hashing, memory access, or trie
traversal bottlenecks.

<LangBar />

## Install tools

<Rust>
  All commands on this page run from the root of the
  [MerkleForge](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge) repository.

  ```bash
  make install-profiling-tools
  ```

  On Linux, `cargo-flamegraph` uses `perf`. Depending on your distribution:

  ```bash
  sudo apt install linux-tools-common linux-tools-generic
  ```

  If kernel settings block profiling, lower the restriction temporarily:

  ```bash
  sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Nothing to install: Node.js 22 and newer include the V8 CPU and heap profilers and the inspector
  used by Chrome DevTools. To profile the comparison suite, build the
  [MerkleForge-ts](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts) packages and install the
  `bench/` dependencies first:

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts.git
  cd MerkleForge-ts
  pnpm install && pnpm build
  cd bench
  npm install   # comparison libraries, kept out of the pnpm workspace
  ```

  To profile your own workload instead, write a small script that does only the work you care
  about, for example:

  ```js [build-tree.mjs]
  import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Keccak256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const leaves = Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, (_, i) => utf8(`leaf-${i}`))
  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, leaves)
  console.log(tree.root())
  ```
</TypeScript>

## CPU profiles and flamegraphs

<Rust>
  ```bash
  ./scripts/flamegraph.sh baseline_construction
  ```

  This writes `flamegraph.svg`. Open it in a browser and inspect the widest frames first; width is
  sampled CPU time. Useful targets: `baseline_construction`, `hash_throughput`, `binary_tree`,
  `sparse_tree`, `patricia_trie`, `comparison`.

  `profiling/flamegraph.svg` in the repository is a reference artifact showing the expected shape.
  Regenerate a machine-specific flamegraph before reporting numbers.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `--cpu-prof` starts the V8 CPU profiler and writes a `.cpuprofile` file to the current directory
  when the process exits:

  ```bash
  node --cpu-prof build-tree.mjs

  # The bench suite, from bench/ (npm run bench runs node --expose-gc run.mjs).
  # SIZES limits the tree sizes.
  SIZES=131072 node --expose-gc --cpu-prof run.mjs
  ```

  Open the `.cpuprofile` in the **Performance** panel of Chrome DevTools to see a flame chart, and
  inspect the widest frames first. The bench suite also runs the comparison libraries, so filter
  the profile to MerkleForge frames, or profile a script of your own.

  To profile interactively, start Node.js with the inspector and attach Chrome DevTools from
  `chrome://inspect`:

  ```bash
  node --inspect-brk build-tree.mjs
  ```

  `--inspect-brk` pauses before the first line so you can start recording first; `--inspect` starts
  without pausing.
</TypeScript>

## Hardware counters and memory

<Rust>
  ```bash
  perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references \
    cargo bench --bench hash_throughput
  ```

  Per tree:

  ```bash
  perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references cargo bench --bench binary_tree
  perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references cargo bench --bench sparse_tree
  perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references cargo bench --bench patricia_trie
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `--heap-prof` starts the V8 sampling heap profiler and writes a `.heapprofile` file when the process
  exits. Load it in the **Memory** panel of Chrome DevTools to see which functions allocated the
  most:

  ```bash
  node --heap-prof build-tree.mjs
  ```

  On Linux, `perf stat` counts cycles, instructions, and cache events around any process, including
  Node.js:

  ```bash
  perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references node build-tree.mjs
  ```

  The counts include V8 startup and JIT compilation, so compare runs of the same script.
</TypeScript>

## Energy

<TypeScript>
  :::note
  The energy workload and helper scripts below are part of the Rust repository. The `perf`,
  `turbostat`, and `powertop` commands measure any process, so you can replace the `cargo bench`
  command with a Node.js command such as `node build-tree.mjs`.
  :::
</TypeScript>

The default energy workload builds a 100,000-leaf binary tree with SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3.
Criterion measures wall-clock time; Linux `perf` collects CPU package energy externally.

```bash
cargo bench --bench bench_energy   # wall clock → target/criterion/bench_energy/
```

### RAPL counters with `perf`

On Intel and some AMD machines the kernel exposes RAPL counters through the `power/*` PMU. Check
support, then run the helper script:

```bash
perf list 'power/energy-*'
./scripts/energy-perf.sh bench_energy
```

The script collects `power/energy-pkg/` (package Joules), `power/energy-cores/` and
`power/energy-ram/` when available, `cycles`, `instructions`, `cache-references`, `cache-misses`,
and `duration_time`. Some machines need elevated privileges:

```bash
sudo ./scripts/energy-perf.sh bench_energy
# or
sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=0
```

Use the privileged path only on a machine you control. The explicit command behind the script:

```bash
sudo perf stat -a -r 3 \
  -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,duration_time,power/energy-pkg/ \
  -- cargo bench --bench bench_energy
```

`-a` records across all CPUs, which matters because package energy is a socket-level reading.

### Fallbacks

If `perf` doesn't show `power/energy-pkg/`, try `turbostat`:

```bash
sudo turbostat --Summary --Joules --out profiling/turbostat-energy.txt -- \
  cargo bench --bench bench_energy
```

`powertop` is less precise but can capture a repeatable system-level profile while the benchmark
runs in another terminal:

```bash
sudo powertop --time=60 --html=profiling/powertop-energy.html
```

### Interpreting results

* Lower elapsed time: construction finished sooner.
* Lower `power/energy-pkg/` Joules: the CPU package used less energy.
* Fewer cycles for the same workload: less CPU work.
* Cache misses explain why runs with similar hash speed differ in time or energy.

Energy measurements are hardware-specific. Report the machine, kernel, CPU governor, Rust version,
and command line with every table. BLAKE3's lower cycles per byte usually means less energy per
proof, which is why the suite measures all three algorithms.

The full guide lives in
[`benchmarks/ENERGY.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/benchmarks/ENERGY.md)
and [`profiling/README.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/profiling/README.md).

# API overview

This page maps the public API of each library. Both expose the same trees, hashes, and proof
formats; the switch shows the Rust crates or the TypeScript packages.

<LangBar />

<Rust>
  For full signatures and doc comments, see docs.rs.

  | Crate | Import as | docs.rs |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `merkle-core` | `merkle_core` | [docs.rs/merkle-core](https://docs.rs/merkle-core) |
  | `merkleforge-hash` | `merkleforge_hash` | [docs.rs/merkleforge-hash](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash) |
  | `merkle-variants` | `merkle_variants` | [docs.rs/merkle-variants](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants) |

  :::note
  docs.rs documents the latest release (v0.5.1). Items marked *v0.5.0* or *v0.5.1* below were
  added in that release.
  :::
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Every package ships TypeScript declarations with TSDoc, so your editor shows full signatures and
  the errors each function throws. All six are ESM only and versioned together.

  | Package | Role | npm |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `@merkleforge/core` | Interfaces, proof types, errors, byte helpers, proof codecs | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/core) |
  | `@merkleforge/hash` | `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, `Blake3` | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash) |
  | `@merkleforge/variants` | The three trees, multiproofs, codecs, Solidity formatting | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants) |
  | `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` | WebAssembly `Keccak256` and `Sha256` | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash-wasm) |
  | `@merkleforge/ethereum` | `eth_getProof` verification | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/ethereum) |
  | `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` | Drop-in `StandardMerkleTree` and `SimpleMerkleTree` | [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/openzeppelin) |

  For how each Rust item maps to TypeScript, see [TypeScript packages](/docs/reference/typescript).
</TypeScript>

## Core

<Rust>
  `merkle-core`: traits, types, and errors shared by every crate. `no_std` + `alloc` capable
  ([details](/docs/guides/no-std)).

  `merkle_core::prelude` re-exports `MerkleError`, `HashFunction`, `MerkleTree`, `ProofVerifier`, `Serializable`,
  `LeafIndex`, `MerkleProof`, `NodeIndex`, `ProofNode`, `ProofSide`, and `TreeMetadata`.

  ```rust
  use merkle_core::prelude::*;

  fn main() {
      let index = LeafIndex(3);
      assert_eq!(index.value(), 3);
      assert_eq!(NodeIndex::from(index), NodeIndex(3));
      assert_eq!(NodeIndex::root(4), NodeIndex(6)); // [L0 L1 L2 L3 P01 P23 Root]
  }
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `@merkleforge/core`: interfaces, proof types, errors, and helpers shared by every package. It has
  no runtime dependencies.

  ```ts
  import { isMerkleError, isTrivialProof, MerkleError, proofDepth, utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
  import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
  import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

  const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'].map(utf8))
  const proof = tree.generateProof(3)

  console.assert(proof.leafIndex === 3 && proof.leafCount === 4)
  console.assert(proofDepth(proof) === 2 && !isTrivialProof(proof))
  console.assert(tree.leafCount === 4 && tree.height === 3)

  try {
    tree.generateProof(9)
  } catch (error) {
    console.assert(isMerkleError(error, 'IndexOutOfBounds') && error instanceof MerkleError)
  }
  ```
</TypeScript>

### Traits and interfaces

<Rust>
  In `merkle_core::traits`:

  | Trait | Methods |
  | --- | --- |
  | [`HashFunction`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/hash_function/trait.HashFunction.html) | `type Digest`; `hash`, `algorithm_name`, `digest_size`; provided `hash_nodes`, `hash_encoded_node` (*v0.5.0*), `empty` |
  | [`MerkleTree<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/merkle_tree/trait.MerkleTree.html) | `insert`, `remove`, `root`, `leaf_count`, `is_empty`, `height`, `generate_proof`, `metadata` |
  | [`ProofVerifier<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/merkle_tree/trait.ProofVerifier.html) | `verify(expected_root, leaf_data, proof) -> bool` |
  | [`Serializable`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/serializable/trait.Serializable.html) | `to_bytes`, `from_bytes`, `serialized_size`; blanket impl for `Serialize + DeserializeOwned` |
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  | Interface | Members |
  | --- | --- |
  | `HashFunction` | `algorithmName`, `digestSize`; `hash`, `hashNodes`, `hashEncodedNode`, `empty` |
  | `MerkleTree` | `hasher`; `insert`, `remove`, `root`, `isEmpty`, `generateProof`, `metadata`; `leafCount`, `height` |
  | `ProofVerifier` | `(hasher, expectedRoot, leafData, proof) => boolean`, the type of every `verify` |

  `defineHashFunction(spec)` builds a `HashFunction` from `algorithmName`, `digestSize`, and
  `hash`, deriving `hashNodes`, `hashEncodedNode`, and `empty` unless you supply them.
  `LEAF_PREFIX` (`0x00`) and `NODE_PREFIX` (`0x01`) are the domain-separation bytes.
</TypeScript>

### Types

<Rust>
  In `merkle_core::types`:

  | Type | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `LeafIndex(pub usize)` | Index into the leaf layer. `value()`, `to_node_index()` |
  | `NodeIndex(pub usize)` | Index into a flat node array. `value()`, `root(leaf_count)` |
  | `ProofSide` | `Left` or `Right`: where the sibling sits |
  | `ProofNode<D>` | `hash: D`, `side: ProofSide` |
  | `MerkleProof<D>` | `leaf_index`, `leaf_count`, `path: Vec<ProofNode<D>>`; `depth()`, `is_trivial()` |
  | `TreeMetadata` | `leaf_count`, `height`, `node_count`, `hash_algorithm`, `variant` |
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  | Type | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `Bytes` | `Uint8Array`: leaf data, digests, and encoded proofs |
  | `ProofSide` | `'left'` or `'right'`: where the sibling sits |
  | `ProofNode` | `hash: Bytes`, `side: ProofSide` |
  | `MerkleProof` | `leafIndex`, `leafCount`, `path: ProofNode[]`; with `proofDepth(proof)` and `isTrivialProof(proof)` |
  | `TreeMetadata` | `leafCount`, `height`, `nodeCount`, `hashAlgorithm`, `variant` |
</TypeScript>

### Errors

<Rust>
  `MerkleError`, a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum. See [Errors](/docs/guides/errors).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `MerkleError` extends `Error`. Its `code` (and `detail`) is one of `EmptyTree`,
  `IndexOutOfBounds`, `InvalidProof`, `InvalidProofStructure`, `EmptyLeafData`,
  `SerializationError`, `DeserializationError`, `HashError`, `UnsupportedOperation`, or `RlpError`.
  `isMerkleError(error, code?)` narrows an unknown error. See [Errors](/docs/guides/errors).
</TypeScript>

### Helpers and codecs

<Rust>
  Proofs serialize through the `Serializable` trait and serde. See [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  | Function | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `utf8`, `toHex`, `fromHex`, `bytesEqual`, `concatBytes` | Byte helpers; `toHex` returns a `0x`-prefixed string |
  | `encodeMerkleProof`, `decodeMerkleProof` | Same bytes as Rust's bincode `Serializable` |
  | `merkleProofToSerdeJSON`, `merkleProofFromSerdeJSON` | Same JSON as Rust's `serde_json` |
  | `BincodeWriter`, `BincodeReader`, `byteArrayFromJSON` | Building blocks for the codecs |
</TypeScript>

## Hash functions

<Rust>
  `merkleforge-hash`:

  | Item | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | [`Sha256`](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash/latest/merkleforge_hash/struct.Sha256.html) | SHA-256 with `0x00`/`0x01` domain prefixes |
  | [`Keccak256`](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash/latest/merkleforge_hash/struct.Keccak256.html) | Keccak-256 with `0x00`/`0x01` prefixes; plain Keccak for Patricia nodes |
  | [`Blake3`](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash/latest/merkleforge_hash/struct.Blake3.html) | BLAKE3 `derive_key` with leaf and internal-node contexts |
  | `HashFunction` | Re-export of `merkle_core::traits::HashFunction` |

  All three are zero-sized, `Copy`, and produce `[u8; 32]`. See [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `@merkleforge/hash` (built on [`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes)):

  | Item | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `Sha256` | SHA-256 with `0x00`/`0x01` domain prefixes |
  | `Keccak256` | Keccak-256 with `0x00`/`0x01` prefixes; plain Keccak for Patricia nodes |
  | `Blake3` | BLAKE3 `derive_key` with leaf and internal-node contexts |

  Each is a frozen `HashFunction` object producing 32-byte digests, identical to the Rust adapters.
  Pass it to a tree's constructor and to the static verifiers.

  `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` adds `createKeccak256Wasm()` and `createSha256Wasm()`, async factories
  for WebAssembly versions with the same output and `algorithmName` (3–7x faster Keccak-256 tree
  builds than the pure-JS adapter in Node, [measured](/docs/performance/benchmarks)). See [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions).
</TypeScript>

## Trees

<Rust>
  `merkle-variants`. Top-level re-exports: `BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`,
  `MerklePatriciaTrie`, `MptProof`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `@merkleforge/variants`. Every tree takes its `HashFunction` in the constructor; verifiers are
  static and take the hash function first. Trees serialize with `toJSON()` and load with
  `fromJSON(hasher, json)`, which rejects JSON written with a different hash.
</TypeScript>

### Binary Merkle tree

<Rust>
  [`BinaryMerkleTree<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants/latest/merkle_variants/binary/struct.BinaryMerkleTree.html):

  | Method | Notes |
  | --- | --- |
  | `new()`, `with_capacity(n)`, `Default` | Empty tree |
  | `from_leaves(iter)` | One-pass `O(n)` build (*v0.5.0*) |
  | `insert(&[u8]) -> Result<LeafIndex>` | Append a leaf |
  | `remove(LeafIndex)` | Replace with `H::empty()` |
  | `root()`, `leaf_count()`, `is_empty()`, `height()` | Queries |
  | `generate_proof(LeafIndex) -> Result<MerkleProof>` | Inclusion proof |
  | `verify(root, leaf, &proof) -> bool` | Stateless, associated function |
  | `generate_multi_proof(&[LeafIndex]) -> Result<BinaryMultiProof>` | One proof for several leaves (*v0.5.1*) |
  | `verify_multi_proof(root, &leaves, &proof) -> bool` | Stateless; leaves in `proof.leaf_indices` order (*v0.5.1*) |

  Implements `MerkleTree<H>`, `ProofVerifier<H>`; `Clone`, `Debug`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`
  (*v0.5.0*). `BinaryMultiProof<D>` (`leaf_indices`, `leaf_count`, `hashes`) serializes in the
  same format as the TypeScript package (*v0.5.1*).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `BinaryMerkleTree`:

  | Member | Notes |
  | --- | --- |
  | `new BinaryMerkleTree(hasher)`, `BinaryMerkleTree.withCapacity(hasher, n)` | Empty tree |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(hasher, leaves)` | One-pass `O(n)` build |
  | `insert(data): number` | Append a leaf; returns its index |
  | `remove(index)` | Replace with `hasher.empty()` |
  | `root()`, `isEmpty()`, `leafCount`, `height` | Queries (`leafCount` and `height` are getters) |
  | `generateProof(index): MerkleProof` | Inclusion proof |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree.verify(hasher, root, leaf, proof)` | Stateless |
  | `generateMultiProof(indices): BinaryMultiProof` | One proof for several leaves |
  | `BinaryMerkleTree.verifyMultiProof(hasher, root, leaves, proof)` | Stateless; leaves in `proof.leafIndices` order |
  | `metadata()`, `toJSON()`, `BinaryMerkleTree.fromJSON(hasher, json)` | Metadata and JSON |

  Implements `MerkleTree`. `BinaryMultiProof` (`leafIndices`, `leafCount`, `hashes`) uses the same
  bincode and JSON format as Rust; `verifyBinaryMultiProof` is the standalone verifier.
</TypeScript>

Guide: [Binary Merkle tree](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree).

### Sparse Merkle tree

<Rust>
  [`SparseMerkleTree<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants/latest/merkle_variants/sparse/struct.SparseMerkleTree.html):

  | Method | Notes |
  | --- | --- |
  | `new()`, `Default` | Empty 256-depth tree |
  | `insert(key, &[u8])`, `batch_insert(&[(key, Vec<u8>)])` | Insert or overwrite |
  | `remove(key)`, `batch_remove(&[key])` | Remove existing keys |
  | `get(key) -> Option<&Digest>` | Stored leaf hash |
  | `generate_membership_proof(key) -> Result<SparseMerkleProof>` | Membership or non-membership |
  | `verify_membership(root, key, leaf, &proof)` | Checks key, value, path (*v0.5.0*) |
  | `verify_non_membership(root, key, &proof)` | Absence proof |
  | `verify(root, leaf, &proof)` | **Deprecated**: doesn't check the key |
  | `root()`, `empty_root()`, `leaf_count()`, `is_empty()`, `height()`, `depth()` | Queries |
  | `empty_hash_at(level)`, `empty_hashes()` | Empty-subtree cache |
  | `stored_node_count()`, `last_node_access_count()`, `unbatched_node_count_estimate()` | Storage introspection |

  Also: `SparseMerkleProof<D>` (`key`, `siblings`, `leaf`; `is_membership()`,
  `is_non_membership()`), `NodeEntry<D>` (with `commitment()`, *v0.5.0*), `SubtreeBatch<D>`,
  `bit_at`, and the constants `SPARSE_TREE_DEPTH`, `EMPTY_HASH_LEVELS`, `BATCH_DEPTH`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `SparseMerkleTree` (keys are 32-byte `Uint8Array`s):

  | Member | Notes |
  | --- | --- |
  | `new SparseMerkleTree(hasher)` | Empty 256-depth tree |
  | `insert(key, data)`, `batchInsert([[key, data], …])` | Insert or overwrite |
  | `remove(key)`, `batchRemove(keys)` | Remove existing keys |
  | `get(key)` | Stored leaf hash, or `undefined` |
  | `generateMembershipProof(key): SparseMerkleProof` | Membership or non-membership |
  | `SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership(hasher, root, key, leaf, proof)` | Checks key, value, and path |
  | `SparseMerkleTree.verifyNonMembership(hasher, root, key, proof)` | Absence proof |
  | `root()`, `emptyRoot()`, `isEmpty()`, `leafCount`, `height`, `depth` | Queries |
  | `emptyHashAt(level)`, `emptyHashes()` | Empty-subtree cache |
  | `storedNodeCount`, `lastNodeAccessCount`, `unbatchedNodeCountEstimate()` | Storage introspection |
  | `indexed()` | A `MerkleTree` view addressed by leaf index |
  | `metadata()`, `toJSON()`, `SparseMerkleTree.fromJSON(hasher, json)` | Metadata and JSON |

  Also: `SparseMerkleProof` (`key`, `siblings` with `null` for empty subtrees, `leaf`),
  `isSparseMembershipProof`, `bitAt`, and the constants `SPARSE_TREE_DEPTH`, `EMPTY_HASH_LEVELS`,
  `BATCH_DEPTH`, `SPARSE_KEY_BYTES`. There is no key-blind `verify`.
</TypeScript>

Guide: [Sparse Merkle tree](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree).

### Merkle Patricia trie

<Rust>
  [`MerklePatriciaTrie<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants/latest/merkle_variants/patricia/struct.MerklePatriciaTrie.html):

  | Method | Notes |
  | --- | --- |
  | `new()`, `Default` | Empty trie |
  | `insert(key, value)`, `remove(key)`, `get(key) -> Option<&[u8]>` | Key-value operations |
  | `generate_proof(key) -> Result<MptProof>` | RLP witness, membership or non-membership |
  | `verify_proof(root, &proof) -> bool` | Stateless |
  | `root()`, `is_empty()`, `leaf_count()`, `node_count()`, `height()` | Queries |

  Also: `MptProof<D>` (`key`, `value`, `proof_nodes`; `new`, `is_membership`, `is_non_membership`),
  `MptNode<D>`, `NodeRef<D>`, `NibblePath`, `hp_encode`, `hp_decode`, `rlp_encode`, `rlp_decode`,
  `hash_node`, `compute_root_hash`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  `MerklePatriciaTrie`:

  | Member | Notes |
  | --- | --- |
  | `new MerklePatriciaTrie(hasher)` | Empty trie |
  | `insert(key, value)`, `remove(key)`, `get(key)` | Key-value operations; `get` returns `undefined` when absent |
  | `generateProof(key): MptProof` | RLP witness, membership or non-membership |
  | `MerklePatriciaTrie.verifyProof(hasher, root, proof)` | Stateless |
  | `MerklePatriciaTrie.proveValue(hasher, root, key, proofNodes)` | Returns the proven value or `null`; accepts `eth_getProof`-style witnesses |
  | `root()`, `isEmpty()`, `leafCount`, `nodeCount`, `height`, `entries()` | Queries |
  | `indexed()` | A `MerkleTree` view addressed by leaf index |
  | `metadata()`, `toJSON()`, `MerklePatriciaTrie.fromJSON(hasher, json)` | Metadata and JSON |

  Also: `MptProof` (`key`, `value` or `null`, `proofNodes`), `MptNode` and `NodeRef` (`{ kind }`
  unions), `bytesToNibbles`, `hpEncode`, `hpDecode`, `rlpEncode`, `rlpDecode`, `encodeRlp`,
  `decodeRlp`, `hashNode`, and `computeRootHash`.
</TypeScript>

Guide: [Merkle Patricia trie](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie).

## Proof formats

<Rust>
  Every proof type implements `Serialize`, `Deserialize`, and `Serializable` (bincode). See
  [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  Each proof type has a bincode codec and a `serde_json`-compatible JSON codec, with the same bytes
  and JSON as the Rust crates:

  | Proof | Bincode | JSON |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `MerkleProof` | `encodeMerkleProof` / `decodeMerkleProof` | `merkleProofToSerdeJSON` / `merkleProofFromSerdeJSON` |
  | `BinaryMultiProof` | `encodeBinaryMultiProof` / `decodeBinaryMultiProof` | `multiProofToSerdeJSON` / `multiProofFromSerdeJSON` |
  | `SparseMerkleProof` | `encodeSparseProof` / `decodeSparseProof` | `sparseProofToSerdeJSON` / `sparseProofFromSerdeJSON` |
  | `MptProof` | `encodeMptProof` / `decodeMptProof` | `mptProofToSerdeJSON` / `mptProofFromSerdeJSON` |

  For the Solidity verifiers, `toSolidityBinaryProof`, `toSolidityBinaryMultiProof`, and
  `toSoliditySparseProof` reshape proofs into hex strings (and a `bigint` bitmap for sparse
  proofs). See [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization) and
  [Proofs](/docs/guides/proofs#verifying-on-chain).
</TypeScript>

## TypeScript-only packages

<Rust>
  These packages have no Rust equivalent. Switch to TypeScript to see their API, or read
  [TypeScript packages](/docs/reference/typescript).
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  **`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`**

  | Function | Returns |
  | --- | --- |
  | `createKeccak256Wasm()` | `Promise<HashFunction>`: WebAssembly Keccak-256, same output as `Keccak256` |
  | `createSha256Wasm()` | `Promise<HashFunction>`: WebAssembly SHA-256, same output as `Sha256` |

  **`@merkleforge/ethereum`**

  | Item | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `verifyEthGetProof(stateRoot, response, options?)` | Verifies a full `eth_getProof` response; returns the account (or `null`) and storage values. Throws `InvalidProof` on any mismatch |
  | `verifyAccountProof({ stateRoot, address, proof }, options?)` | Account proof only; returns `EthAccount` or `null` |
  | `verifyStorageProof({ storageRoot, slot, proof }, options?)` | One storage slot; returns its value as a `bigint` (`0n` when empty) |
  | `mappingSlot(key, slot)` | Storage slot of `mapping[key]` for a mapping declared at `slot` |
  | `keccak256`, `toBytes32`, `bytesToBigInt` | Helpers |
  | `EMPTY_TRIE_ROOT`, `EMPTY_CODE_HASH` | Constants |

  `options.hasher` swaps the trie hash, for example `await createKeccak256Wasm()`. Types:
  `EthGetProofResponse`, `EthAccount`, `VerifiedEthProof`, `BytesLike`.

  **`@merkleforge/openzeppelin`**

  | Item | Description |
  | --- | --- |
  | `StandardMerkleTree.of(values, leafEncoding)` | ABI-encoded leaves, the same tree as `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree` |
  | `SimpleMerkleTree.of(values)` | `bytes32` leaves |
  | `getProof`, `getMultiProof`, `verify`, `verifyMultiProof`, `root`, `entries()`, `dump()` | The same instance API |
  | `StandardMerkleTree.load(dump)`, `SimpleMerkleTree.load(dump)` | Load an existing `dump()` unchanged |
  | `StandardMerkleTree.verify(…)`, `SimpleMerkleTree.verify(…)` | Static verifiers |
  | `abiEncode(types, values)`, `standardLeafHash`, `standardNodeHash`, `formatLeaf` | Helpers |
</TypeScript>

## Safety

<Rust>
  Every published crate uses `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` and `#![deny(missing_docs)]`.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  The packages compile with `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`,
  document every public API with TSDoc (including what it throws), and return copies of internal
  `Uint8Array` state rather than the buffers themselves. The tree verifiers (`verify`,
  `verifyMultiProof`, `verifyMembership`, `verifyNonMembership`, `verifyProof`) return `false` for
  malformed proofs instead of throwing; `proveValue` and the `@merkleforge/ethereum` functions throw
  `InvalidProof`, because they return the proven value. Releases are published with provenance
  through npm trusted publishing.
</TypeScript>

# TypeScript packages

MerkleForge for TypeScript and JavaScript is published on npm under the
[`@merkleforge`](https://www.npmjs.com/org/merkleforge) scope. It implements the same trees,
hashes, and proof formats as the Rust crates, with an idiomatic TypeScript API. The source lives
in [1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts).

* **Runtimes:** Node.js 22+, browsers, Deno, and Bun. ESM only.
* **Dependencies:** the only runtime dependency is [`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes).
* **Compatibility:** roots and proofs match the Rust crates byte for byte. A proof generated by a
  Rust server verifies in a browser, and the other way round. This is tested against vectors
  generated by the Rust crates.

## Packages

| Package | Role | Rust equivalent |
|---------|------|-----------------|
| [`@merkleforge/core`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/core) | `HashFunction` and `MerkleTree` interfaces, proof types, `MerkleError`, byte helpers, proof codecs | `merkle-core` |
| [`@merkleforge/hash`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash) | `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, `Blake3` | `merkleforge-hash` |
| [`@merkleforge/variants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants) | `BinaryMerkleTree` (with multiproofs), `SparseMerkleTree`, `MerklePatriciaTrie`, proof codecs, Solidity proof formatting | `merkle-variants` |
| [`@merkleforge/hash-wasm`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/hash-wasm) | WebAssembly `Keccak256` and `Sha256` with identical output; Keccak-256 tree builds 3–7x faster than pure JS ([measured](/docs/performance/benchmarks)) | TypeScript only |
| [`@merkleforge/ethereum`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/ethereum) | Verify `eth_getProof` account and storage proofs against a state root | TypeScript only |
| [`@merkleforge/openzeppelin`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/openzeppelin) | Drop-in `StandardMerkleTree` and `SimpleMerkleTree` for `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`: same roots, proofs, and dumps | TypeScript only |

The repository also contains Solidity verifiers for every Keccak-256 proof type
(`MerkleForgeBinary`, `MerkleForgeSparse`, `MerkleForgePatricia`, `MerkleForgeEthereum`); see
[contracts/](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/tree/main/contracts).

```bash
npm i @merkleforge/core @merkleforge/hash @merkleforge/variants
```

Staging builds from the `develop` branch are published under the `next` dist-tag
(`npm i @merkleforge/variants@next`).

Releases are published from CI through npm trusted publishing with provenance, and a maintainer
approves each version with 2FA before it goes live.

### Downloads

Live from npm. The headline numbers are the last 7 days, npm's "weekly downloads", which track ongoing use. All-time totals also count the registry mirrors and scanners that fetch every new version, and include the packages' earlier `@1888-labs/merkle-*` names.

<NpmDownloads />

## How the API maps

| Rust | TypeScript |
|------|------------|
| `BinaryMerkleTree::<Keccak256>::new()` | `new BinaryMerkleTree(Keccak256)` |
| `BinaryMerkleTree::<Keccak256>::from_leaves(data)?` | `BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, data)` |
| Generic `H: HashFunction` type parameter | `HashFunction` object passed at construction and to static verifiers |
| `BinaryMerkleTree::<H>::verify(root, leaf, &proof)` | `BinaryMerkleTree.verify(H, root, leaf, proof)` |
| `Result<T, MerkleError>` | Throws `MerkleError`; check `error.code` or use `isMerkleError(error, 'EmptyTree')` |
| `[u8; 32]` digests, `&[u8]` data | `Uint8Array` (`Bytes`) |
| `b"alice"` | `utf8('alice')` |
| `LeafIndex(usize)` | `number` |
| `ProofSide::Left` / `Right` | `'left'` / `'right'` |
| `proof.depth()` / `proof.is_trivial()` | `proofDepth(proof)` / `isTrivialProof(proof)` |
| `tree.leaf_count()`, `tree.height()` | `tree.leafCount`, `tree.height` (getters) |
| `snake_case` methods | `camelCase` methods (`generate_proof` → `generateProof`) |
| `impl MerkleTree for SparseMerkleTree` (index-addressed) | `smt.indexed()` returns a `MerkleTree` view |
| `serde` on proofs | `merkleProofToSerdeJSON` / `merkleProofFromSerdeJSON` (same JSON as `serde_json`) |
| `Serializable::to_bytes` on proofs (bincode) | `encodeMerkleProof` / `decodeMerkleProof` (same bytes) |
| `no_std` + `alloc` | Not applicable |

The guides show both languages side by side: use the **Rust / TypeScript** switch in the sidebar
(or the bar at the top of the page on small screens).

## Versioning

The npm packages are versioned independently of the Rust crates (for example npm `0.2.1` alongside
crates `0.5.1`). Compatibility is defined by the **formats**, not the version numbers: the hashing
scheme, proof structure, and the bincode and JSON proof encodings are shared, and the TypeScript
test suite checks them in CI against vectors generated by the Rust crates. Release notes are on
[GitHub Releases](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/releases).

## What only one language has

| Feature | Rust | TypeScript |
|---------|------|------------|
| Binary, Sparse, and Patricia trees, multiproofs | ✓ | ✓ |
| SHA-256, Keccak-256, BLAKE3 | ✓ | ✓ |
| `no_std` support | ✓ | — |
| WebAssembly hashes | — | ✓ `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` |
| OpenZeppelin `StandardMerkleTree` drop-in | — | ✓ `@merkleforge/openzeppelin` |
| `eth_getProof` verification | — | ✓ `@merkleforge/ethereum` |
| Solidity proof formatting and verifier contracts | — | ✓ |

# Changelog

The Rust crates and the TypeScript packages are released separately and versioned independently.
Compatibility comes from the shared proof formats, not from matching version numbers. Both follow
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## Rust crates

The full changelog lives in the repository:
**[CHANGELOG.md on GitHub](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)**.

`merkle-core`, `merkleforge-hash`, and `merkle-variants` are versioned together; one entry covers
all published crates. `merkle-bench` is never published. The changelog follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).

### v0.5.1 (2026-10-20)

* **Added:** `BinaryMerkleTree::generate_multi_proof` and `verify_multi_proof`, with the new
  `BinaryMultiProof` type: one proof for several leaves, sharing sibling hashes. Its serde and
  bincode format matches the TypeScript package
  [`@merkleforge/variants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/variants), so multiproofs
  move between Rust and TypeScript unchanged.

### v0.5.0 (2026-10-14)

Correctness and performance fixes. Roots and proofs for the shipped hash adapters are unchanged.

* **Added:** `BinaryMerkleTree::from_leaves` (one-pass `O(n)` build),
  `SparseMerkleTree::verify_membership` (checks the proof's key),
  `HashFunction::hash_encoded_node`, `NodeEntry::commitment`, and `Clone` / `Debug` / `Serialize` /
  `Deserialize` for all three trees.
* **Fixed:** sparse and Patricia inserts and removals recompute only the changed path (4,000
  sparse inserts: about 223 s to 0.2 s; one sparse proof: 151 ms to 25 µs; 4,000 Patricia inserts:
  about 5.9 s to 0.02 s). `MerkleTree::insert` on sparse and Patricia trees no longer overwrites a
  leaf after a removal.
* **Breaking:** the default `HashFunction::hash_nodes` now hashes `0x01 ‖ left ‖ right`;
  `MerklePatriciaTrie` selects plain Keccak through `hash_encoded_node` instead of the algorithm
  name; the hidden `MptNode::__DigestMarker` variant is gone.
* **Deprecated:** `SparseMerkleTree::verify`. Use `verify_membership`.
* **Docs:** this Vocs documentation site replaces the old React website, and the repository moved
  to `1888-Labs/MerkleForge`.

### v0.4.1 (2026-09-05)

Packaging and documentation refresh for the MerkleForge Framework rebrand: crate metadata,
rewritten crate READMEs, and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### v0.4.0 (2026-07-27)

Adds the Ethereum-compatible `MerklePatriciaTrie<H>` with RLP and hex-prefix encoding,
EIP-1186-style `MptProof` witnesses, and validation against official Ethereum trie vectors.

## TypeScript packages

Release notes for each version are on
**[GitHub Releases](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/releases)**, and each package has a
`CHANGELOG.md` generated by [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets).

All six `@merkleforge/*` packages are versioned together. Versions up to 0.1.1 were published as
`@1888-labs/merkle-*`, which are now deprecated. `next` snapshots from the `develop` branch are not
listed here.

### v0.2.2 (2026-10-27)

* **Changed:** releases are published from CI through npm trusted publishing (OIDC) with
  provenance, and a maintainer approves each version with 2FA before it goes live. There is no
  long-lived npm token.

### v0.2.1 (2026-10-20)

* **Added:** [`@merkleforge/openzeppelin`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@merkleforge/openzeppelin),
  a drop-in replacement for `@openzeppelin/merkle-tree`. `StandardMerkleTree` and
  `SimpleMerkleTree` produce identical roots, proofs, multiproofs, and `dump()` JSON, so proofs
  verify with OpenZeppelin's `MerkleProof` on-chain and existing dumps load unchanged. Includes a
  dependency-free `abiEncode`.

### v0.2.0 (2026-10-18)

* **Changed:** the packages moved to the `@merkleforge` scope: `@1888-labs/merkle-core` is now
  `@merkleforge/core`, and likewise `hash`, `hash-wasm`, `variants`, and `ethereum`. The API is
  unchanged; update your imports. The `@1888-labs/merkle-*` packages are deprecated.

### v0.1.1 (2026-10-18)

* **Changed:** rewritten package READMEs with API tables and more examples.

### v0.1.0 (2026-10-18)

Initial TypeScript release, as `@1888-labs/merkle-*`.

* `BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`, and an Ethereum-compatible `MerklePatriciaTrie`, with
  roots and proofs that match the Rust crates.
* SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 adapters, plus WebAssembly Keccak-256 and SHA-256 in
  `hash-wasm`.
* Binary multiproofs.
* Proof codecs that are byte-compatible with Rust's bincode and `serde_json` output.
* Helpers that shape proofs for the MerkleForge Solidity verifiers.
* `eth_getProof` account and storage proof verification in `ethereum`.

# Security

Audit status, how to report vulnerabilities, and what verifiers must trust, for the Rust crates and
the TypeScript packages.

<LangBar />

## Audit status

:::warning
**MerkleForge has not completed an independent security audit.** This applies to both the Rust
crates and the TypeScript packages.

The <Rust inline>Rust codebase is tested with unit, integration, property-based, benchmark, and
Ethereum test-vector tests</Rust><TypeScript inline>TypeScript codebase is tested with unit,
property-based (fast-check), cross-implementation (vectors generated from the Rust crates), and
Ethereum test-vector tests, plus real mainnet `eth_getProof` responses</TypeScript>, but tests are
not an audit. Review the code, your threat model, and the test
coverage before using MerkleForge in production systems, financial applications, or other
security-critical environments.
:::

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please **do not** report vulnerabilities in public issues.

1. Open the **Security** tab of the
   <Rust inline>[MerkleForge repository](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/security)</Rust><TypeScript inline>[MerkleForge-ts repository](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/security)</TypeScript> and click
   **Report a vulnerability** to use GitHub Security Advisories.
2. Or email the details to [dicethedev@gmail.com](mailto\:dicethedev@gmail.com).

Include as much as you can:

* a clear description of the issue;
* steps to reproduce, ideally with proof-of-concept code;
* affected versions or components;
* potential impact and severity, and whether you believe it is being actively exploited.

Don't disclose publicly until the issue is confirmed and fixed, and don't access, modify, or destroy
data that isn't yours. The maintainers will acknowledge and investigate reports, may contact you
for details, and will coordinate disclosure once a fix is available.

There is no formal bug bounty. With your consent, your contribution may be credited in the
changelog or release notes.

The canonical policy is
<Rust inline>[`.github/SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/.github/SECURITY.md)</Rust><TypeScript inline>[`.github/SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts/blob/main/.github/SECURITY.md)
in MerkleForge-ts</TypeScript>.

## Design properties

<Rust>
  * `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in every published crate.
  * **Domain separation** between leaves (`0x00`) and internal nodes (`0x01`), or BLAKE3 context
    strings, to prevent second-preimage attacks. See [Mental model](/docs/mental-model#domain-separation-0x00-and-0x01).
  * **Empty leaves rejected** so inserted data can't be confused with padding.
  * **Verifiers never panic** on malformed proofs; they return `false`.
  * **Deserialization rebuilds** internal nodes from leaves and rejects data from another hash
    algorithm, so a decoded tree is always internally consistent.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  * **Small dependency surface.** `@merkleforge/core` has no runtime dependencies, and the only
    third-party runtime dependency of the core, hash, and tree packages is
    [`@noble/hashes`](https://github.com/paulmillr/noble-hashes). The optional
    `@merkleforge/hash-wasm` package uses [`hash-wasm`](https://github.com/Daninet/hash-wasm).
  * **Domain separation** between leaves (`0x00`) and internal nodes (`0x01`), or BLAKE3 context
    strings, to prevent second-preimage attacks. See [Mental model](/docs/mental-model#domain-separation-0x00-and-0x01).
  * **Empty leaves rejected** (`MerkleError` with code `EmptyLeafData`) so inserted data can't be
    confused with padding.
  * **Verifiers never throw** on malformed proofs; they return `false`.
  * **Deserialization rebuilds** internal nodes from leaves and rejects data from another hash
    algorithm, so a decoded tree is always internally consistent.
  * **No internal buffers handed out.** Methods return copies of internal `Uint8Array` state.

  **Releases**

  * Releases are published from GitHub Actions through **npm trusted publishing** (OIDC) with
    **provenance**. There is no npm token.
  * Each release is **staged** first and goes live only after a maintainer approves every package
    with **2FA**.
  * The packages are set to require 2FA and to disallow publishing tokens.

  Check the registry signatures and provenance attestations of your installed packages with:

  ```bash
  npm audit signatures
  ```
</TypeScript>

## What integrators must get right

* **Trust the root, not the prover.** A proof shows consistency with a root; it says nothing about
  whether that root is the right one.
* **<Rust inline>`MerkleProof::leaf_count`</Rust><TypeScript inline>`MerkleProof.leafCount`</TypeScript> is not committed** by the binary root. Obtain it independently if it
  matters.
* **Check the key** on sparse proofs with <Rust inline>`verify_membership`. The deprecated
  `SparseMerkleTree::verify` accepts a valid proof for *any* key holding the value.</Rust><TypeScript inline>`SparseMerkleTree.verifyMembership`, which takes the
  key and rejects a proof for a different one.</TypeScript>
* **Canonical leaf encoding.** Prover and verifier must hash exactly the same bytes.
* **Custom hash adapters** must keep leaf and node domains separate. <Rust inline>Since v0.5.0, the default
  `hash_nodes` applies the `0x01` prefix for you.</Rust><TypeScript inline>`defineHashFunction` fills in a
  default `hashNodes` that applies the `0x01` prefix for you.</TypeScript> See
  [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions#writing-a-custom-adapter).

# Brand assets

The MerkleForge mark is the **Forged block**: a solid rounded block with a Merkle root and two
branches cut out of it. It reads as a tree, an anvil-struck block, and a sealed hash at once.

<BrandPreview />

## Files

All assets live in
[`assets/brand/`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/tree/main/assets/brand) in the
repository. Wordmark text is converted to outlines, so the SVGs need no fonts.

| Folder | What | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `svg/mark/`, `png/mark/` | Mark alone, black or white, transparent cut-outs (64–1024 px) | Avatars, docs headers, small spaces |
| `svg/lockup/`, `png/lockup/` | Mark + wordmark, horizontal and stacked | README, website header, slides |
| `svg/wordmark/`, `png/wordmark/` | Wordmark only | Where the mark already appears nearby |
| `svg/icon/`, `png/icon/` | App icon (dark/light, 1024) and avatar (512/1024) | GitHub org, crates.io, X, Discord |
| `favicon/` | `favicon.svg` (adapts to dark mode), `.ico`, 16/32/48 PNG, apple-touch, 192/512, `site.webmanifest` | Website and docs |
| `svg/banner/`, `png/banner/` | GitHub social preview, README, X header, LinkedIn (dark + light) | Social and repository cards |

## Colour

Monochrome by design: black, white, and a short grey ramp. **No accent colour.**

<BrandSwatches />

| Name | Hex | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Forge Black | `#000000` | Primary ground, mark on light |
| Ink | `#141414` | Raised surfaces, ghost mark in banners |
| Steel | `#262626` | Borders, dividers on dark |
| Graphite | `#6B6B6B` | Secondary text on light, large only on dark |
| Slate | `#5C5C5C` | "Forge" in the wordmark on light |
| Ash | `#A3A3A3` | "Forge" in the wordmark on dark, captions on dark |
| White | `#FFFFFF` | Mark on dark, primary text on dark |

## Type

* **Space Grotesk**: wordmark (Merkle 700 / Forge 400, tracking −3%), headings 500–700.
* **JetBrains Mono**: code, hashes, technical labels (400–500).

Both are free on Google Fonts under the SIL Open Font License.

## Usage

* **Clear space:** keep at least ¼ of the mark's height empty on every side.
* **Minimum size:** mark 16 px; horizontal lockup 24 px tall.
* Use the black mark on light grounds and the white mark on dark grounds.
* Don't recolour, rotate, outline, stretch, add shadows or gradients, or rearrange the mark and
  wordmark.
* Don't place the mark on busy photos; use a solid black or white panel.

open infrastructure for verifiable, distributed, and intelligent systems.

<OwnerPreview />

When you credit the project, use **"MerkleForge by 1888 Labs"**. Use the 1888 Labs horizontal
logo from the [1888 Labs brand kit](https://github.com/1888-Labs/brandkit), not a retyped
wordmark. Use the `on-light` file on light grounds and the `on-dark` file on dark grounds. The
1888 Labs Signal orange belongs to the 1888 Labs mark only. Don't add it to MerkleForge assets,
which stay monochrome.

# Contributing

Contributions are welcome across correctness, documentation, benchmarks, examples, developer
experience, and performance analysis. By participating, you agree to follow the
[Code of Conduct](/docs/community/code-of-conduct).

The Rust crates live in [1888-Labs/MerkleForge](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge) and the
TypeScript packages in [1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts).

<LangBar />

## Good first contributions

<Rust>
  * Improve docs, Rustdoc, examples, or these pages (every page has a *Suggest changes* link).
  * Add benchmark reproduction notes for different hardware.
  * Add test vectors for Binary, Sparse, or Patricia trees.
  * Improve error messages or API examples.
  * Investigate performance with Criterion, `perf`, or flamegraphs.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  * More test vectors and property-style tests (tampered proofs, edge sizes).
  * Docs and examples for browser, Deno, and Bun usage.
  * Benchmarks for tree builds and proof verification.
  * Issues labelled `good first issue`.
  * Improve these pages (every page has a *Suggest changes* link).
</TypeScript>

## Development setup

<Rust>
  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
  cd MerkleForge
  cargo test --workspace
  ```

  The workspace pins Rust 1.97.1 in `rust-toolchain.toml`; `rustup` installs it automatically.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  You need Node.js 22+ and pnpm. The pnpm version is pinned in `package.json`; run
  `corepack enable` to pick it up.

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge-ts.git
  cd MerkleForge-ts
  pnpm install
  pnpm check   # lint, typecheck, test, and package checks
  ```

  | Command | What it does |
  | --- | --- |
  | `pnpm build` | Compile every package with `tsc -b` into `dist/` |
  | `pnpm typecheck` | Type-check sources and tests |
  | `pnpm test` | Run Vitest against the sources (no build needed) |
  | `pnpm coverage` | Tests with V8 coverage |
  | `pnpm lint` / `pnpm format` | Biome lint and format check / auto-fix |
  | `pnpm check:packages` | publint and arethetypeswrong on what npm will ship |
  | `pnpm fixtures:solidity` | Regenerate `contracts/test/fixtures` from the TypeScript packages |
  | `pnpm test:solidity` | Foundry tests for the Solidity verifiers (needs [Foundry](https://getfoundry.sh)) |
</TypeScript>

This website lives in its own repository,
[1888-Labs/merkleforge-docs](https://github.com/1888-Labs/merkleforge-docs), built with
[Vocs](https://vocs.dev):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/merkleforge-docs.git
cd merkleforge-docs
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Recommended workflow

<Rust>
  1. Open or comment on an issue first for large API, storage, or cryptography changes.
  2. Create a focused branch, for example `fix/docs-links` or `feat/sparse-proof-tests`.
  3. Keep the pull request small enough to review comfortably.
  4. Add or update tests for behaviour changes.
  5. Update docs when public APIs, examples, or benchmark behaviour change.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  1. Branch from `develop` (`feat/...`, `fix/...`, `docs/...`).
  2. Make a focused change with tests.
  3. If it changes a published package, run `pnpm changeset` and describe the change for users.
     Docs, CI, and test-only changes do not need one.
  4. Run `pnpm check`.
  5. Open a pull request into `develop`. `develop` is merged into `main` to release.

  Commits use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/): `feat(sparse): ...`,
  `fix(binary): ...`, `test(patricia): ...`, `docs: ...`.

  The Rust crates are the reference implementation: roots, proofs, and encodings must match them
  byte for byte. When changing tree logic, read the matching Rust source first, and add or regenerate
  test vectors from the Rust crates rather than hand-writing expected hashes. Never edit an expected
  value just to make a test pass.
</TypeScript>

## Required checks

Run these before opening a pull request:

<Rust>
  ```bash
  make fmt    # rustfmt
  make lint   # Clippy across the workspace, warnings denied
  make test   # all workspace tests in release mode
  ```
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  ```bash
  pnpm check   # pnpm lint, pnpm typecheck, pnpm test, and pnpm check:packages

  # When touching contracts/ or proof shapes
  pnpm fixtures:solidity && pnpm test:solidity
  ```
</TypeScript>

For website changes, run `npm run build` in the docs repository.

## Pull request guidelines

<Rust>
  * Explain the problem, the change, and how you verified it.
  * Link related issues.
  * Keep `target/`, local benchmark noise, editor files, and temporary artifacts out of commits.
  * Include benchmark numbers only with the environment and command recorded.
  * Avoid unrelated refactors in feature or bug-fix pull requests.
</Rust>

<TypeScript>
  * Explain the problem, the change, and any compatibility or security impact.
  * List the commands you ran.
  * Link related issues.
  * Keep unrelated refactors out of the pull request.
</TypeScript>

## Security

Don't report vulnerabilities in public issues. Follow the disclosure process on the
[Security](/docs/reference/security) page.

# Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in the
MerkleForge community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of
age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex
characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience,
education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race,
caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming,
diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our
community include:

* Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
* Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
* Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
* Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes,
  and learning from the experience
* Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall
  community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

* The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances
  of any kind
* Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
* Public or private harassment
* Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address,
  without their explicit permission
* Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a
  professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of
acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in
response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive,
or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject
comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are
not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for
moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, including the
MerkleForge repository, issues, pull requests, discussions, and project chat
channels, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the
community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include
using an official email address, posting via an official social media account,
or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Reporting

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be
reported to the project maintainers at
[dicethedev@gmail.com](mailto\:dicethedev@gmail.com). All complaints will be
reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the
reporter of any incident.

Security vulnerabilities are not Code of Conduct matters. Please report them
through the process in the [security policy](/docs/reference/security).

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining
the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed
unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing
clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the
behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of
actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No
interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with
those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This
includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels
like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent
ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including
sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public
communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or
private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction
with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period.
Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community
standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an
individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the
community.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage],
version 2.1, available at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html).

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by
[Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][mozilla coc].

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq). Translations are available at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations).

[homepage]: https://www.contributor-covenant.org

[mozilla coc]: https://github.com/mozilla/diversity

# Projects using MerkleForge

## ProofStream

ProofStream turns live indexed DEX activity into portable proof receipts. It normalizes blockchain
records into deterministic rows, commits them with a MerkleForge `BinaryMerkleTree<Keccak256>`,
and lets a browser verify one selected activity using only the row, its compact proof, and the
dataset root.

* [ProofStream repository](https://github.com/1888-Labs/ProofStream)
* [ETHGlobal Online 2026 showcase](https://ethglobal.com/showcase/proofstream-jvup1)

## Add your project

Building something with MerkleForge? Open a pull request that adds a short section to
[this page](https://github.com/1888-Labs/merkleforge-docs/edit/main/pages/docs/community/projects.mdx)
with a one-paragraph description and links.

    <div>
      <Rust>
        ```rust [src/main.rs]
        use merkle_core::prelude::*;
        use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
        use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

        fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
            let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves([
                "alice:100", "bob:250", "carol:75",
            ])?;

            let root = tree.root().expect("tree is non-empty");
            let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(1))?;

            // Stateless: only the root, the leaf bytes, and the proof.
            assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, b"bob:250", &proof));
            Ok(())
        }
        ```
      </Rust>

      <TypeScript>
        ```ts [index.ts]
        import { utf8 } from '@merkleforge/core'
        import { Sha256 } from '@merkleforge/hash'
        import { BinaryMerkleTree } from '@merkleforge/variants'

        const tree = BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Sha256, ['alice:100', 'bob:250', 'carol:75'].map(utf8))

        const root = tree.root()!
        const proof = tree.generateProof(1)

        // Stateless: only the root, the leaf bytes, and the proof.
        console.assert(BinaryMerkleTree.verify(Sha256, root, utf8('bob:250'), proof))
        ```
      </TypeScript>
    </div>
  </div>
